items.title: PolicyStack
items.text:
PolicyStack configures OpenShift clusters from Git through Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) governance policies. It is for admins who run an ACM hub and want every cluster's operators and settings reviewed in Git, rolled out cluster by cluster, and reported as compliant or not. It adds no controller of its own: a Helm chart points the hub's OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD) at your repository, and ACM does the rest.

You create your own repository from PolicyStack's releases with copier, describe each cluster in it, and turn on the elements you want. An element is a Helm chart under stack/ that configures one product, such as cert-manager, MetalLB or the Compliance Operator.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. You edit Git. Each cluster has a fleet file, fleet/<cluster>.yaml, that picks the revision (branch, tag or commit) the cluster renders from and the values files it reads. Values files turn elements on and set their options.
  2. Argo CD on the hub renders each element once per cluster into ACM Policies, using that cluster's revision and values, and writes them to the pstack namespace on the hub.
  3. Each Policy targets exactly one cluster. ACM's governance add-on on that cluster enforces the Policy or only reports differences, and ACM shows the compliance result on the hub.
flowchart LR
  subgraph git["Your repository"]
    fleet["fleet/#lt;cluster#gt;.yaml"]
    stack["stack/#lt;element#gt;/"]
    vals["values files"]
  end
  subgraph hub["ACM hub"]
    appset["ApplicationSet<br>policystack"]
    app["Application<br>#lt;element#gt;-#lt;cluster#gt;"]
    pol["Policies + Placement<br>in pstack"]
    rep["Replicated Policies<br>in #lt;cluster#gt;"]
  end
  spoke["Managed cluster<br>governance add-on"]
  fleet -->|"revision, valueFiles"| appset
  stack -->|"one Application per directory"| appset
  stack -->|"chart"| app
  appset -->|"one per element × cluster"| app
  vals --> app
  app -->|"helm template, sync"| pol
  pol -->|"Placement: one cluster"| rep
  rep -->|"pulled and applied"| spoke
  spoke -.->|"compliance"| rep
Box What it is fleet/<cluster>.yaml One file per cluster, read from the default branch. Without it the cluster gets nothing (Fleet files). stack/<element>/ The elements, read at the revision the fleet file pins (How an element is built). values files On top of the element's own defaults: the root values.yaml, then the layers the fleet file lists, then values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml. Later files win (Values cascade). ApplicationSet policystack Installed once per hub. Creates one Argo CD Application per element for each ACM managed cluster on this hub that has a fleet file (ApplicationSets). Application <element>-<cluster> Renders one element for one cluster with Helm and syncs the result to the hub. Policies + Placement in pstack The rendered ACM objects. The Placement selects only this cluster (ACM policies in brief). Replicated Policies in <cluster> ACM's copy of each Policy in the cluster's namespace on the hub. Where you read that cluster's compliance. Governance add-on ACM's policy controllers on the managed cluster. They apply the Policy (enforce) or only report differences (inform), and send the status back.

The install chart also creates a second ApplicationSet, policystack-lifecycle, which builds and destroys clusters whose fleet file has hub: (Cluster lifecycle). It does nothing for clusters you import.

items.title: Why it works this way
items.text:
• Each cluster gets one Application per element, rendered from that cluster's own revision and values files, so a commit reaches a cluster only through them. You promote a change cluster by cluster and roll back by moving the pin back (Rolling out changes).
  • Elements render ACM Policies instead of plain manifests. A Policy can enforce its state or only report drift, and every cluster's compliance is visible on the hub. For a dry run, set global.remediationAction: inform in a values layer: every Policy of the clusters reading that layer becomes report-only (Dry run).
  • Argo CD writes Policies to the hub only and never deploys to managed clusters. Each cluster's governance add-on pulls its own Policies, the same way ACM delivers every policy.

New here?

Skim How PolicyStack works before installing. It maps the repository, what lives on the hub, how a commit reaches a cluster, and the terms the rest of the docs use. Installation and First cluster link the other concept pages where they need them.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: This page is for changes to PolicyStack itself, sent upstream: the framework (install/, lifecycle/, lib/, tools/, .github/, docs/) and the starter elements in stack/. Running PolicyStack from your own repository and taking upstream releases into it is covered in Upgrading PolicyStack; elements you write or eject there are yours and need nothing here.

items.title: Repositories and versions
items.text:
Repository Holds Versioned by PolicyStack The framework, the starter elements and the policy-library chart (lib/) Release tags vX.Y.Z, one tag line for the framework and every element, cut by release-please (Releases). Adopters copy and update from them with copier. policy-library has its own chart version in lib/policy-library/Chart.yaml (Library changes) PolicyStack/.github Org defaults, including the Renovate preset Not versioned

Element versions, deprecating a key or an element, and when to contribute instead of ejecting: Versions and deprecation. What each version promises adopters: Compatibility.

"Release" means two things in these docs: the Helm release name Argo CD gives each element on each cluster (<element>-<cluster>), and a PolicyStack GitHub release.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
Tool versions live in mise.toml. mise installs each at the version CI uses: Go, Helm, Python, copier, prek (the hook runner) and the linters.

git clone https://github.com/<you>/PolicyStack.git && cd PolicyStack
mise install    # run `mise trust` first if mise says the config is not trusted
eval "$(mise activate bash)"   # put this in your shell rc; see `mise activate --help` for others
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt -r tools/requirements-docs.txt
prek install    # optional: run the hooks on each commit

mise install only downloads the tools. Until mise activate puts them on PATH, prek and go are missing, and make silently uses whatever helm your system has, which may not render the way the hub does. The hooks call the mise tools directly, so they need the same PATH.

Before opening a PR, run what each job of CI and Upstream runs:

prek run --all-files                       # lint
make -C tools/validator validate           # validate (Helm floor leg)
make -C tools/validator lint test          # validator
helm dependency update --skip-refresh lib/tests/fixtures/policy-stack-test && untt --strict lib/tests/fixtures/policy-stack-test   # library
python -m unittest tools/test_doc_generator.py && zensical build --strict   # docs

The library job also runs ct lint (the version bump check, Library changes). mise does not install chart-testing, so that step runs in CI only.

The first validate needs network access to download Go modules; the CRDs are committed. make lint also fetches the Go vulnerability database (govulncheck). CI also runs validate with Helm 4.2.1; that leg is advisory (Policy Validate).

items.title: Pull requests
items.text:
• The title is a Conventional Commit, such as feat(validator): real POLICY080. Squash merges make it the commit subject and the release-note line (PR Title).
  • A breaking change is anything that changes the framework's Public API, a stable element's values keys or Policy names for existing users, a stable lifecycle engine, or anything Lifecycle holds for a major at every maturity. Mark it with ! in the title: release-please reads it from the squash commit and bumps the major (Releases). Any other breaking change to a preview element or a preview lifecycle engine ships in a minor: no !, and a subject that starts with breaking: and says what to change, such as feat(odf): breaking: rename config.pools to config.ipAddressPools or feat(lifecycle): breaking: .... The notes then list it under odf: with a subject starting breaking:, which adopters search for (Element stability).
  • ci, upstream and pr-title must pass, plus one approval from .github/CODEOWNERS: any member of @PolicyStack/maintainers.
  • Update docs/ in the same PR.
  • A fix for a bad render or policy that reached a cluster adds a test that would have caught it: extend the validator rule that covers it, or add a rule. Check files are named by topic, not rule ID: grep -l POLICY033 tools/validator/internal/checks/*.go finds prune.go, tests in prune_test.go. ACM template evaluation is in internal/acmtemplates/.
  • A new rule needs a row in the rules table of tools/validator/README.md (Validator rules includes it; make test fails without it) and in the phase table of What it checks, which nothing tests.

items.title: Validator rules
items.text: A rule ID is never reused, even after its rule is removed. The severity is the Severity of the Finding the rule's Run returns. A new rule, or a new error case in an existing rule, that can fail a repository that passes today ships as a warning for at least one framework minor before it becomes an error. The release notes of the minor that adds the warning and of the minor that makes it an error say so. A rule that prevents an outage or a security problem may be an error from the start. The comment above All() in tools/validator/internal/checks/checks.go carries the same rule for whoever adds one.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
release-please cuts every release. There is one package, the whole repository, and one tag line, vX.Y.Z: each release holds the framework and every element. On each main push, the release job of Upstream opens or updates one release PR. Merging it tags its merge commit and creates the GitHub release with the notes from the PR. .release-please/config.json configures the package, and .release-please/manifest.json records the last release.

Tag Counts commits that change Version written to vX.Y.Z Anything except .release-please/, docs/, values/, lib/tests/ and the validator fixtures CHANGELOG.md, and the version lines of install/Chart.yaml and lifecycle/Chart.yaml marked x-release-please-version

The squash commit's type sets the bump: fix a patch, feat a minor, ! a major. docs, chore, ci, test and refactor commits release nothing. The scope becomes the release-note prefix, so scope an element change with the element's name, such as feat(odf): add config.flexibleScaling: the notes then list it as odf: add config.flexibleScaling, which is how adopters find the changes to the elements they track. Element Chart.yaml version lines are never bumped.

exclude-paths matches whole directories only. Some files copier leaves out of copies sit outside those directories: README.md, zensical.toml, .github/workflows/upstream.yml, tools/test_doc_generator.py and the rest of the upstream-only list in copier.yml. A fix or feat that changes only those still cuts a release, and adopters get an update that changes nothing but the version. Title those PRs docs, ci, test or chore.

A new element needs no release setup. tools/create-element.sh adds copier's answers template, and the element ships in the next release.

items.title: Library changes
items.text:
policy-library is the Helm library chart every element renders through. It lives in lib/policy-library, with its helm-unittest suites in lib/tests. Every chart that uses it declares it the same way:

stack/gitops/Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: policy-library
    alias: stack
    version: "^4.0.0"                              # floor: the lowest 4.x this chart needs
    repository: "file://../../lib/policy-library"  # relative to the chart directory

Those charts are each element, lifecycle/ (file://../lib/policy-library), tools/sample-element/ and the validator's test chart. make deps loops over CHARTS in tools/validator/Makefile, so a new chart outside stack/ must be added there.

Helm resolves file:// at render time. Argo CD's repo server and the validator package lib/policy-library into the chart's charts/ from the same Git revision they render. charts/ and Chart.lock are gitignored. A cluster pinned to a tag therefore renders the library as it was at that tag, and a library change reaches a cluster in the same commit as the element changes that use it. Nothing is published, and there is no chart repo to reach.

version is a floor, not a pin. ^4.2.0 accepts any 4.x at or above 4.2.0, and the chart always gets whatever lib/ holds. If that does not satisfy the constraint, Helm fails with a generic can't get a valid version for 1 subchart(s); POLICY060 reports the same mistake with the fix (Validator rules).

A library change is one PR:

  1. Change lib/policy-library, and in the same PR the elements, validator and docs that depend on it.
  2. Bump version in lib/policy-library/Chart.yaml. Patch: a fix, which may change output only where it was a bug. Minor: a new optional key or define. Major: anything removed or renamed, or any other change to output for unchanged values (policy-library versions). ct lint in the Upstream library job fails a PR that changes lib/policy-library without a bump.
  3. An element that needs the new minor raises its floor to ^4.N.0. The others keep theirs.

  4. Run the suites and commit the updated snapshots (lib/tests/**/__snapshot__). A snapshot diff for values that don't use a new key means the change is a major, unless the PR names the bug the diff fixes.

    helm dependency update --skip-refresh lib/tests/fixtures/policy-stack-test
untt --strict lib/tests/fixtures/policy-stack-test  # -u rewrites snapshots
make -C tools/validator validate test

A major moves every floor to ^5.0.0 in that same PR, with the element and values changes it needs, and is a breaking change (!). It also adds 5 to the list in install/templates/_helpers.tpl, keeping 4. Both ApplicationSets pass that list to every Application as policystack.libraryMajors, and policy-library fails the render of a revision whose library major the hub's install chart doesn't list. A cluster pinned to a 4.x revision keeps rendering on a hub upgraded to the new install chart, and a cluster moved to 5.x fails, naming the fix, on a hub that hasn't been upgraded. TestTemplatePatch fails when the list lacks the major in lib/policy-library/Chart.yaml. To roll back, revert the PR; fleet revisions from before it keep rendering the library they had.

items.title: Adding a lifecycle engine
items.text:
An engine is the tool the hub builds a cluster with: hypershift, hive or siteconfig (Cluster lifecycle). Each fleet file that sets hub gets an Application lifecycle-<cluster> rendering lifecycle/. Its templates/policy.yaml picks the stack.<engine> block (a component) of lifecycle/values.yaml that install.engine names, and turns on its present or absent Policy by state. That Policy's templates run in order, each rendering one converter. Adding an engine adds converters, one component and schema keys; the ApplicationSet and the fleet keys don't change.

HyperShift as the worked example:

lifecycle/
├── converters/
│   ├── guard.yaml, manifests.yaml, detach.yaml,   # shared by every engine
│   │   managedcluster.yaml, destroy.yaml
│   └── _hypershift/
│       ├── root.yaml           # the HostedCluster by identity alone
│       ├── credentials.yaml    # pull secret, SSH key, etcd encryption key
│       ├── hostedcluster.yaml  # the cluster: HostedCluster and NodePools
│       ├── ready.yaml          # gate: waits for the rollout
│       └── cleanup.yaml        # deletes what credentials copied, then install.manifests
├── values.yaml                 # stack.hypershift: the present and absent Policies
└── values.schema.json          # install.engine enum and per-engine keys

Rendered for fixture hcp-kubevirt, Policy present-lifecycle-hcp-kubevirt holds, in order, present-guard-hcp-kubevirt (InformOnly), present-credentials-hcp-kubevirt, present-manifests-hcp-kubevirt, present-cluster-hcp-kubevirt (enforced) and present-ready-hcp-kubevirt (InformOnly).

  1. Converters in converters/_<e>/. The _ keeps policy-library from discovering the directory as a Policy <e> of every component. Without it, every lifecycle render runs those converters, which fails the render for clusters of the other engines (install.siteconfig.nodes is required) or ships an extra enforced Policy <e>-lifecycle-<cluster>. Shared converters sit directly in converters/ for the same reason (Partials). An engine needs:

    • root.yaml: the object the engine creates first and deletes to destroy the cluster, with only apiVersion, kind, name and namespace. The shared destroy step, the destroyed gate and the ownership check read it.
    • credentials.yaml, the cluster converter, a ready gate (ready.yaml; Hive's is installed.yaml) and cleanup.yaml, which ends with include "lifecycle.cleanupManifests" so the hub objects from install.manifests are deleted once the cluster is gone.

    Some fields can't change after create: Hive rejects provisioning.releaseImage changes. Read those back from the live object, so a later version bump never produces a rejected update:

    lifecycle/converters/_hive/clusterdeployment.yaml
    {{ "{{-" }} $releaseImage := dig "spec" "provisioning" "releaseImage" {{ $image | quote }} (lookup "hive.openshift.io/v1" "ClusterDeployment" {{ $c | quote }} {{ $c | quote }}) {{ "}}" }}

  2. Ownership (Ownership). In the cluster converter, merge the lifecycle.marker helper (lifecycle/templates/_helpers.tpl, like the other lifecycle.* helpers below) into the root object's annotations. If the engine creates the ManagedCluster itself, mark that too: Hive writes the marker on it, SiteConfig passes it through extraAnnotations. When the root object doesn't exist, as after a failed create, the guard falls back to the ManagedCluster, and an unmarked one reads as an imported cluster that every step refuses to touch. Start every enforced converter except manifests with include "lifecycle.refuse", before its first object entry (Helm variables may come first). It fails the step in the same evaluation as the write, so a stale guard result can never let a step touch a cluster lifecycle didn't build. Because it is an ACM template, the step renders as object-templates-raw; TestEnforceIsRaw (tools/validator/internal/acmtemplates/ownership_test.go) checks that. An engine that can adopt an existing object (SiteConfig's ClusterDeployment) also adds a branch to lifecycle.foreign.

  3. Component in values.yaml. Copy an existing stack.<engine> block whole and change its file: paths. Keep:

    • enabled: true. Without it policy-library renders nothing and reports no error: the cluster is never built.
    • suffixTemplateNames: true. Every lifecycle release lands on the hub, so without the -<cluster> suffix two clusters' templates share a name and ACM rejects the second.
    • file: on every template: there is no converters/present/, so a template without one fails the render.
    • The template names of the block you copied (hypershift and hive: guard, credentials, manifests, cluster, ready; guard, detach, detached, destroy, destroyed, cleanup; siteconfig's absent chain has no detach/detached) and orderManifests, which makes each wait for the one before. TestOwnership (tools/validator/internal/acmtemplates/ownership_test.go) finds the guard and skips ready and manifests by name.
    • default.remediationAction: enforce with every gate InformOnly, which ACM keeps inform under a Policy-level enforce. No pruneObjectBehavior: it lets a Policy delete a cluster.

  4. Schema. Add <e> to the install.engine enum in values.schema.json. For engine settings, add an install.<e> object and an allOf entry that requires its keys when engine is <e> and sets maxProperties: 0 otherwise, as hive and siteconfig do. install allows no other keys, so a fleet file setting install.<e> fails the render until the schema has it. POLICY090 fails when the enum and the stack keys differ.

  5. Validator. Add every kind the converters lookup to kinds in tools/validator/internal/acmtemplates/acmtemplates.go, or POLICY081 fails. Add a present and an absent fixture to tools/validator/testdata/clusters/, to the want lists of TestLoadDir_testdata and TestResolve_testdata, and to the fixture list. Add a TestOwnership row (fixtures and the root's apiVersion, kind and namespace) and an <e>_test.go in internal/acmtemplates: profiles never reach lifecycle/.

  6. Engine-specific code. Check each and extend it if the engine needs it: lifecycle.releaseImage picks -x86_64 for siteconfig and -multi for every other engine; POLICY052 checks only that a pinned revision has lifecycle/converters/_hypershift/, so a fleet file pinned to a revision without the new engine passes CI and then fails to render; POLICY051 reads only install.siteconfig.nodes.

  7. Docs. An example in Building clusters, a row in Pick an engine, and its tab or column in every table of Lifecycle keys.

An engine that upgrades from the hub writes version into its objects on every evaluation, as hypershift does with the HostedCluster and NodePool release. One that only installs uses version at create, reads the field back afterwards, and leaves upgrades to the upgrade element, which sets ClusterVersion on the cluster from the fleet file's version and channel (OpenShift upgrades).

items.title: Docs layout
items.text:
Write for a first-time reader: model first, every rule with its reason, worked examples, failure modes. Explain a concept in full on one page and link it everywhere else.

Each page belongs to one section:

Section Holds Home (index.md) What PolicyStack is, the diagram, where each section starts Get started (start/) The path from an empty hub to the first configured cluster, in order Concepts (concepts/) How PolicyStack works and why, in reading order: overview, ACM policies, elements, values, placement, lifecycle, removal, ApplicationSets. No procedures Guides (guides/) One operator task per page. Link Concepts for the model and Reference for key lists Elements (elements/) One page per stack/<el> that needs more than its README. No settings tables Develop (develop/) Writing, previewing and validating elements Reference (reference/) Complete key, rule and workflow tables, each opening with what it is for. No narrative Contributing (contributing.md) Changing PolicyStack itself
  • Element READMEs (stack/*/README.md) are generated (Hooks) and only on GitHub, not the site. An element with a page here sets home: in its Chart.yaml to the page URL, and its README links it.
  • A new page needs a nav entry in zensical.toml. Strict mode doesn't check nav: a missing entry leaves the page out of the menu, and an entry pointing at a missing file ships as a dead link.
  • A moved page or section needs a redirect_maps entry in zensical.toml.
  • reference/rules.md includes the rules section of tools/validator/README.md. A relative link resolves against the including page, not the README, so it breaks on one side: keep that section free of relative links.

  • Preview from the repo root, where snippet paths resolve:

    zensical serve            # live preview; restart it after editing the README rules table
zensical build --strict   # what CI runs, after python -m unittest tools/test_doc_generator.py

items.title: ACM policies in brief
items.text: PolicyStack never applies anything to a managed cluster itself. It renders Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) governance objects onto the hub, in namespace pstack (created by PolicyStack's install chart, Where Policies live), and ACM does the rest: it copies each Policy to the cluster it targets, applies or checks it there, and reports compliance back. An element is one Helm chart under stack/ (metallb, gitops, …), rendered once per cluster; how its files become these objects is on How an element is built.

items.title: The objects
items.text: Object Lives in What it does Policy pstack on the hub A wrapper. It holds one or more policy templates, a remediationAction, optional dependencies and compliance annotations. ACM never applies a Policy directly; it delivers it. Policy template Inside a Policy, under spec.policy-templates One unit of work. PolicyStack uses two kinds: ConfigurationPolicy and OperatorPolicy. On the hub they are not separate objects, so oc get configurationpolicy -n pstack returns nothing; read them in the Policy's YAML. ConfigurationPolicy Created on the managed cluster Lists Kubernetes objects and how each must compare with the live cluster (ConfigurationPolicy). OperatorPolicy Created on the managed cluster Installs and maintains one OLM operator (OperatorPolicy). Placement pstack on the hub Selects managed clusters by label. PolicyStack renders one per element per cluster, selecting only that cluster (Placement). PlacementBinding pstack on the hub Links Policies to a Placement. A Policy with no binding goes nowhere. ManagedClusterSet, ManagedClusterSetBinding Hub Clusters are grouped into ManagedClusterSets; ACM's built-in set global holds every cluster. A Placement only sees clusters from sets bound to its own namespace by a ManagedClusterSetBinding. PolicyStack binds global into pstack (Cluster sets).

items.title: How a Policy reaches a cluster
items.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph hub["Hub"]
    root["Policy<br>pstack/config-metallb-c1"]
    pl["Placement + PlacementBinding<br>pstack/metallb-c1"]
    rep["Replicated Policy<br>c1/pstack.config-metallb-c1"]
  end
  subgraph spoke["Managed cluster c1"]
    fw["governance-policy-framework"]
    cp["ConfigurationPolicy<br>c1/config-metallb-instance"]
    cpc["config-policy-controller"]
    obj["MetalLB metallb<br>in metallb-system"]
  end
  pl -->|"picks c1"| rep
  root -->|"propagator copies"| rep
  rep -->|"syncs"| fw
  fw -->|"creates"| cp
  cp --> cpc
  cpc -->|"checks or applies"| obj
  cpc -.->|"status"| rep
  rep -.->|"status"| root

Names in this example: the Helm release is metallb-c1 (<element>-<cluster>), Policies are <policy>-<release> and templates <policy>-<template>, so template names don't carry the cluster (Rendered names).

  1. Argo CD syncs the root Policy (the one from Git; ACM's per-cluster copies are replicated Policies) into pstack on the hub, with its Placement and PlacementBinding. Look with oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack (the full resource name, because policies can resolve to another policy engine's kind); the compliance column there sums up every cluster the Policy reaches.
  2. For each cluster the Placement selects, ACM's policy propagator on the hub copies the Policy into the hub namespace named after the cluster (ACM creates one per managed cluster at import; local-cluster for the hub itself), as <namespace>.<name>: pstack.config-metallb-c1 in namespace c1. Hub templates are resolved in this step (Hub and managed-cluster templates). Per-cluster compliance is read from this copy. The name doubles as a label value, so it is capped at 63 characters (Naming limits).
  3. Each managed cluster runs two ACM governance add-ons: governance-policy-framework copies the replicated Policy into the cluster-named namespace on the managed cluster and creates each policy template there as a real object; config-policy-controller evaluates them (next step).
  4. config-policy-controller compares every ConfigurationPolicy and OperatorPolicy with the live cluster, changes the cluster under enforce, and writes compliance into the template's status. The framework sends it back up to the replicated Policy, and the propagator rolls it up into the root Policy.

Template names are per cluster, not per Policy

Every template of every Policy placed on a cluster lands in the same namespace there, so two Policies can't ship a template with the same name. The second one reports Template name must be unique. Policy template with kind: ConfigurationPolicy name: <name> already exists in policy <policy>. CI catches this before merge (POLICY002 within an element, POLICY003 across elements; Validator rules).

This is the config Policy of the metallb element as Argo CD syncs it for cluster c1 (render it with the helm template command in Placement, release metallb-c1, plus --set stack.metallb.enabled=true; without selector, the cluster selector the ApplicationSet passes into every Application, the render fails):

Policy pstack/config-metallb-c1
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: config-metallb-c1
  namespace: pstack
  annotations: # (1)!
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/categories: "SC System and Communications Protection"
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/controls: "SC-7 Boundary Protection"
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/standards: "NIST SP 800-53"
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce # (2)!
  disabled: false # (3)!
  copyPolicyMetadata: false # (4)!
  dependencies: # (5)!
    - apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
      kind: Policy
      name: install-metallb-c1
      namespace: pstack
      compliance: Compliant
  policy-templates:
    - extraDependencies: # (6)!
        - apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
          kind: ConfigurationPolicy
          name: install-metallb-status
          compliance: Compliant
      ignorePending: true
      objectDefinition:
        apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
        kind: ConfigurationPolicy
        metadata:
          name: config-metallb-instance
        spec:
          remediationAction: enforce
          severity: medium # (7)!
          object-templates:
            - complianceType: musthave # (8)!
              objectDefinition:
                apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
                kind: MetalLB
                metadata:
                  name: metallb
                  namespace: metallb-system
  1. Metadata only (Severity and compliance annotations).
  2. Overrides the remediationAction of every template below (inform, enforce and InformOnly).
  3. true stops ACM delivering the Policy while it stays on the hub. To remove a Policy, see Removal and pruning.
  4. Keeps Argo CD's tracking labels off the replicated copies, so Argo CD never sees them as its own and never prunes them.
  5. The whole Policy waits until Policy install-metallb-c1 is Compliant on this cluster (Dependencies and ignorePending).
  6. This one template also waits for the operator's install check.
  7. Shown in the console; changes no behavior.
  8. The MetalLB object must exist with these fields (ConfigurationPolicy).

items.title: ConfigurationPolicy
items.text:
A ConfigurationPolicy lists objects under object-templates. Each entry is an objectDefinition (the object, written like a manifest) and a complianceType that says how it must compare with the cluster. The controller only looks at the fields you list, except where mustonlyhave says otherwise.

complianceType Compliant when Under enforce musthave (PolicyStack's default) The object exists and every listed field matches. Unlisted fields are ignored; a listed list must contain the listed items, and may hold more. Creates the object, or patches the listed fields. Other fields and list items stay. mustonlyhave The object exists and matches exactly: listed maps and lists hold nothing else, and the object has no top-level field you didn't list (metadata and status aside). Creates the object, or replaces those fields and removes the extra ones. Anything another controller added to them is removed on every evaluation. mustnothave No object with that name exists. Deletes it.

Take a live ConfigMap app with data: {a: "1", b: "2"} and a template listing data: {a: "1"}: musthave is Compliant, mustonlyhave is NonCompliant and enforce removes b, mustnothave is NonCompliant and enforce deletes the ConfigMap.

Two shapes are checks only, whatever the action:

  • An object with no metadata.name and no objectSelector matches any object of that kind (in that namespace) with the listed fields. musthave is Compliant if one matches, mustnothave if none do. ACM can't create or delete by an unknown name, so it evaluates these as inform. With objectSelector, each selected object is handled by name and enforce acts on it.
  • Fields under status are compared but never written; a mismatch stays NonCompliant.

PolicyStack generates one such check per operator, named install-<key>-status after the operator's key in the element (install-metallb-status for MetalLB): a ClusterServiceVersion with no name, spec.displayName set to the operator's display name, and status.phase: Succeeded. It turns Compliant once the operator finished installing, which is what other templates wait on.

object-templates-raw is the same list written as one string, so ACM templates on the cluster can decide how many objects there are; PolicyStack picks it from the output shape of a converter (an element file that renders a template's objects) (Converter shapes). What happens to objects when a ConfigurationPolicy goes away (pruneObjectBehavior) is on Removal and pruning.

items.title: OperatorPolicy
items.text:
An OperatorPolicy manages one OLM operator: it creates and maintains the operator's Subscription and OperatorGroup, and approves the InstallPlans OLM proposes (an InstallPlan is OLM's proposal to install or upgrade to a ClusterServiceVersion, one operator version). The fields that matter:

  • complianceType: musthave keeps the operator installed; mustnothave uninstalls it under enforce, as removalBehavior says (by default the Subscription and CSV go, the OperatorGroup goes if nothing else uses it, CRDs stay).
  • upgradeApproval (required): None approves the first install only; Automatic also approves later upgrades.
  • versions lists the CSV names it may approve, for the first install and for upgrades. Empty allows any.

The OperatorPolicy owns approval: ACM rejects an OperatorPolicy whose subscription sets installPlanApproval, and CI fails it first (POLICY030). Under inform it approves nothing: a fresh cluster gets no operator, and the Policy reports NonCompliant. Pinning, bumping and uninstalling are on Operator versions.

items.title: inform, enforce and InformOnly
items.text:
Action Where it is set What the controller does inform Policy Compares and reports. Never changes the cluster, never approves an InstallPlan. On new config every missing object reads NonCompliant: the list of what enforce would change. enforce Policy Creates, patches or deletes objects until they match, and approves InstallPlans. InformOnly One template Keeps that template inform even when its Policy enforces.

The Policy's remediationAction overrides the action of every template inside it. The only exception is a template set to InformOnly, which the add-on turns into inform on the cluster. Use it for checks that must never act: a readiness check, or a mustnothave that should report an object rather than delete it (the compliance element's findings templates are mustnothave ComplianceCheckResults; enforced, ACM would delete the scan results).

Which action each Policy gets, and how to force every Policy to inform for a dry run, is on Inform or enforce.

Enforced means applied, not ready

An enforced ConfigurationPolicy turns Compliant as soon as the API server accepts the create or patch. It says nothing about whether the operator behind the object finished its work. An OperatorPolicy is the exception: it stays NonCompliant until the CSV reaches Succeeded and its deployments are available. Wait on a separate inform check for that, as Cluster lifecycle does after each step.

items.title: Compliance states
items.text:
The controller reports a state per template; the add-on rolls them up to the Policy.

State Template Policy Compliant The cluster matches. Every template is Compliant. NonCompliant The cluster differs, a check failed, or the template could not be processed (message starts with template-error;). At least one template is NonCompliant. This wins over Pending. Pending A dependency is unmet, so the template isn't evaluated (Dependencies and ignorePending). No template is NonCompliant and at least one is Pending.

An empty state means nothing has reported. If oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n c1 doesn't list the Policy at all, the Placement selected no cluster: check oc get placementdecisions -n pstack and Cluster sets. If the copy exists but is empty, the cluster hasn't reported, for example because it is unreachable.

Read the reason on the hub, from the replicated Policy:

# one line per Policy on cluster c1
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n c1
# NAME                        REMEDIATION ACTION   COMPLIANCE STATE   AGE
# pstack.config-metallb-c1    enforce              Compliant          5m
# pstack.install-metallb-c1   enforce              Compliant          6m

# one line per template: name, state, latest message
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io pstack.config-metallb-c1 -n c1 \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.details[*]}{.templateMeta.name}{"\t"}{.compliant}{"\t"}{.history[0].message}{"\n"}{end}'

Messages name the object and what is wrong with it:

Message Means NonCompliant; violation - metallbs [metallb] not found in namespace metallb-system musthave under inform, object missing. NonCompliant; violation - metallbs [metallb] in namespace metallb-system is missing, and cannot be created, reason: ... Enforce tried to create it and the API refused. NonCompliant; violation - metallbs [metallb] found but not as specified in namespace metallb-system Exists, a listed field differs. Compliant; notification - metallbs [metallb] was created successfully in namespace metallb-system Enforce created it. Pending; Dependencies were not satisfied: 1 is still pending (Policy pstack.install-metallb-c1) Waiting on a dependency. Compliant; Dependencies were not satisfied: 2 are still pending (ConfigurationPolicy install-metallb-status, Policy pstack.install-metallb-c1) but ignorePending is true Waiting, but reported Compliant because of ignorePending: config-metallb-instance before the operator is installed. NonCompliant; template-error; ... The template could not be processed, for example a failed hub template.

On the managed cluster, oc get configurationpolicies,operatorpolicies -n c1 lists the templates and oc describe shows each one's related objects. In the console, the same data is under Governance, per Policy and per cluster.

items.title: Dependencies and ignorePending
items.text:
A dependency makes something wait until another policy object reaches a given compliance state (PolicyStack writes Compliant unless the values entry sets compliance).

  • spec.dependencies on a Policy holds back every template in it.
  • extraDependencies on one policy template holds back that template only.

Either may name a Policy or a template (ConfigurationPolicy, OperatorPolicy) on the same cluster. While a dependency is unmet, the template is Pending and does not exist on the managed cluster: the add-on doesn't create it, or deletes it if it was there. A dependency that goes NonCompliant later, for example while an operator upgrades and its CSV leaves Succeeded, removes the dependent templates until it recovers. With pruneObjectBehavior, removing a template also deletes its objects, so every operator upgrade would delete and recreate, for example, the MetalLB instance. That is why PolicyStack rejects pruneObjectBehavior on any template with a dependency (POLICY033, Removal and pruning).

ignorePending: true on a template reports a Pending template as Compliant, with the message ending but ignorePending is true. The Policy can then read Compliant while the template hasn't run.

In the metallb example, Policy config waits for Policy install, and its config-metallb-instance template also waits for install-metallb-status. The waits exist because the MetalLB CRD only exists once the operator is installed. Until then the template is Pending and not created, and because of ignorePending the config Policy reads Compliant instead of Pending. Check install-metallb-c1 before trusting a green config.

The values keys that render these (dependencies, extraDependencies, waitForOperator, orderManifests) are on How an element is built.

items.title: Severity and compliance annotations
items.text:
All four are metadata; none changes what ACM does.

  • severity (low, medium, high, critical) sits on each template and shows in the console next to its violations.
  • categories, controls and standards become policy.open-cluster-management.io/* annotations on the Policy. The Governance dashboard groups Policies by them, so claiming a control the Policy doesn't implement misreports compliance.

items.title: Hub and managed-cluster templates
items.text:
ACM resolves Go templates inside policy templates, in two places:

Syntax Resolved by When Can read {{hub ... hub}} The propagator, on the hub When it replicates the Policy for each cluster, and again when a hub object the template reads changes Hub objects in the Policy's namespace (pstack), and the target ManagedCluster (.ManagedClusterName, .ManagedClusterLabels). Other namespaces need hubTemplateOptions.serviceAccountName on the Policy, naming a ServiceAccount in pstack with read access. {{ ... }} config-policy-controller, on the managed cluster On every evaluation Objects on that cluster (lookup, fromSecret, fromConfigMap, fromClusterClaim).

Hub templates are how a secret on the hub reaches a cluster without being stored in Git (Secrets). A failed hub template shows on the cluster as a template-error on that template. Converters are Helm templates too, so an ACM template inside one is written escaped, for example {{ "{{" }}hub fromSecret … hub{{ "}}" }}, so that Helm prints it instead of evaluating it (Helm templates and ACM templates).

items.title: Further reading
items.text:
• ACM Governance: the policy framework, ConfigurationPolicy, OperatorPolicy, templates and dependencies.
  • ACM Clusters: ManagedClusterSets and Placements.

items.title: ApplicationSets
items.text:
How the hub turns fleet files and stack/ into Argo CD Applications, and what each Application does. Read it when an Application is missing, has the wrong name, or will not sync. How PolicyStack works gives the big picture first; ACM policies in brief covers what happens after the Policies reach pstack.

Argo CD deploys only to the hub. Every Application's destination is the hub itself, and everything it syncs is a Policy, Placement or PlacementBinding in pstack, the policy namespace the install chart creates. ACM, not Argo CD, delivers those policies to managed clusters.

items.title: ApplicationSets in brief
items.text:
An Argo CD Application renders one Helm chart from one Git path at one revision and keeps the result applied. An ApplicationSet is a template for Applications plus a list of generators. Each generator produces sets of parameters, and the ApplicationSet controller creates one Application per parameter set, filling the template with them. It re-runs the generators every 3 minutes. When a parameter set disappears, its Application is deleted.

PolicyStack uses four generator types:

Generator Produces one parameter set per Parameters used here clusters Argo CD cluster secret .name (the ManagedCluster name), .metadata.labels git files YAML file matching a path Every top-level key of the file, such as .revision, .valueFiles, .hub git directories Directory matching a path .path.path (stack/gitops), .path.basenameNormalized (gitops) matrix Combination of its two child generators Both children's parameters. The second child can use the first's, which is how stack/* is read at each cluster's own revision.

A selector on a generator drops parameter sets that do not match, like a label selector on the parameters.

helm install of the install chart creates two ApplicationSets in openshift-gitops:

ApplicationSet Creates Who needs it policystack One Application per element per cluster: Day-2 configuration of clusters that already run. Everyone policystack-lifecycle One Application per cluster this hub builds, from fleet files with hub: <hubName> (Cluster lifecycle). Only hubs that build clusters. Fleet files without hub never match it.

items.title: Cluster secrets
items.text:
The clusters generator lists Argo CD cluster secrets: Secrets in openshift-gitops labelled argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster. PolicyStack needs one per ManagedCluster only as an entry in that list. Argo CD never connects to the clusters they describe.

The install chart's GitOpsCluster argo-acm-importer-global creates them. ACM puts every ManagedCluster, the hub included, in the built-in ManagedClusterSet global. The install chart binds that set into openshift-gitops with a ManagedClusterSetBinding, because a Placement only sees clusters from sets bound into its own namespace (ACM policies in brief); its Placement global there selects every cluster in it. The GitOpsCluster creates one secret per selected cluster and copies the ManagedCluster's labels onto it, so the generators can read clusterID, local-cluster and the Global Hub deploy-mode label.

The Placement tolerates unreachable and unavailable. Without that, a cluster that loses contact drops out of the Placement, the GitOpsCluster deletes its secret, and the ApplicationSet deletes its Applications and every Policy they rendered (What deletes an Application).

items.title: policystack
items.text:
For every cluster secret, the policystack ApplicationSet:

  1. Keeps it only if it has the clusterID label. ACM sets that label once the cluster's klusterlet, the ACM agent on the managed cluster, has joined the hub, so clusters still importing are skipped.
  2. Reads the cluster's fleet file from the default branch (HEAD). A cluster without a fleet file gets no Applications, and the ApplicationSet reports no error.
  3. Lists every directory under stack/ at the fleet file's revision.
  4. Creates one Application per directory, named <element>-<cluster>.
flowchart LR
  S["Cluster secret<br>prod-east-1"] --> F["fleet/prod-east-1.yaml<br>at HEAD<br>revision: main"]
  F --> D["stack/* at main<br>acm, compliance, gitops, ..."]
  D --> A["acm-prod-east-1<br>compliance-prod-east-1<br>gitops-prod-east-1<br>..."]

The fleet file is read at HEAD; everything else at its revision. Fleet files explains why.

The cluster secret decides which fleet file is read:

Cluster secret Fleet file The hub's own (label local-cluster) fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml (The hub) A managed hub imported into a Global Hub in default mode (label global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/deploy-mode: default) fleet/hubs/<cluster>.yaml (Global Hub) Any other cluster fleet/<cluster>.yaml

Without Global Hub, only the first and last rows apply.

Two consequences of generating from directories:

  • An element exists per revision. An element added on a branch gets Applications only on clusters whose revision contains it.
  • Disabled elements still get an Application. Generators read files, not merged Helm values, so they cannot tell whether a values layer enabled an element. Every directory under stack/ gets an Application on every cluster, and a disabled element renders zero objects and shows Synced with no resources.
policystack generators, rendered with hubName=acm-dc1 
generators:
  - matrix:
      generators:
        - matrix:
            generators:
              - clusters: # (1)!
                  selector:
                    matchExpressions:
                      - key: clusterID
                        operator: Exists
              - git: # (2)!
                  repoURL: 'https://github.com/acme/policystack.git'
                  revision: HEAD
                  pathParamPrefix: fleet # (3)!
                  files:
                  - path: 'fleet/{{if index .metadata.labels "local-cluster"}}hubs/acm-dc1{{else if eq (index .metadata.labels "global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/deploy-mode") "default"}}hubs/{{.name}}{{else}}{{.name}}{{end}}.yaml'
        - git: # (4)!
            repoURL: 'https://github.com/acme/policystack.git'
            revision: '{{.revision}}'
            directories:
            - path: 'stack/*'
  1. Every cluster secret with clusterID.
  2. The cluster's fleet file at HEAD, picked by the table above. Its top-level keys become parameters, such as {{.revision}}.
  3. Both git generators emit a path parameter. This renames the fleet file's to fleet.path, so {{.path.path}} and {{.path.basenameNormalized}} still mean the element directory, which builds the Application name and source path.
  4. Every stack/* directory at the cluster's revision.

items.title: Lifecycle generator
items.text:
Skip this unless the hub builds clusters.

policystack-lifecycle reads fleet files that set hub, and creates lifecycle-<cluster> for each one this hub should build. That Application renders lifecycle/ at the fleet file's revision into Policies that are placed on the building hub, not on the new cluster, which does not exist yet. On the hub they create the HostedCluster, ClusterDeployment or ClusterInstance and wait for it (Cluster lifecycle).

A fleet file with hub renders on exactly one hub:

Fleet file has Rendered by Policies placed on hub: <this hub's hubName>, and this hub manages itself (local-cluster exists) This hub local-cluster hub: <name> of a managed hub that this Global Hub imports in default mode The Global Hub That managed hub (Global Hub lifecycle) No hub Nobody. The cluster is imported, not built.

A hub whose MultiClusterHub disables self-management has no local-cluster secret and builds nothing itself.

policystack-lifecycle generators, rendered with hubName=acm-dc1 
generators:
  - matrix: # (1)!
      generators:
        - clusters:
            selector:
              matchExpressions:
                - key: local-cluster
                  operator: Exists
        - git: &fleet
            repoURL: 'https://github.com/acme/policystack.git'
            revision: HEAD
            files:
            - path: 'fleet/*.yaml'
            - path: 'fleet/*/*.yaml' # (2)!
              exclude: true
          selector:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: hub
                operator: In
                values:
                  - "acm-dc1"
  - matrix: # (3)!
      generators:
        - git: *fleet
          selector:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: hub
                operator: Exists
        - clusters:
            selector:
              matchLabels:
                apps.open-cluster-management.io/cluster-name: '{{ if regexMatch "^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$" (toString .hub) }}{{ .hub }}{{ end }}' # (4)!
                global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/deploy-mode: default
  1. Fleet files with hub: acm-dc1, paired with this hub's own cluster secret.
  2. Argo CD's * crosses /. This drops hubs/ and other subdirectories, so a hub file is never a lifecycle fleet file.
  3. Global Hub only: fleet files naming a managed hub imported in default mode. Fleet files come first because Argo CD templates a child generator's fields but not its selector.
  4. A hub that is not a DNS label matches nothing instead of failing the whole ApplicationSet.

items.title: Applications
items.text:
Field policystack policystack-lifecycle Name <element>-<cluster>, <element>-<hubName> for the hub lifecycle-<cluster> Source stack/<element> at the fleet file's revision lifecycle/ at the fleet file's revision Values files values.yaml, root values.yaml, each valueFiles entry, values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml (Order) Same files Injected values selector for the cluster, version, channel selector for the building hub, hub, state, install, version, channel (Order) Destination The hub (https://kubernetes.default.svc) Same Project default Same Sync Automated, prune, selfHeal, allowEmpty Automated, prune, selfHeal

The Application name is also the Helm release name. The Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding names include it: Policy install-gitops-prod-east-1, Placement and PlacementBinding gitops-prod-east-1. ConfigurationPolicy and OperatorPolicy names do not (Rendered names). Renaming an element, a cluster or hubName renames the release, so its Policies are deleted and recreated. Where a template prunes, the objects on the cluster are deleted and recreated too (Removal and pruning).

What the sync options do, all on the hub:

  • Automated: every change at the revision syncs without anyone pressing Sync.
  • prune: an object that drops out of the render, such as a policy you set enabled: false, is deleted from pstack.
  • selfHeal: a hand edit to a Policy or Placement in pstack is reverted to what Git renders.
  • allowEmpty: Argo CD normally refuses an automated sync that would leave an Application with no objects. This lets a disabled element prune to zero (Removal and pruning). Lifecycle Applications leave it off: lifecycle/ always renders the present or absent Policy, so an empty render can only be an error, and Argo CD refuses to prune everything.

The destination namespace, open-cluster-management, is unused. Every rendered object sets its own namespace, policyNamespace (pstack).

Application compliance-prod-east-1 fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
revision: main
channel: stable-4.20
valueFiles:
  - environments/prod.yaml
  - datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - platforms/aws.yaml

renders:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: compliance-prod-east-1
  namespace: openshift-gitops
  labels:
    velero.io/exclude-from-backup: "true" # (1)!
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths: '.;../../lib;../../values.yaml;../../values/environments/prod.yaml;../../values/datacenters/dc1.yaml;../../values/platforms/aws.yaml;../../values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml' # (2)!
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io # (3)!
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: 'https://github.com/acme/policystack.git'
    targetRevision: main
    path: stack/compliance
    helm:
      ignoreMissingValueFiles: true # (4)!
      valueFiles:
        - values.yaml
        - ../../values.yaml
        - ../../values/environments/prod.yaml
        - ../../values/datacenters/dc1.yaml
        - ../../values/platforms/aws.yaml
        - ../../values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
      valuesObject:
        channel: "stable-4.20"
        policystack:
          libraryMajors: [4] # (5)!
        selector: # (6)!
          matchExpressions:
            name:
              key: name
              operator: In
              values:
                - "prod-east-1"
  destination:
    server: 'https://kubernetes.default.svc'
    namespace: open-cluster-management
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true # (7)!
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
      allowEmpty: true
  1. Kept out of ACM backup (Install chart).
  2. Render cache.
  3. Added by the ApplicationSet controller because preserveResourcesOnDeletion is false. Deleting the Application deletes its objects in pstack.
  4. A listed file that does not exist is skipped without an error (Missing files).
  5. The policy-library majors this hub supports. A revision built on another major fails its render (Order).
  6. Becomes the element's single-cluster Placement (Placement).
  7. No effect: no Application sets ignoreDifferences.

items.title: When an Application fails
items.text:
Two different steps can fail, with different blast radius:

Step What runs Typical cause What you see Effect Generation The ApplicationSet controller evaluates its generators. A fleet file that does not parse, lacks revision, or pins a revision that does not exist. ErrorOccurred condition on the ApplicationSet No Application is created, updated or deleted until it is fixed; existing ones keep their Policies (One bad fleet file stops the hub). Render Argo CD runs helm template for one Application. A values key the schema rejects, a policies.<p> naming a policy that has no converter, or a revision whose policy-library major the hub's install chart doesn't support. ComparisonError on that Application, sync status Unknown That Application neither syncs nor prunes; its Policies stay as they were. A converter error affects one element. A schema error in a layer fails every Application that reads the layer, all elements and lifecycle-<cluster> included (Schema).

A render error carries the Helm message. With stack.gitops.policies.bogus.enabled: true in a layer:

policy-library: policies.bogus has no templates - add converters/bogus/<template>.yaml

oc get applicationset policystack -n openshift-gitops \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ErrorOccurred")].message}'
oc get application gitops-prod-east-1 -n openshift-gitops \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ComparisonError")].message}'

Your repository's CI renders every element for every fleet file and checks every pin, so both normally fail the PR instead of the hub (Validation).

items.title: Deletion
items.text:
Both ApplicationSets set preserveResourcesOnDeletion: false, so each Application gets Argo CD's resources finalizer and deleting it deletes its Policies, Placement and PlacementBinding from pstack. Applications are deleted when their generator stops producing them, for example when a fleet file is deleted (What deletes an Application). ACM then removes the policies from the cluster; what they created stays unless a template prunes (What happens on the managed cluster). No lifecycle template prunes, so deleting lifecycle-<cluster> leaves the cluster running, unmanaged (Abandon).

Every Policy sets copyPolicyMetadata: false, so Argo CD never treats ACM's replicated copies as its own and never prunes them (Removal and pruning).

items.title: Render cache
items.text:
Background; nothing to configure.

Each Application lists the files its render reads in manifest-generate-paths. Paths are relative to the source path, stack/<element>: . is the element directory, ../../lib is the policy-library chart (Helm reads it from Git through file://), and ../../ is the repo root. For a new commit, Argo CD compares the changed files with this list, with or without a webhook, and reuses the cached render when none match.

A commit to values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml therefore re-renders only prod-east-1's Applications, and a commit to stack/compliance/ only the compliance-* Applications at that revision. A commit to the root values.yaml or to lib/ re-renders all of them, lifecycle-* included (its paths start at lifecycle/, so the library is ../lib). Fleet files are not listed: a fleet change alters the Application spec, which always re-renders.

items.title: The hub
items.text:
ACM manages the hub as a ManagedCluster too, named local-cluster by default and labelled local-cluster. PolicyStack configures it like any cluster, with one difference: it is known by hubName, the name you give it at helm install (Install chart). The secret with the local-cluster label switches the generator to the hub's names:

Managed cluster Hub Fleet file fleet/<cluster>.yaml fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml (Hub file) Cluster values file values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml values/clusters/<hubName>.yaml Applications (releases) <element>-<cluster> <element>-<hubName> Policies in pstack <policy>-<element>-<cluster> <policy>-<element>-<hubName> Placement selector name In [<cluster>] name In [<hub's ManagedCluster name>], local-cluster by default Replicated Policies Namespace <cluster> The hub's ManagedCluster namespace, local-cluster by default Lifecycle fleet files it builds Those with hub: <hubName>

For the hub's compliance, run oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n local-cluster (or the MultiClusterHub's localClusterName), not -n <hubName>. The ManagedCluster keeps its ACM name; hubName changes only what PolicyStack derives from Git.

Why not use the cluster name?

Nothing on a hub is both stable and unique. Every hub's own ManagedCluster is local-cluster unless the MultiClusterHub sets localClusterName, so hubs reading one repo would collide. clusterID is unique but changes when a hub is rebuilt or replaced, which would rename every hub Application. A name you choose stays put. fleet/hubs/ keeps hub files apart from a managed cluster that happens to have the same name.

items.title: Several hubs, one repo
items.text:
Each hub only sees cluster secrets for the ManagedClusters it imports. fleet/prod-east-1.yaml therefore renders only on the hub that manages prod-east-1, and a lifecycle fleet file only on the hub its hub names. Every active hub needs its own hubName, because they all share the name local-cluster. Two active hubs with the same hubName both read fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml and both try to build every cluster whose fleet file names that hub.

A DR hub is the exception: it does not run PolicyStack while passive, and at takeover it is installed with the hubName of the hub it replaces, so it reads the same hub file and adopts the restored clusters (Hub disaster recovery).

A managed hub imported into a Global Hub in default mode has no local-cluster. The Global Hub reads fleet/hubs/<cluster>.yaml for it and names its Applications <element>-<cluster>. Name its ManagedCluster after its hubName so both modes read the same file (Global Hub).

items.title: Changing hubName
items.text:
Warning

The hub's Applications are renamed, so they and their Policies are deleted and recreated under the new name. Fleet files with hub: <old> stop matching; their lifecycle-<cluster> Applications are deleted and those clusters keep running, unmanaged, until the fleet files name the new hub.

Check the current value with helm get values policystack -n openshift-gitops. To change it:

  1. Merge copies of fleet/hubs/<old>.yaml and values/clusters/<old>.yaml under the new name, and change hub: <old> to the new name in lifecycle fleet files.
  2. helm upgrade policystack ./install -n openshift-gitops --reset-then-reuse-values --set hubName=<new>.
  3. Delete the old files.

items.title: How an element is built
items.text:
An element is one product's configuration, packaged as a Helm chart under stack/<element>/: gitops installs OpenShift GitOps and its Argo CD instance, metallb installs MetalLB and its address pools. Argo CD on the hub renders every element once per cluster, as an Application named <element>-<cluster>; a disabled element renders nothing. The output is ACM Policies in the pstack namespace on the hub. Nothing in an element is applied to a cluster directly: ACM delivers the Policies and enforces them (ACM policies in brief).

The examples below follow stack/gitops from its files to its Policies. To write an element, read this first, then follow Writing an element.

items.title: Anatomy
items.text:
stack/gitops/
├── Chart.yaml                   # (1)!
├── values.yaml                  # (2)!
├── templates/policy.yaml        # (3)!
├── converters/                  # (4)!
│   ├── instance/
│   │   ├── argocd.yaml
│   │   └── ca-bundle.yaml
│   └── link/
│       └── argocd-console.yaml
└── README.md                    # (5)!
  1. name: gitops, equal to the directory name, and one dependency: the policy-library chart with alias: stack, version: "^4.0.0" and repository: file://../../lib/policy-library. The library does all the rendering. It lives in this repo, so Helm takes it from lib/ at the same Git revision as the element; version is the lowest 4.x the element needs (Library changes). Helm passes a subchart the values under its alias and checks them against the subchart's values.schema.json, so everything under stack: is validated: a misspelled key such as enabeld fails the render instead of being ignored.
  2. The element's defaults, all under stack.gitops. A chart named user-monitoring reads stack.userMonitoring: the library camelCases the chart name, because Go templates can't read a key containing - with dot syntax. Below, <el> stands for this key. A key that doesn't match the chart name renders nothing (POLICY090, a validator rule your repository's CI runs).
  3. One line, {{- include "policy-library.render" . -}}, in nearly every element (compliance and upgrade add validation before it).
  4. The manifests. A converter is one file here: a Kubernetes manifest with Helm templating that "converts" the element's settings into the objects ACM enforces.
  5. Generated from Chart.yaml, values.yaml and converters/ by tools/doc-generator.py. See Reading an element's README.

Keep the directory name equal to the chart name. The ApplicationSet names the release <directory>-<cluster>, and the library recovers the cluster by stripping <chart name>- from it. With a mismatch the stripping fails, and any element: dependency (Waiting and ordering) or suffixTemplateNames fails the render: requires Release.Name (...) to start with the chart name.

items.title: Files create, values configure
items.text:
Converter files create policies and templates; values.yaml only configures them, with two exceptions: operatorPolicies and templates.<t>.file. The library scans converters/<policy>/<template>.yaml. A folder name becomes a Policy, a file name (minus .yaml) a template, and the file's contents the objects that template enforces. In ACM terms a template is one entry in the Policy's policy-templates, here a ConfigurationPolicy named <policy>-<template>. It is not a Helm template.

Rendering gitops for cluster c1 (release gitops-c1: the Application and Helm release name, <element>-<cluster>) gives:

Placement         gitops-c1
PlacementBinding  gitops-c1                    # binds the three Policies to the Placement
Policy            install-gitops-c1            # from operatorPolicies.gitops
  ConfigurationPolicy   install-gitops-ns
  ConfigurationPolicy   install-gitops-status
  OperatorPolicy        install-gitops
Policy            instance-gitops-c1           # from converters/instance/
  ConfigurationPolicy   instance-argocd        #   argocd.yaml
  ConfigurationPolicy   instance-ca-bundle     #   ca-bundle.yaml
Policy            link-gitops-c1               # from converters/link/
  ConfigurationPolicy   link-argocd-console    #   argocd-console.yaml

The gitops values.yaml has entries for instance, link and their templates, but deleting every one of them would still render the same three Policies. They only set options: descriptions, dependencies, severity, per-template config. policies.<p> and policies.<p>.templates.<t> configure what the folders created.

You add You get converters/<p>/<t>.yaml Template <p>-<t> in Policy <p>-<release>. The first file in a new folder creates the Policy. operatorPolicies.<k> with subscription.name, in the element's values.yaml (a layer may only override existing entries; POLICY032) Three templates in Policy install-<release>: install-<k>-ns, install-<k>-status and OperatorPolicy install-<k> (The install Policy). policies.<p>.templates.<t>.file Template <p>-<t> rendered from the file(s) named, and Policy <p> if it is new. The other values key that creates something (Reusing files). A new policy belongs in the element's values.yaml; a layer may only add templates to existing policies (POLICY035). Any other policies or templates key Options on an entry that already exists. Nothing new.

items.title: Names that don't exist
items.text:
A values layer (a values file under values/ that the cluster reads; Values cascade) can't invent a policy or a template by naming it: anything it names must be backed by a file, a file key or an operator, and the library fails the render rather than ignore a typo. The checks run before enabled is applied, so enabled: false on a misspelled template fails too. All errors below come from rendering gitops:

In a values layer Result policies.ghost.enabled: true policies.ghost has no templates - add converters/ghost/<template>.yaml policies.instance.templates.typo.enabled: false policies.instance.templates.typo has no file - add converters/instance/typo.yaml or set file policies.extra.templates.cm.file: instance/nope converters/instance/nope.yaml, a file of extra-cm, is missing or empty operatorPolicies.typo.namespace: x operatorPolicies.typo has no subscription.name - a values layer may set an operator the element does not define stack.gitops.enabeld: true Schema error: gitops: Additional property enabeld is not allowed stack.gitOps.enabled: true (wrong element key) Renders nothing, no error. Only POLICY035 in CI catches it. stack.gitops.config.bogus: 1 Renders; the converters never read it. POLICY035 catches unknown top-level config keys, nothing checks deeper ones.

A render error stops the whole Application: Argo CD shows a ComparisonError with the message, and nothing for that element on that cluster syncs or prunes until the layer is fixed (Applications). A typo in a layer stops this element on every cluster that reads it; a schema error under stack stops every element there (Schema). Your repository's CI (Your repository's CI) runs the same render on every pull request, so these normally fail there first (Validation).

items.title: The install Policy
items.text:
install exists when operatorPolicies is non-empty. Each entry becomes three templates:

Template Kind Does install-<k>-ns ConfigurationPolicy Creates the operator's Namespace. Left out when operatorPolicies.<k>.complianceType: mustnothave (uninstall). install-<k> OperatorPolicy Manages the Subscription, OperatorGroup and InstallPlan approval (Operator versions). install-<k>-status ConfigurationPolicy Checks that a CSV whose spec.displayName equals operatorPolicies.<k>.displayName (default subscription.name) reached Succeeded. It takes the Policy's action but names no CSV, so even under enforce it only reports. Templates with waitForOperator: <k> wait on it; if displayName doesn't match the CSV exactly (oc get csv -n <namespace>), it never passes and they never run.

Files in converters/install/ join the same Policy, rendered before the operators. The sample element does both: its my-element-instance template (a ConfigMap) and its operator both sit in Policy install-my-element-<cluster>. Turning off policies.install therefore turns off every operator of the element.

Don't confuse this Policy with the install/ chart or a fleet file's install: key (Words with more than one meaning).

items.title: Partials and reuse
items.text:
Discovery (the scan of converters/<policy>/<template>.yaml above) skips two kinds of file, which render only when a templates.<t>.file names them:

  • Partials: a file or folder whose name starts with _, such as findings/_findings.yaml or _shared/. Prefix a file meant only for file with _; otherwise discovery also renders it as a template of its own.
  • Files directly under converters/, such as converters/guard.yaml of the lifecycle chart.

A .yml file never renders: discovery skips it and file always appends .yaml. Rename it.

POLICY021 warns about a converter nothing renders.

items.title: Reusing files
items.text:
templates.<t>.file says "this template's contents come from this other file". It is a path under converters/ without .yaml, or a list of them, and it replaces the file discovery would have used. Two uses:

One file, several templatesSeveral files, one template

stack/compliance reports findings per severity. high, medium and low have no file of their own: file creates all three from one partial, each with its own config.

stack/compliance/values.yaml (excerpt)
policies:
  findings:
    templates:
      high:
        file: findings/_findings
        config:
          severity: "compliance.openshift.io/check-severity=high"   # (1)!
      medium:
        file: findings/_findings
        severity: medium                                            # (2)!
        config:
          severity: "compliance.openshift.io/check-severity=medium"
  1. Read by the partial as .Config.severity, a label selector.
  2. The ACM severity of ConfigurationPolicy findings-medium. Unrelated to config.severity.

stack/acs needs its namespace in both central and secured, because either can be on a cluster without the other. central/central is the file discovery would use anyway; the list puts the shared namespace in front of it, concatenating the objects of each file into one ConfigurationPolicy:

stack/acs/values.yaml (excerpt)
policies:
  central:
    templates:
      central:
        file: [_shared/acs-namespace, central/central]
  secured:
    templates:
      tls:
        file: [_shared/acs-namespace, secured/tls]

Rule of thumb: if you are about to copy a converter, use file. Otherwise add a file.

items.title: Settings: config and .Config
items.text:
stack.<el>.config holds the element's settings: the curated, typed values an admin is meant to change, such as gitops ha.enabled or rbacPolicies. Converters read it as .Config. Values never carry a raw CR spec: the converter builds the manifest from the settings, so layers stay small and typed, and a CR API change is fixed once in the converter rather than in every layer.

For each template, .Config is the element config deep-merged with that template's own templates.<t>.config, the template winning. gitops sets the console text this way:

stack/gitops/values.yaml (excerpt)
stack:
  gitops:
    policies:
      link:
        templates:
          argocd-console:
            config:
              consoleText: Red Hat OpenShift GitOps   # .Config.consoleText in argocd-console.yaml only

Layers change config like any other values: maps merge key by key, lists are replaced whole (Merge rules). The library schema does not validate config. POLICY022 fails a converter that reads a top-level key missing from the element's values.yaml, and POLICY035 fails a layer that sets one.

items.title: What renders
items.text:
• The element is off until a values layer sets stack.<el>.enabled: true. Every shipped element is off except upgrade, which drives and reports OpenShift version upgrades and renders nothing until a fleet file sets version or channel, or a layer sets stack.upgrade.config.upstream (OpenShift upgrades).
  • Everything inside it is on. Every policy, template and operator renders unless it sets enabled: false. Elements ship a piece off when it needs per-cluster input, is one of several alternatives (platform, storage backend), or is risky to apply by default; the README lists those under Optional pieces.
  • null means unset. A layer setting enabled: null on an entry an earlier layer turned off turns it back on.
  • A Policy with nothing enabled renders nothing. Disable instance-argocd and instance-ca-bundle and Policy instance-gitops-<cluster> disappears. Its dependents are not adjusted: link-gitops-<cluster> still waits for it and stays Pending, so turn them off in the same layer (policies.link.enabled: false).
  • operatorPolicies.<k>.enabled: false stops managing the operator; it doesn't uninstall it. It also fails the render while a template waits on that operator: waitForOperator "gitops" on policy "instance" matches no enabled entry in operatorPolicies. Turn the waiting templates off in the same layer (Stopping and uninstalling).

A template whose converter renders no objects still renders, with object-templates-raw: [] (the string field converter output goes into when it starts with an ACM template or a list; Converter shapes), and ACM reports it Compliant without checking anything. POLICY082 fails a Policy whose templates are all empty.

items.title: Inform or enforce
items.text:
Each Policy gets a remediationAction, the first one set of:

  1. policies.<p>.remediationAction
  2. default.remediationAction (stack.<el>.default, the element-wide defaults block)
  3. inform

gitops sets default.remediationAction: enforce, so enabling it changes the cluster at once.

Setting Rule Dry run global.remediationAction: inform in any layer a cluster reads overrides every Policy of every element (Global keys, Dry run) Template action Only InformOnly; any other value fails the schema (inform, enforce and InformOnly) severity template or operator → policies.<p> → default → low

Full defaults: What you leave out. What inform and enforce do on the cluster: ACM policies in brief.

items.title: Waiting and ordering
items.text:
Policies and templates render in name order, but that is output order only. ACM evaluates them independently unless something says to wait. Until a dependency is met, ACM does not create the waiting template on the cluster and reports it Pending, and deletes it again if the dependency later stops being met (Dependencies and ignorePending).

Key Waits for policies.<p>.dependencies: [{name: install}] Policy install-<release> of the same element to be Compliant. dependencies: [{name: ready, element: odf}] Policy ready-odf-<cluster>: another element on the same cluster. If odf isn't enabled there, that Policy never exists and the wait never ends. templates.<t>.extraDependencies: [{name: central-ready}] Template central-ready of the same Policy (name is the template key, rendered <p>-central-ready). templates.<t>.waitForOperator: <k> install-<k>-status, the operator's CSV reaching Succeeded. Also sets ignorePending: true, so the Policy reads Compliant while waiting. templates.<t>.ignorePending: true Adds no wait. While the template is Pending, the Policy's compliance ignores it, so the Policy can read Compliant. policies.<p>.orderManifests: [a, b, c] Chains every template of Policy p: a, b, c first, then the unlisted templates in name order, then its operators, each waiting for the one before to be Compliant. Used by lifecycle for its build steps.

gitops chains its three Policies: instance depends on install, link on instance, and instance-argocd waits for the operator, because the ArgoCD CR can't be created before its CRD exists. The rendered instance Policy:

Policy instance-gitops-c1 (excerpt)
spec:
  dependencies:
    - kind: Policy
      name: install-gitops-c1      # policies.instance.dependencies: [{name: install}]
      namespace: pstack
      compliance: Compliant
  policy-templates:
    - extraDependencies:           # waitForOperator: gitops
        - kind: ConfigurationPolicy
          name: install-gitops-status
          compliance: Compliant
      ignorePending: true
      objectDefinition:
        kind: ConfigurationPolicy
        metadata:
          name: instance-argocd

On a new cluster this reads: install the operator, wait for its CSV, then create the ArgoCD instance, then the console link. Dependency entry fields (kind, compliance, release, raw) are listed in the library README.

items.title: Helm templates and ACM templates
items.text:
Here "template" means a Go template expression {{ }}, not a policy template. A converter can hold two kinds, evaluated at different times in different places:

Data Template expressions evaluated by Write values.yaml, layers, .Config Helm, when Argo CD renders on the hub {{ .Config.x }} Objects on the managed cluster (lookup, fromConfigMap) ACM's config-policy controller on the managed cluster, every evaluation {{ "{{" }} lookup ... {{ "}}" }} Hub objects and cluster labels (copySecretData, .ManagedClusterLabels) ACM's policy propagator on the hub, before it copies the Policy to the cluster and again when an object it reads changes {{ "{{" }}hub ... hub{{ "}}" }}

Helm runs first and would evaluate ACM's braces too, so they are escaped: Helm prints {{ "{{" }} as {{. Anything known from values belongs to Helm. The gitops console link uses both:

ConverterAfter Helm (in the Policy)On the managed cluster converters/link/argocd-console.yaml (excerpt)
text: {{ .Config.consoleText | quote }}
