href: '{{ "{{" }} $host := (lookup "route.openshift.io/v1" "Route" "{{ .Config.namespace }}" "openshift-gitops-server").spec.host {{ "}}" }}{{ "{{" }} skipObject (not $host) {{ "}}" }}https://{{ "{{" }} $host {{ "}}" }}'

text: "Red Hat OpenShift GitOps"
href: '{{ $host := (lookup "route.openshift.io/v1" "Route" "openshift-gitops" "openshift-gitops-server").spec.host }}{{ skipObject (not $host) }}https://{{ $host }}'

Helm filled in the text and the namespace. The rest is now an ACM template.

ACM looks up the cluster's own Route and writes href: https://<route host>. Until the Route exists, skipObject leaves the ConsoleLink out instead of creating a broken link.

Forgetting to escape usually fails at render: Helm's lookup returns an empty map, so reading a field from it fails (nil pointer evaluating interface {}.<field>), and Helm doesn't know ACM-only functions (function "fromSecret" not defined). Some mistakes render silently instead: an unescaped .ManagedClusterName becomes an empty string. Check the rendered Policy (Validation).

Helm evaluates only converter files; strings from values are inserted as-is. So ACM templates inside values, such as policies.<p>.templates.<t>.customMessage.noncompliant (the ConfigurationPolicy's violation message), are written unescaped: noncompliant: "{{ .DefaultMessage }}: ...". Reading hub secrets with hub templates is covered in Secrets.

items.title: Rendered names
items.text:
<release> is the Application name, <element>-<cluster>; on the hub itself, hubName (the name given at helm install, since ACM calls the hub local-cluster) stands in for the cluster name (The hub).

Object Name gitops on c1 Policy <policy>-<release> instance-gitops-c1 ConfigurationPolicy <policy>-<template> instance-argocd OperatorPolicy install-<k> install-gitops Placement, PlacementBinding <release> gitops-c1

Everything lives in pstack on the hub; ConfigurationPolicies and OperatorPolicies are read inside the Policy YAML there (The objects).

Template names must be unique per cluster (ACM) but carry neither element nor cluster, so include the product in them (Naming). CI fails clashes (POLICY002 within, POLICY003 between elements). Lifecycle places every cluster's release on the hub, so it appends the cluster to its template names (suffixTemplateNames, see Cluster lifecycle). ACM also copies each Policy as pstack.<policy>-<release>, which limits name lengths (Naming limits).

Renaming deletes and recreates Policies

Element, policy and template names are part of every object name. Renaming one deletes its Policies and creates new ones on every cluster that has the element (Removal and pruning).

items.title: Reading an element's README
items.text:
Each stack/<element>/README.md is generated from the element's files and lists what a values layer can set. Browse them on GitHub.

Section Shows You set Title and first paragraph What the element does stack.<el>.enabled: true Optional pieces Entries shipped enabled: false The Turn on with key, under stack.<el> Settings Every config key with its default stack.<el>.config.<setting> Operators Each operator's package, channel, source, namespace and pinned versions stack.<el>.operatorPolicies.<k>.versions and the other operatorPolicies keys, where <k> is the Operator policy name minus install- (Operator versions) Policies Each Policy's name on the hub (<policy>-<element>-<cluster>), its dependencies, and every template with its action, severity, waits and source file stack.<el>.policies.<p>...

In the Policies tables, inform (always) marks an InformOnly template, (off) an optional one, and "compliant while pending" a template with ignorePending. The full list of keys is in the policy-library README.

items.title: Cluster lifecycle
items.text:
Lifecycle is how a hub builds and destroys clusters from fleet files (fleet/<cluster>.yaml, one per cluster, saying which Git revision and values layers it gets: Fleet files). You add hub, version and an install block to a cluster's fleet file and merge to the default branch, the only branch fleet files are read from. The hub you named creates the cluster with ACM's own installers and imports it. From then on the same fleet file gives it Day-2 config (the element Policies that configure a running cluster), like any imported cluster. Set state: absent and the hub destroys it.

A cluster whose fleet file has no hub is one you build and import yourself. Lifecycle never touches it.

PolicyStack adds no controller for this. The lifecycle/ chart renders only an ACM Policy, a Placement and a PlacementBinding. The install itself is done by components that ship with ACM and its multicluster engine (MCE): HyperShift, Hive, or SiteConfig with the assisted or image-based installer. You provide the credential Secret on the hub (Install keys), plus a BMC Secret for siteconfig and the InfraEnv and Agents for hypershift on Agent (Examples). Steps: Building clusters. Keys: Lifecycle keys.

items.title: Fleet keys
items.text:
hub: in a fleet file names the building hub by its hubName (Words with more than one meaning).

Five fleet-file keys drive lifecycle. Only Application lifecycle-<cluster> (below) reads hub, state and install; the per-element Day-2 Applications ignore them. revision and valueFiles work as for any cluster: revision also pins which lifecycle/ chart renders, and layers can set install defaults.

Key What it does hub The hubName of the hub that builds the cluster, as set at helm install on that hub. That hub also imports it. CI fails (POLICY050) when fleet/hubs/<hub>.yaml does not exist, which catches typos. state present (default) builds the cluster, then keeps applying the changes the engine accepts (Immutable fields). absent destroys it. version OpenShift release, x.y.z. Required while state: present: the render fails with version is required. Bumping it upgrades the cluster (OpenShift upgrades). channel Upgrade channel, such as stable-4.20. Optional. On hypershift, a bump waits until the channel's update graph offers version (Upgrades). install What to build: engine, credential, domain, nodes. Any values layer can set install defaults; the fleet file's install wins over every layer.

version and channel go only in the fleet file. The two ApplicationSets (policystack for Day-2, policystack-lifecycle) pass them from there to the lifecycle chart and to the upgrade element, the Day-2 element that upgrades a running cluster. A layer value would silently upgrade every cluster that reads the layer, so CI rejects it (POLICY034, why).

The fleet file name is the cluster name: a DNS label of at most 30 characters, so every element's Policy names fit (Naming limits).

items.title: Pick an engine
items.text:
install.engine picks which ACM component builds the cluster. Never change it on an existing cluster: destroy first, otherwise the hub can build a second cluster with the same name (Changing engine).

You want install.engine install.platform Upgraded by OpenShift on AWS, GCP, Azure or vSphere hive upgrade element on the cluster OpenShift on bare metal with a BMC siteconfig upgrade element on the cluster Hosted control plane, workers as VMs on the hub hypershift (default) KubeVirt lifecycle-<cluster> on the hub, on a version bump Hosted control plane, bare-metal workers hypershift Agent lifecycle-<cluster> on the hub, on a version bump Hosted control plane, workers you boot yourself hypershift None lifecycle-<cluster> on the hub, on a version bump
  • hypershift creates a HostedCluster and NodePools. The control plane runs as pods on the hub, so the hub upgrades it. install.platform has no default: leave it out and the render fails with install.platform is required. Set it in the fleet file or a layer, as upstream's example values/platforms/kubevirt.yaml and agent.yaml do.
  • hive creates a ClusterDeployment, and Hive runs the OpenShift installer against your cloud or vCenter. It ignores install.platform; the cloud goes in install.hive.platform.<aws|gcp|azure|vsphere>.
  • siteconfig creates a ClusterInstance. SiteConfig boots your hosts through their BMCs and installs them with the assisted installer (ai, default) or from a seed image (ibi, single node).

items.title: How a Policy builds a cluster
items.text:
flowchart LR
  F[fleet/ocp-aws.yaml<br>hub: acm-dc1] --> A[Application<br>lifecycle-ocp-aws]
  A --> P[Policy<br>present-lifecycle-ocp-aws]
  P --> O[ClusterDeployment<br>on the hub]
  O --> H[Hive installs<br>the cluster]
  H --> M[ManagedCluster<br>imported]
  M --> D[Day-2 Applications]
  1. On the hub whose hubName matches hub, ApplicationSet policystack-lifecycle creates Application lifecycle-<cluster> in openshift-gitops. Fleet files are read at the head of the default branch; the Application renders lifecycle/ at the fleet file's revision, so a change to the lifecycle chart reaches only clusters whose revision contains it.
  2. The render is a Placement and PlacementBinding lifecycle-<cluster> and one Policy in pstack, the hub namespace that holds every PolicyStack Policy (Where Policies live): present-lifecycle-<cluster>, or absent-lifecycle-<cluster> when state: absent. Flipping state makes Argo CD delete one and create the other; deleting a lifecycle Policy removes nothing from the hub (Why Policies).
  3. The Placement selects the hub's own ManagedCluster (local-cluster by default). ACM copies the Policy into namespace local-cluster, and the governance add-on on the hub evaluates it against the hub's own API. Nothing is placed on the new cluster; it does not exist yet.
  4. The Policy's steps create the engine's objects on the hub. The engine builds the cluster from them.
  5. ACM imports the finished cluster, and the Day-2 ApplicationSet takes over (Day-2 handoff).

The cluster is built when present-lifecycle-<cluster> is Compliant. Compliant does not mean its Day-2 elements have applied; those are separate Policies.

The hub must manage itself

The lifecycle ApplicationSet only runs on a hub that is registered as its own ManagedCluster, local-cluster, which ACM does by default. Without it, no lifecycle-<cluster> Application appears and nothing reports an error. Check with oc get managedcluster -l local-cluster. The one exception is a hub imported into Multicluster Global Hub in default mode, which has no local-cluster: the global hub renders the Application and places the Policy on that hub (Global Hub).

items.title: Worked example
items.text:
fleet/ocp-aws.yaml with a copy of upstream's example platforms/aws.yaml layer (full example in Building clusters):

# fleet/ocp-aws.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
valueFiles:
  - platforms/aws.yaml      # engine: hive, credential hive-credentials/aws, machine sizes
install:
  baseDomain: aws.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      aws:
        region: us-east-2

renders on hub acm-dc1:

Application openshift-gitops/lifecycle-ocp-aws
├ Placement, PlacementBinding pstack/lifecycle-ocp-aws    selects local-cluster
└ Policy pstack/present-lifecycle-ocp-aws                 enforce
  ├ present-guard-ocp-aws        InformOnly  refuses a same-named cluster it did not build
  ├ present-credentials-ocp-aws  enforce     Namespace ocp-aws; Secrets ocp-aws-pull-secret,
  │                                          ocp-aws-creds, ocp-aws-install-config
  ├ present-manifests-ocp-aws    enforce     install.manifests (none here)
  ├ present-cluster-ocp-aws      enforce     ClusterDeployment ocp-aws/ocp-aws, ManagedCluster ocp-aws,
  │                                          KlusterletAddonConfig ocp-aws/ocp-aws
  └ present-ready-ocp-aws        InformOnly  ClusterDeployment spec.installed: true

Hive then installs the cluster, about 45 minutes on AWS.

items.title: Why Policies
items.text:
Argo CD could apply a ClusterDeployment from Git. A Policy evaluated on the hub can do four things Argo CD cannot:

  • Keep secrets out of Git. You create the credential Secret (a console credential works) and, for siteconfig, the BMC Secret on the hub by hand. The credentials step copies their keys into per-cluster Secrets with fromSecret, an ACM template function that reads a Secret when the Policy is evaluated. The Policy is evaluated on the hub itself, so they can sit in any hub namespace. Edits reach the copies on the next evaluation. Lifecycle never deletes them.
  • Run steps in order and wait on the engine's status between them (The step chain).
  • Read live fields back. The Hive release image, the SiteConfig ClusterImageSet image and the ClusterInstance sshPublicKey are read from the live objects, so a later version bump never hits an immutable field (Immutable fields).
  • Refuse what it did not build, checked in the same evaluation as each write (Ownership).

No lifecycle template sets pruneObjectBehavior, the ACM setting that deletes a Policy's objects when the Policy is deleted (Removal and pruning). Deleting a lifecycle Policy therefore deletes nothing on the hub. Only state: absent destroys a cluster.

items.title: The step chain
items.text:
Each step is a ConfigurationPolicy inside the Policy, named <state>-<step>-<cluster>, such as present-guard-hcp-kubevirt. The -<cluster> suffix comes from the policy-library option suffixTemplateNames: true: every lifecycle Policy lands on the same hub, and ACM requires template names to be unique across all Policies on one cluster.

The lifecycle chart lists the steps in orderManifests, a policy-library key that makes each step depend on the one before it being Compliant (Waiting and ordering). Until it is, ACM does not evaluate the step and reports it Pending.

flowchart LR
  subgraph present
    pg[guard] --> pc[credentials] --> pm[manifests] --> pcl[cluster] --> pr[ready]
  end
  subgraph absent
    ag[guard] --> ad[detach] --> adt[detached] --> ax[destroy] --> axd[destroyed] --> acl[cleanup]
  end
Step Mode Does guard InformOnly NonCompliant while a same-named cluster exists that lifecycle did not build (Ownership). Stops the chain. credentials enforce Namespace and the Secrets copied from the credential. manifests enforce install.manifests: extra hub objects, such as a MetalLB address pool the cluster's API needs. cluster enforce The engine's objects: HostedCluster and NodePools, ClusterDeployment, or ClusterInstance. ready InformOnly Waits for the install, or a HyperShift upgrade, to finish. detach enforce Deletes the ManagedCluster while the cluster still runs, so ACM's agents clean up. detached InformOnly Waits for the ManagedCluster to be gone. destroy enforce Deletes the engine's root object; the engine then deletes the cluster. destroyed InformOnly Waits for the root object to be gone. cleanup enforce Deletes the copied Secrets or Namespace <cluster>, and install.manifests.

The InformOnly steps are gates. An enforced create or delete is Compliant as soon as the API accepts it, long before the engine finishes, so each enforced step that hands work to an engine is followed by a gate that checks the engine's status. InformOnly is a template-level action ACM never enforces, even inside an enforced Policy (ACM policies in brief), so a gate never changes anything.

siteconfig has no detach or detached: SiteConfig owns the ManagedCluster and would re-create it. Per-engine detail for every step: Policy chains.

NonCompliant during a build is normal

present-ready-<cluster> stays NonCompliant with Waiting for … until the install finishes, and on hypershift during every upgrade; Argo CD shows lifecycle-<cluster> Degraded. Diagnosis: Watching a build, When a build fails.

Dry run applies to lifecycle

global.remediationAction: inform in any layer the cluster reads turns the lifecycle Policy to inform too (Dry run). The hub then builds nothing, and state: absent destroys nothing.

items.title: Ownership
items.text:
Lifecycle acts only on clusters it built. Without this, adding hub to the fleet file of an imported or console-built cluster with the same name would let the hub patch that cluster's objects, and state: absent would destroy a cluster PolicyStack never built.

The cluster step writes the annotation lifecycle.policystk.io/hub: <hubName> (the marker) on the engine's root object in the same create. The root object is the engine object whose deletion destroys the cluster:

Engine Root object Also marked hypershift HostedCluster <install.namespace>/<cluster> hive ClusterDeployment <cluster>/<cluster> ManagedCluster <cluster> siteconfig ClusterInstance <cluster>/<cluster> ManagedCluster <cluster>, through extraAnnotations

Each evaluation checks the first of these that exists:

  1. the root object;
  2. ManagedCluster <cluster>;
  3. siteconfig only: ClusterDeployment <cluster>/<cluster>, which SiteConfig would adopt.

If it lacks the marker, it is foreign. The others are not checked, so a hypershift cluster's ManagedCluster, which the hypershift-addon creates without the marker, never counts once the HostedCluster exists. A marked ManagedCluster with no root object, as after a failed ClusterDeployment create, is owned.

When an object is foreign:

  • guard goes NonCompliant and names it, which stops the chain.
  • Every enforced step except manifests repeats the check in the same evaluation and fails with <Kind> <cluster> was not built by lifecycle (no lifecycle.policystk.io/hub annotation); refusing. A stale guard result can therefore never let a step write or delete. manifests writes hub objects not tied to the cluster name, so it skips the check, but it runs only after credentials passed it.

Only the key counts; the value records the hub that last wrote it. A root object restored onto a new hub, as in hub disaster recovery, stays owned. An imported cluster is never adopted: remove hub, state and install from its fleet file.

Not marked: Namespace and hypershift Secrets

Namespace <cluster> and the hypershift Secrets carry no marker. A same-named Namespace or Secret created after a destroy, with no root object left, is deleted by a still-present absent Policy, so delete the fleet file once a destroy finishes. Only install.namespace is checked for a HostedCluster: a same-named HostedCluster in another namespace is not seen, and lifecycle builds a second one whose ManagedCluster name collides. Keep HostedCluster names unique on the hub.

Changing engine

The lookup starts at the new engine's root object, so it can miss an engine switch. Switching from hive to hypershift or siteconfig, or from siteconfig to hypershift, finds the old engine's marked ManagedCluster, so the guard passes and the hub builds a second cluster under the same name while the first keeps running. Other switches are refused, because the new root object or the ManagedCluster exists without the marker. Destroy before changing engine.

items.title: Immutable fields
items.text:
Most install keys are fixed at create, because the engine's API rejects changes to the fields they set. Changing one never rebuilds the cluster. The cluster step tries the update, the API denies it, and present-cluster-<cluster> goes NonCompliant with the API's message while the live object stays as it was. The update is all or nothing: while the denial stands, no other change to that object goes through either, including a version bump on a HostedCluster and every node change on a ClusterInstance.

To recover, revert the value, or destroy and build again. Which fields are fixed per object: Immutable fields.

What does apply after create: version and channel on hypershift, NodePool replicas and new pools, siteconfig worker add and remove, manifests, and the credential's contents. Everything else: check the table.

siteconfig is the strictest. Its ClusterInstance is mustonlyhave, so the whole rendered spec must match, and SiteConfig refuses almost every change after install. A shared layer change or a new revision whose lifecycle/ renders the ClusterInstance differently is denied on every evaluation. Before moving a siteconfig cluster to a new revision, render both and compare the ClusterInstance.

items.title: Destroy and abandon
items.text:
Destroy removes the cluster. Set state: absent and keep install and every layer that sets it; without them the absent Policy targets the wrong engine (Destroy).

The absent chain:

  1. detach deletes the ManagedCluster while the cluster still runs, so ACM's agents remove themselves. The cluster leaves Argo CD, and its Day-2 Applications and hub Policies are deleted.
  2. destroy deletes the root object. HyperShift deletes the control plane and NodePools; Hive deprovisions the cloud resources with <cluster>-creds; SiteConfig deletes the BareMetalHosts, then the ManagedCluster.
  3. cleanup deletes the copied Secrets or Namespace <cluster>, the siteconfig ClusterImageSet, and install.manifests. The credential stays.

The cluster is gone when absent-lifecycle-<cluster> is Compliant. Then delete the fleet file: a lingering absent Policy deletes any Namespace <cluster> created later (Not marked). Or set state: present to build a new cluster under the same name. Procedure and what each engine leaves behind: Destroy.

Abandon stops lifecycle without touching the cluster. Delete the fleet file, or remove hub, state and install together. Application lifecycle-<cluster> and its Policy are deleted, and since no lifecycle template prunes, the cluster keeps running and stays an ACM ManagedCluster.

  • Removing only hub while the fleet file still sets state or install fails CI (POLICY050). If install comes only from layers, CI passes and the cluster is abandoned.
  • Removing the keys keeps the cluster's Day-2 Applications. Deleting the whole fleet file deletes them too (Removal and pruning).
  • Deleting the fleet file while absent-lifecycle-<cluster> is not yet Compliant abandons the cluster halfway through destroy.

Restore the keys with the same install to re-adopt it: the root object still carries the marker. Changing hub abandons the cluster on the old hub, and the new hub builds a second one unless the root object was moved there with its marker (Abandon).

items.title: Day-2 handoff
items.text:
A cluster the hub builds gets Day-2 config the same way as an imported one:

  1. The ManagedCluster appears. hypershift: the hypershift-addon creates it once the HostedCluster is available, and runs the cluster's klusterlet (ACM's agent for that cluster) on the hub in hosted mode. hive: the cluster step created it, and ACM imports it once Hive marks the install done. siteconfig: SiteConfig created it, and ACM imports it.
  2. Like every ManagedCluster, it joins ACM's global ManagedClusterSet. The install chart's GitOpsCluster turns that into an Argo CD cluster secret (Install chart). Once the cluster reports in, ACM labels it with its clusterID, and only then does the Day-2 ApplicationSet select it, so a cluster still installing gets no Day-2 Applications.
  3. The Day-2 ApplicationSet pairs the secret with the same fleet file and creates one <element>-<cluster> Application per element, at the fleet file's revision with its valueFiles.

hive and siteconfig render their own KlusterletAddonConfig with every add-on on, replacing SiteConfig's stock one, which turns off the application manager that ACM needs to create the cluster's Argo CD secret.

items.title: How PolicyStack works
items.text: The rest of the docs assume you know what is in your repository, what PolicyStack creates on the hub, how a commit reaches a cluster, how fleet files work, what your repository's CI checks, and the terms below. Read this page before Installation.

items.title: The repository
items.text:
You create your own repository from upstream PolicyStack with copier and pass its URL as gitRepo when you install the chart on the hub (Installation). Upstream ships no fleet files, so it configures no cluster until you add yours. Several hubs can read one repository; each acts only on the fleet files of clusters it manages or builds, plus its own fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml (Several hubs, one repo).

copier copies two kinds of things from upstream release tags, each recorded in a .copier-answers.yml: the framework, once, at the repository root, and each element you want, into stack/<element>/. Everything else is yours. Each path belongs to one owner:

Path What it is Owner Updated by install/ The Helm chart you run once per hub. It creates the two ApplicationSets, a GitOpsCluster that registers every ACM managed cluster with Argo CD (so the ApplicationSets can list them), the pstack namespace and RBAC (Install chart). install/operators/ renders ACM, OpenShift GitOps and a MultiClusterHub for a hub that doesn't run them yet. Framework A framework update. Don't edit. lifecycle/ The chart that builds and destroys clusters (Cluster lifecycle). Framework Same lib/ policy-library, the Helm library chart every element and lifecycle/ renders through (How an element is built). Framework Same tools/ The validator, the sample element, create-element.sh and the README generator. Framework Same .github/workflows/, .pre-commit-config.yaml, mise.toml CI workflows, lint hooks and pinned tool versions (CI workflows). Framework Same /.copier-answers.yml The framework release you have, such as _commit: v1.2.0. copier A framework update. Never edit by hand. stack/<element>/ with a .copier-answers.yml A tracked element, copied from a release tag vX.Y.Z no newer than the framework's. Upstream, until you edit it An element update, which merges upstream's changes with your edits. stack/<element>/ without one An element you wrote, or one you ejected from tracking. You You fleet/ One fleet file per cluster. You You values/ Values layers, such as environments/prod.yaml or clusters/<cluster>.yaml. You You values.yaml Values every cluster gets. It holds only policyNamespace: pstack, the namespace the install chart creates. Don't edit it: changing that key renames, so deletes and recreates, every Policy (Where Policies live), and fleet-wide settings go in a layer (Order). Framework A framework update .github/CODEOWNERS, README.md Reviewers, your own notes. You You

You take updates by hand: copier update merges a newer release of the framework or of one element into a branch, you open it as a PR, and the merge reaches clusters like any other (Upgrading PolicyStack). Upstream promises compatibility only for the framework and for elements you haven't edited (Compatibility). Settings belong in values/: an element you edit is yours to merge on every update.

Every element ships with enabled: false except upgrade, which renders nothing until a fleet file sets version or channel, or a layer sets stack.upgrade.config.upstream. Then it enforces them on merge: version starts an OpenShift upgrade (OpenShift upgrades). A cluster gets nothing from an element until a values layer it reads sets stack.<elementKey>.enabled: true, where the key is the element name in camelCase: cert-manager reads stack.certManager (How an element is built).

A layer that turns elements on enforces them as soon as the PR that lists the layer merges. Read a layer before listing it, or start with a dry run. A cluster always reads the values/clusters/ file matching its name, without listing it.

items.title: What lives on the hub
items.text:
Every object Argo CD creates is on the hub. Only ACM changes managed clusters, through the Policies.

Object Where One per Created by ApplicationSets policystack and policystack-lifecycle openshift-gitops Hub helm install policystack ./install GitOpsCluster argo-acm-importer-global, its Placement global, and its Argo CD cluster secrets openshift-gitops Secret per ManagedCluster, the hub included The install chart, then ACM. The secrets only let the ApplicationSets list clusters (ApplicationSets). ManagedClusterSetBinding global openshift-gitops, pstack Namespace The install chart. Lets Placements there select clusters; without it they select nothing (Cluster sets). Namespace pstack, ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding openshift-gitops-policy-admin Cluster Hub The install chart. Lets Argo CD manage Policies, Placements and PlacementBindings. Application <element>-<cluster> openshift-gitops Element directory per cluster with a fleet file, enabled or not. A disabled element's Application renders nothing. policystack Application lifecycle-<cluster> openshift-gitops Cluster this hub builds policystack-lifecycle (Cluster lifecycle) Policies, Placement, PlacementBinding pstack One Policy per policy the element defines: one per converters/<policy>/ directory, plus install when it manages operators (How an element is built). One Placement per enabled element per cluster; one PlacementBinding when at least one Policy renders The Applications Replicated Policies pstack.<policy name> The cluster's namespace, named like the cluster Policy per cluster it targets ACM (ACM policies in brief)

For example, with the gitops element enabled for the managed cluster prod-east-1:

Application   openshift-gitops/gitops-prod-east-1
├─ Placement         pstack/gitops-prod-east-1           selects prod-east-1 only
├─ PlacementBinding  pstack/gitops-prod-east-1
├─ Policy            pstack/install-gitops-prod-east-1   → prod-east-1/pstack.install-gitops-prod-east-1
├─ Policy            pstack/instance-gitops-prod-east-1  → prod-east-1/pstack.instance-gitops-prod-east-1
└─ Policy            pstack/link-gitops-prod-east-1      → prod-east-1/pstack.link-gitops-prod-east-1

install comes from the element's operatorPolicies, instance and link from its converters/instance/ and converters/link/ directories.

The Application name is also the Helm release name, and Policy names are <policy>-<release> (Rendered names). On the hub itself, hubName, the name you give the hub at helm install, takes the cluster's place in the Application name, and the replicated Policies sit in the hub's ManagedCluster namespace, local-cluster by default (The hub).

items.title: How a change reaches a cluster
items.text:
1. You merge a commit. A cluster whose fleet file pins a branch, such as revision: main, takes every commit to that branch. A cluster pinned to a tag or commit SHA takes nothing until its fleet file's revision changes.
  2. For each Application whose inputs changed, Argo CD runs helm template on stack/<element> at the cluster's revision, with the cluster's values cascade: the element's values.yaml, the root values.yaml, each valueFiles entry, then values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml (Values cascade). It syncs the result into pstack and deletes the objects that dropped out of the render.
  3. The Placement selects exactly one ManagedCluster, and ACM replicates each Policy into that cluster's namespace on the hub (Placement and naming).
  4. The governance add-on, ACM's policy controllers on the managed cluster, pulls the replicated Policy. Under enforce it creates or patches objects to match the Policy; under inform it only reports differences. The status goes back to the replicated Policy and the Policy in pstack (ACM policies in brief).
Branch pinTag pin fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
revision: main

Merge a change to values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml on main. It reaches the cluster within about 6 minutes (Default branch only).

fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
revision: v1.4.0

Merge the change to main, tag it v1.5.0, then merge a second PR that sets revision: v1.5.0. Until that second merge, the cluster keeps rendering v1.4.0. Production clusters pinned this way change only through a reviewed edit under fleet/ (Rolling out changes).

When a change doesn't arrive, check each stage in order:

Stage Check Usual cause and effect Generation oc get applicationset policystack -n openshift-gitops -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ErrorOccurred")].message}' A bad fleet file stops generation for the whole hub (One bad fleet file stops the hub). Application exists oc get applications.argoproj.io -n openshift-gitops \| grep <cluster> None: no fleet file named exactly like the ManagedCluster at fleet/<cluster>.yaml on the default branch (subdirectories and other branches are ignored), or the cluster's Argo CD secret lacks the clusterID label (oc get secret -n openshift-gitops -l argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type=cluster -L clusterID). ACM adds the label once the cluster has joined. Render oc get application <element>-<cluster> -n openshift-gitops -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].message}' A ComparisonError with the Helm error: a key the library schema rejects (an unknown key directly under stack.<elementKey>), a wrong type, a values entry that names no policy. Argo CD syncs and deletes nothing for that Application, so the cluster keeps its last good Policies. Other Applications are unaffected, except that a schema error under stack in a shared layer fails every Application, lifecycle-<cluster> included, of every cluster reading that layer (When an Application fails). Render is empty oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack \| grep <element>-<cluster> (<element>-<hubName> for the hub) No Policies: no layer the cluster reads enables the element, or a values file name is misspelled, which Argo CD skips silently (Missing files). Compliance oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n <cluster> (local-cluster for the hub) Under inform, NonCompliant means the cluster differs and nothing will change it. Under enforce, oc describe policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io pstack.<policy> -n <cluster> shows each template's latest message (Compliance states).

A misspelled element key, or a misspelled top-level key under config, renders without error and is ignored; only POLICY035 in CI catches it. Nothing catches a misspelled nested config key (Schema).

items.title: Fleet files
items.text:
A fleet file enrolls one cluster. fleet/<cluster>.yaml is named exactly like the cluster's ManagedCluster. A hub's own ManagedCluster is named local-cluster by default, so its name can't tell hubs apart. A hub, recognized by its local-cluster label, uses fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml instead, kept in its own directory so it can't collide with a managed cluster's file.

fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
revision: main # (1)!
valueFiles: # (2)!
  - environments/prod.yaml
  - datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - platforms/aws.yaml
  1. The branch, tag or commit SHA every Application of this cluster renders stack/ and values/ from.
  2. Values layers under values/, lowest precedence first. values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml is always added last.

The file decides three things: whether the cluster gets Applications at all, the revision it renders from, and the layers it reads. Optional keys set the OpenShift version and channel, or have a hub build the cluster (Fleet file keys).

A fleet file does not import a cluster. The cluster must also exist in ACM, imported by you or built by a hub, and have joined. Without hub: <hubName>, which asks that hub to build the cluster (Cluster lifecycle), a fleet file for a cluster ACM doesn't manage does nothing. Once the cluster joins, its Applications appear and its Policies apply without any further commit, so a fleet file written ahead of an import takes effect at import.

items.title: Default branch only
items.text:
The ApplicationSets read fleet files from the latest commit of the default branch (Argo CD's HEAD). Everything else, stack/ and values/, is read at the revision the file names. The revision is a key inside the file, so the file has to come from one fixed branch. It also means only merges to the default branch decide which revision each cluster renders: a commit on another branch can't re-pin a cluster. A cluster pinned to a branch still takes every commit to that branch.

What follows from that:

  • fleet/ on any other branch does nothing.
  • Subdirectories other than fleet/hubs/ are ignored. fleet/prod/prod-east-1.yaml enrolls nothing.
  • Changing the repository's default branch re-points every cluster. A cluster with no file on the new default branch loses its Applications.
  • Deleting a fleet file deletes the cluster's Applications and with them its Policies on the hub. ACM then removes the policies from the cluster; what they created stays unless the template sets pruneObjectBehavior (Removal and pruning). A cluster a hub built is abandoned, not destroyed: it keeps running, unmanaged (Cluster lifecycle).

A fleet file change lands within about 6 minutes: the ApplicationSet re-reads Git every 3 minutes, and Argo CD remembers which commit a branch points to for 3 minutes. An ApplicationSet webhook makes it immediate, except the fix for a failed generation, which waits for the 3-minute retry.

items.title: One bad fleet file stops the hub
items.text:
A broken fleet file freezes generation

policystack reads the fleet files of the clusters registered on this hub. If one of them fails to parse, lacks revision, or pins a revision that doesn't exist, generation fails: no Application for any cluster on this hub is created, updated or deleted until it is fixed. Existing Applications and Policies stay as they are.

policystack-lifecycle parses every fleet/*.yaml (not fleet/hubs/) before it filters by hub, so one unparseable fleet file stops lifecycle on every hub reading the repository, and a fleet file naming this hub that lacks revision stops it on this hub. A revision that doesn't exist breaks only that cluster's lifecycle-<cluster> render.

Your repository's CI rejects these before merge (Your repository's CI). It can't catch a pinned branch deleted after merge, so pin tags, commit SHAs or protected branches. Fleet keys, quoting rules and revision forms are in Fleet files.

items.title: Your repository's CI
items.text:
On every pull request, the CI workflow runs Policy Validate, the validator, which renders every element the way the ApplicationSet does and checks the result (Validator rules, CI workflows).

Check Catches Blocks merge ci Policy Validate: invalid fleet files (POLICY050), pins that don't resolve, lack a file the fleet file uses or are on a framework major the hubs can't render (POLICY052), values keys nothing reads (POLICY035), render errors (RENDER000). Also fails if the lint hooks fail. Once a ruleset requires it pr-title PR titles that aren't Conventional Commits, such as feat: enable metallb on prod-east-1 Once a ruleset requires it Render Diff Nothing; comments each fleet cluster's Policy changes, rendering each cluster at its own revision before and after the merge Never

Nothing is required until you add a ruleset: Protect the repository.

items.title: Words with more than one meaning
items.text: hubinstallcompliance Term Meaning The hub The cluster running ACM, OpenShift GitOps and PolicyStack. ACM also manages it as a cluster, named local-cluster by default. hubName The hub's name in PolicyStack, set once at helm install. Picks fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml and values/clusters/<hubName>.yaml, and names the hub's Applications (The hub). hub: in a fleet file The hubName of the hub that builds and destroys that cluster (Cluster lifecycle). Leave it out for a cluster you import. fleet/hubs/ Hub fleet files (Fleet files). Term Meaning install/ chart helm install policystack ./install, run once per hub (Install chart). install/operators Renders ACM and OpenShift GitOps for a new hub (Installation). The install Policy The Policy an element gets when it manages operators, such as install-gitops-prod-east-1 (How an element is built). install: in a fleet file The cluster a hub builds: engine, platform, nodes (Lifecycle keys). Term Meaning Compliance state ACM's status on every Policy: Compliant, NonCompliant or Pending (ACM policies in brief). The compliance element Installs the Compliance Operator, runs scans and reports their results as the compliance state of its Policies (Compliance).

items.title: Glossary
items.text: Term Meaning Answers file .copier-answers.yml, at the repository root for the framework and in each tracked stack/<element>/. Records the upstream release tag copier copied (The repository). Application An Argo CD object that renders one source with Helm and syncs the result. PolicyStack creates <element>-<cluster> and lifecycle-<cluster>, all with the hub as destination (ApplicationSets). ApplicationSet An Argo CD object that creates Applications from generators, here from cluster secrets, fleet files and stack/* directories (ApplicationSets). Cluster secret An Argo CD Secret registering a cluster. The GitOpsCluster creates one per ManagedCluster so the ApplicationSets can list them (ApplicationSets). ConfigurationPolicy A policy template listing Kubernetes objects that must, or must not, exist on the cluster (ACM policies in brief). Converter A file stack/<element>/converters/<policy>/<template>.yaml. Its directory creates a Policy and the file one ConfigurationPolicy in it; the file's Helm output is the objects it checks or enforces (How an element is built). Day-2 Configuring a cluster that already runs, which is what elements do. Building the cluster is lifecycle. A built cluster gets Day-2 config the same way as an imported one (Day-2 handoff). Element A Helm chart stack/<element>/ that turns curated settings into the Policies for one product. Configured under stack.<elementKey> in values (How an element is built). enforce, inform A Policy's remediation action. enforce changes the cluster to match; inform only reports. Every shipped element enforces by default (ACM policies in brief). Engine How a hub builds a cluster: hypershift (hosted control plane on the hub), hive (installer on AWS, GCP, Azure or vSphere) or siteconfig (bare metal) (Cluster lifecycle). Fleet file fleet/<cluster>.yaml, or fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml for the hub, on the default branch. Enrolls the cluster and sets its revision and layers (Fleet files). Framework Everything in your repository that comes from upstream except the elements: install/, lifecycle/, lib/, tools/, the CI workflows. Versioned vX.Y.Z (Compatibility). GitOpsCluster ACM object that creates an Argo CD cluster secret per ManagedCluster; PolicyStack's is argo-acm-importer-global (ApplicationSets). Governance add-on ACM's policy controllers on each managed cluster. They pull its replicated Policies, apply or check them, and report status (ACM policies in brief). hubName See Words with more than one meaning. Layer A values file under values/ that a cluster reads, either listed in its fleet file's valueFiles or its own values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml. The root values.yaml is read before all layers. Directory names under values/ are conventions (Values cascade). Lifecycle A hub building and destroying clusters from fleet files with hub:, through Policies that run on the hub (Cluster lifecycle). ManagedCluster ACM's record of a cluster. The hub has a namespace of the same name for it, holding its replicated Policies (ACM policies in brief). Managed cluster A cluster ACM manages, imported by hand or built by a hub. It gets Applications once it has a fleet file (First cluster). OperatorPolicy A policy template that installs and upgrades one OLM operator. An element's operatorPolicies create them in its install Policy (ACM policies in brief). Placement, PlacementBinding ACM objects that choose clusters and bind Policies to them. Every PolicyStack Placement selects exactly one cluster (Placement and naming). Policy ACM's unit of compliance on the hub. It wraps one or more policy templates and carries the remediation action (ACM policies in brief). policy-library The Helm library chart every element depends on, aliased stack, in lib/policy-library. It discovers converters and renders the Policies and Placement (How an element is built). pstack The hub namespace holding every Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding PolicyStack renders (policyNamespace) (Placement and naming). Release The Application name, also the Helm release name: <element>-<cluster>, <element>-<hubName> on the hub. Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding names derive from it (Rendered names). Render Argo CD running helm template for one Application. A failed render shows as ComparisonError and changes nothing (How a change reaches a cluster). Replicated Policy ACM's copy of a Policy in the target cluster's namespace on the hub, pstack.<policy name>. Read a cluster's compliance there (ACM policies in brief). Revision The branch, tag or commit SHA a fleet file pins. All of the cluster's Applications render from it (Fleet files). Template One entry in a Policy: a ConfigurationPolicy or an OperatorPolicy (ACM policies in brief). Validator The Go tool in tools/validator that renders and checks every element in CI (Validation). Values cascade The ordered files Helm gets for one Application: the element's values.yaml, the root values.yaml, then every layer. Later files override earlier ones (Values cascade).

items.title: Placement and naming
items.text:
Every enabled element renders, for each cluster, its Policies, one Placement and one PlacementBinding, all in pstack on the hub. The Placement and PlacementBinding are named <element>-<cluster>, which is also the Helm release and the Argo CD Application name (Applications). A Placement picks clusters; a PlacementBinding attaches Policies to it (ACM policies in brief). Here every Placement picks exactly one cluster.

Rendered names lists every name an element renders; Naming limits covers how long they can be.

items.title: Placement
items.text:
The policystack ApplicationSet knows each Application's cluster from the Argo CD cluster secret it generated it from, so it writes the cluster's selector into the Application's valuesObject (Helm values inline in the Application, which outrank every values file, Order). policy-library, the Helm library chart every element depends on, turns each entry of the selector.matchExpressions map into one expression of the Placement's predicate: name In (<cluster>). ACM sets the name label on every ManagedCluster to its own name.

InjectedRendered 
# Application metallb-nonprod-west-1, spec.source.helm
valuesObject:
  selector:
    matchExpressions:
      name: {key: name, operator: In, values: ["nonprod-west-1"]}

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: metallb-nonprod-west-1
  namespace: pstack
spec:
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      labelSelector:
        matchExpressions:
        - key: name
          operator: In
          values:
          - nonprod-west-1
  tolerations: # (1)!
  - key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unreachable
    operator: Exists
  - key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unavailable
    operator: Exists
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PlacementBinding
metadata:
  name: metallb-nonprod-west-1
  namespace: pstack
placementRef:
  name: metallb-nonprod-west-1
  kind: Placement
  apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io
subjects: # (2)!
- apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Policy
  name: addressing-metallb-nonprod-west-1
- apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Policy
  name: config-metallb-nonprod-west-1
- apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Policy
  name: install-metallb-nonprod-west-1
  1. Added unless a layer sets placement.tolerations (Tolerations).
  2. Every Policy this release renders. An element that renders no Policy gets no PlacementBinding.

A Placement selects one cluster because each Application renders from that cluster's own values cascade at that cluster's own revision. Its Policies carry that cluster's settings, so they must reach that cluster and no other. Group clusters with values layers (Values cascade), never with Placement labels.

On the hub, the selector holds the hub's ManagedCluster name, usually local-cluster, while the release name uses hubName: Placement metallb-acm-dc1 selects name In (local-cluster) (The hub).

selector belongs to the ApplicationSet. A values file that sets it fails CI with POLICY035 (top-level key "selector" is read by nothing).

To see the real Placement for a cluster, check out the revision the cluster's fleet file pins, then pass the cluster's layers in fleet-file order: root values.yaml, each valueFiles entry (here environments/nonprod.yaml and datacenters/dc2.yaml), then values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml. Without the three --set lines the render fails with nil pointer evaluating interface {}.matchExpressions, because only the ApplicationSet supplies selector.

helm dependency update stack/metallb # (1)!
helm template metallb-nonprod-west-1 stack/metallb \
  -f values.yaml \
  -f values/environments/nonprod.yaml \
  -f values/datacenters/dc2.yaml \
  -f values/clusters/nonprod-west-1.yaml \
  --set selector.matchExpressions.name.key=name \
  --set selector.matchExpressions.name.operator=In \
  --set 'selector.matchExpressions.name.values={nonprod-west-1}'
  1. Packages lib/policy-library into the gitignored charts/. Re-run it after a change to lib/.

The validator's preview (make -C tools/validator preview ELEMENT=<element>, Preview) supplies operator: Exists instead, so its Placement selects every cluster. The preview is meant to do that.

items.title: Tolerations
items.text:
The default tolerations keep a cluster's Policies bound while ACM taints it unreachable (stopped reporting) or unavailable (reports itself unavailable), so an outage changes nothing. Without them:

  1. The Placement drops the cluster and ACM removes its Policies.
  2. When the cluster reconnects, it deletes them locally, then they come back.
  3. Templates with pruneObjectBehavior delete their objects on reconnect and recreate them when the Policies return (Removal and pruning). Without prune (the default) the objects stay, but the cluster drops out of the hub's compliance view while offline.

Keep them. placement.tolerations: [] in any layer removes them, and nothing validates it.

items.title: Cluster sets
items.text:
A Placement only selects clusters from ManagedClusterSets bound to its own namespace by a ManagedClusterSetBinding. ACM's built-in set global contains every ManagedCluster. The install chart creates ManagedClusterSetBinding global in pstack, and keeps it on uninstall so removing PolicyStack doesn't unbind Placements still in use. If it is missing, every Placement selects nothing and no Policy reaches any cluster, while Argo CD still shows every Application Synced.

Check with oc get managedclustersetbinding global -n pstack. Without it, each Placement's PlacementSatisfied condition is False with reason NoManagedClusterSetBindings. A helm upgrade of the install chart recreates it.

items.title: Overriding the Placement
items.text:
A top-level placement: key in any values layer merges into the generated spec (policy-library Placement). It applies to every element's Placement for every cluster reading that layer. POLICY080 checks the rendered Placement against its CRD (unknown fields, types), but nothing checks what the keys do, so a wrong selector shows up only on the hub.

Key Effect claimSelector, celSelector ANDed into the generated predicate. Can only narrow the selection to this cluster or to nothing, so use them as a guard, such as "only on AWS clusters". predicates Appended as extra predicates, which ACM ORs with the generated one. Almost always a mistake (below). tolerations Replaces the default tolerations. Any other Placement.spec field Passed through. Fields such as numberOfClusters or spreadPolicy change nothing with one cluster. 
# values/platforms/aws.yaml: only place Policies on clusters that really are AWS
placement:
  claimSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: platform.open-cluster-management.io, operator: In, values: [AWS]}

If the guard excludes the cluster, its Policies stop reaching it, which is a removal (Removal and pruning).

placement.predicates sends one cluster's Policies to other clusters

# values/environments/prod.yaml: wrong
placement:
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels: {environment: prod}

Every Application that reads this layer renders a Placement with two predicates, name In (<its cluster>) OR environment=prod. Each prod cluster then also receives every other prod cluster's Policies, built from their values. Their template names collide with its own, which ACM rejects (Template name must be unique).

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text: The lifecycle-<cluster> Application's Policies build a cluster by creating objects on the hub, so its Placement selects the ManagedCluster of the hub that the fleet file's hub: names, not the cluster being built (Cluster lifecycle). The policystack-lifecycle ApplicationSet injects that selector, as for elements.

items.title: Where Policies live
items.text:
Argo CD creates every Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding in pstack on the hub, the policyNamespace set in the root values.yaml. The install chart creates the namespace and keeps it on uninstall. ACM then copies each Policy to every cluster its Placement selects (ACM policies in brief):

Copy Cluster Namespace Name Look with Root Policy, from Git Hub pstack <policy>-<release> oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack Replicated Policy Hub <cluster>, local-cluster for the hub pstack.<policy>-<release> oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n <cluster> Policy and its ConfigurationPolicies, OperatorPolicies Managed cluster <cluster>, local-cluster on the hub Policy as above; ConfigurationPolicy <policy>-<template>, OperatorPolicy install-<key> oc get configurationpolicies,operatorpolicies -n <cluster>

Leave policyNamespace at pstack. Changing it renames every Policy, which deletes and recreates all of them (Removal and pruning), and shifts the name budget below. install/values.yaml must hold the same value, because the install chart creates that namespace and binds the global cluster set into it; CI fails POLICY071 if the two differ.

items.title: Naming limits
items.text:
ACM names the replicated copy <policyNamespace>.<policy>-<release>. Its admission webhook rejects a root Policy whose namespace and name together exceed 62 characters (63 with the dot), so Argo CD's sync fails with the combined length of the policy namespace and name cannot exceed 62 characters and the Policy is never created. CI fails POLICY001 before merge. A ManagedCluster can't be renamed, so a cluster name that is too long means re-importing it under a shorter one.

pstack.addressing-metallb-nonprod-west-1
│      │          │       └ cluster: you choose it
│      │          └ element: fixed by the element
│      └ policy: fixed by the element
└ policyNamespace (7 with the dot, leaves 56)
Policy Replicated name Characters install pstack.install-metallb-nonprod-west-1 37 config pstack.config-metallb-nonprod-west-1 36 addressing pstack.addressing-metallb-nonprod-west-1 40

Keep cluster names and hubName to 30 characters

You only control the last part. hubName counts because it takes the cluster's place in the hub's release names. The longest policy and element pair shipped today, pstack.ingress-cert-cert-manager-, is 33 characters, which leaves 30. Element authors keep to that: an element name is at most 17 characters, policy plus element at most 24 (Naming).

CI (POLICY001) checks every element against a 30-character cluster name, and your fleet files against the elements each one enables (Fixtures). No check rejects a long cluster name by itself, so a 35-character cluster passes until a PR enables a longer-named element.

items.title: Template and lifecycle names
items.text:
ConfigurationPolicy and OperatorPolicy names carry no cluster name, so cluster length doesn't affect them. They must still be unique across every Policy on one cluster: Policy names such as config, install and ready are shared by many elements, so authors pick distinctive template names (metallb-instance, not instance), and CI fails a clash between two elements (POLICY003, Rendered names). They are also capped at 63 characters (POLICY001).

The exception is lifecycle/: it places one release per built cluster on the hub, so it appends the cluster (suffixTemplateNames): present-credentials-<cluster>. Its longest names, pstack.present-lifecycle-<cluster> and present-credentials-<cluster>, fit a 38-character cluster, but a built cluster also gets element Applications once imported (Cluster lifecycle), so keep it to 30.

items.title: Removal and pruning
items.text:
"Prune" means two different things in PolicyStack:

Argo CD prune ACM pruneObjectBehavior Where it acts Hub Managed cluster What it deletes Hub objects that left the render: Policies, Placement, PlacementBinding Objects a ConfigurationPolicy manages: Namespaces, Deployments, CRs Set by The ApplicationSet (prune: true on every Application) You, per template. Off by default.

Argo CD prune always runs. ACM prune is off unless you set it, and no shipped element or lifecycle engine sets it. By default, removing a policy, a template, an element or a cluster's fleet file leaves every object it created on the managed cluster. The procedures are in Rolling out changes.

items.title: The deletion chain
items.text:
Each step runs in a different controller, and each has a place to check:

  1. Argo CD deletes Policy <policy>-<release> from pstack on the hub, or updates it without the removed template. oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack
  2. ACM on the hub deletes the replicated copy pstack.<policy>-<release> from the cluster's namespace on the hub, or updates it. oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n <cluster>
  3. The governance add-on on the managed cluster deletes its copy and the ConfigurationPolicies and OperatorPolicies inside it, or only the removed template. oc get configurationpolicies,operatorpolicies -n <cluster> on the managed cluster
  4. The config-policy controller on the managed cluster deletes the objects those ConfigurationPolicies managed, only if pruneObjectBehavior allows it. Otherwise the objects stay, unmanaged.

Argo CD never deletes the replicated copies itself: it doesn't track them (copyPolicyMetadata: false, Deletion).

items.title: Everyday removals
items.text:
Most removals change what one Application renders. The Application stays; Argo CD prunes what left the render. Renaming an element replaces the Application (What deletes an Application).

Change Hub Managed cluster Element enabled: false Every Policy, the Placement and the PlacementBinding are pruned. The Application stays, with zero resources (allowEmpty). Every Policy of the element is removed. Policy enabled: false, or its converters/<policy>/ deleted together with its policies.<policy> entry in the element's values.yaml and every layer That Policy is pruned. That Policy and its templates are removed. Template enabled: false, or its converter file deleted together with its templates.<template> entry The Policy is updated without it; if it was the Policy's last enabled template, the Policy is pruned. That ConfigurationPolicy is removed. An object drops out of a template's output: an entry removed from a config map, an {{- if }} that stops emitting it, a renamed metadata.name The Policy is updated. The ConfigurationPolicy stays; that object is no longer managed. With prune set, it is deleted. Renamed policy Old Policy pruned, new one created. Old ConfigurationPolicy removed, new one created. With prune set, the objects are deleted and recreated. Renamed template The Policy is updated: the old ConfigurationPolicy is removed and a new one created. Old ConfigurationPolicy removed, new one created. With prune set, the objects are deleted and recreated.

ACM prune fires when a policy change stops managing an object, not only when the policy is deleted. In metallb, the pools template emits one IPAddressPool per config.ipAddressPools entry; on a template like that with prune set, deleting an entry deletes that object on the cluster. (metallb itself can't set prune: every template waits on something, and the CI check POLICY033 rejects prune there.)

A file deleted while values still name it fails the render (has no file). A render that fails removes nothing: the Application shows ComparisonError, Argo CD neither syncs nor prunes, and the cluster keeps the last Policies it had (Applications).

items.title: What deletes an Application
items.text:
Every 3 minutes the policystack ApplicationSet regenerates one Application for each stack/<element> directory, for each cluster that has a fleet file, read at that cluster's revision (ApplicationSets). It deletes an Application it no longer generates, and the Application's finalizer deletes its Policies, Placement and PlacementBinding first (Deletion). Any of these deletes an Application:

Trigger See The cluster's revision no longer has stack/<element>. Clusters pinned to older revisions keep it until their pin moves. Removing an element Fleet file deleted, or renamed, which is the same as deleting it: the file name must equal the ManagedCluster name. Offboarding a cluster stack/<element> renamed, or hubName changed. The Application name changes, so the old one is deleted and a new one created. The hub Global Hub only: a managed hub's deploy-mode label, which makes the global hub read its fleet file from fleet/hubs/, is removed. Its Day-2 Applications are deleted unless fleet/<hub>.yaml exists, and every lifecycle-<cluster> Application with hub: <hub> is deleted, abandoning those clusters. Global Hub Cluster detached. ACM's GitOpsCluster deletes its Argo CD cluster secret, which the ApplicationSet lists clusters from. ApplicationSets The Argo CD cluster secret or its clusterID label disappears, for example during an ACM upgrade. Pausing removals ApplicationSet deleted Teardown

applicationsSync: create-update on the ApplicationSet pauses every row except deleting the ApplicationSet; creates and updates continue (Pausing removals). Don't rename an element or hubName while paused: the old Policies stay next to the new ones and their template names collide.

A broken fleet file deletes nothing: it stops all generation on the hub until fixed (One bad fleet file stops the hub).

items.title: What happens on the managed cluster
items.text:
When the cluster deletes a ConfigurationPolicy (step 3 of the chain), the controller acts on the version it last received (step 4). It deletes the objects only if pruneObjectBehavior is not None and the Policy enforces and the template isn't InformOnly (inform, enforce and InformOnly).

Case Effect None (default), or the Policy is inform Everything stays. Fields that musthave or mustonlyhave changed on objects that existed before keep their last enforced values; nothing reverts them. DeleteIfCreated Deletes the objects this ConfigurationPolicy created, as recorded in its status. One recreated while its objects still exist (cluster re-imported, or a rename made while prune was off) records them as pre-existing and later deletes nothing. DeleteAll Deletes every object the template manages, including ones that existed before the policy, such as a shared namespace. A deleted Namespace takes every workload and PVC in it. OperatorPolicy pruneObjectBehavior doesn't apply. Operator, CSV, CRDs and CRs stay. With versions pinned or upgradeApproval: None (OperatorPolicy), the OperatorPolicy left the Subscription on manual InstallPlan approval, so with the policy gone nothing approves upgrades and they stop. Unpinned, OLM keeps upgrading along the channel. To uninstall, see Stopping and uninstalling. Cluster detached, or governance add-on removed Nothing is deleted: the controller that would prune is gone. Cluster disconnected when the Policy is removed Prunes when it reconnects.

Gatekeeper constraints in a converter follow the rows above; ACM's Gatekeeper-specific removal rule doesn't apply, because they're wrapped in a ConfigurationPolicy.

items.title: Setting prune
items.text:
Set it per template in a values layer; it works whatever shape the converter has (Converter shapes).

stack:
  <element>:
    policies:
      <policy>:
        templates:
          <template>:
            pruneObjectBehavior: DeleteIfCreated

Prune deletes live objects

  • Set it in its own commit, and remove the policy only after that commit reached the cluster. "Reached" is per cluster: in its pinned revision, synced, and replicated. Check with oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io pstack.<policy>-<release> -n <cluster> -o yaml | grep pruneObjectBehavior on the hub. If prune and the removal land together, the cluster never sees prune and deletes nothing.
  • Renames delete and recreate. Renaming an element, policy, template or hubName, or changing policyNamespace, deletes the old ConfigurationPolicy and its objects, then recreates the objects from scratch. Data in a deleted PVC, namespace or CR is gone.
  • Keep the Placement's default tolerations. With placement.tolerations: [], a cluster that drops off the network loses its Policies and prunes on reconnect, then gets them back: a network blip becomes an outage (Tolerations).

POLICY033 fails CI on prune that can't work or would fire by accident (Validator rules):

  • Any dependency. ACM deletes a waiting template whenever its dependency is unmet (Dependencies and ignorePending), so prune would delete its objects every time, for example during each operator upgrade. Waiting keys: Waiting and ordering.
  • Not enforced. ACM prunes only under enforce. Not flagged while a dry run forces inform.
  • DeleteAll is a warning, reported without failing CI: prefer DeleteIfCreated.

If you add prune in your repository, never add it to stack/cim or lifecycle/: deleting the AgentServiceConfig deletes the assisted-service volumes, and deleting a lifecycle Policy must never delete a cluster.

items.title: Deleting objects without prune
items.text:
Turn the template into a deletion first, then remove it:

  1. Set stack.<element>.policies.<policy>.templates.<template>.complianceType: mustnothave under an enforced Policy:

    # values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  metallb:
    policies:
      config:
        templates:
          metallb-instance:
            complianceType: mustnothave

  2. Wait until pstack.config-metallb-prod-east-1 is Compliant in namespace prod-east-1 on the hub: the objects are gone. Every cluster must reach that state at its own pin before you go on.

  3. Disable or delete the template.

Warning

If the template includes the Namespace, mustnothave deletes it and everything in it.

This only works for converters that emit plain documents. Open the converter: if it emits - complianceType: entries, it is a raw list, and the values key is ignored without an error (acs central hub-access is). For those, disable the template and delete the objects with oc delete. For operators, use the OperatorPolicy's own mustnothave (Stopping and uninstalling).

items.title: Values cascade
items.text: Everything a cluster runs is set in plain Helm values files under values/, called layers. Each cluster has a fleet file, fleet/<cluster>.yaml, that names the Git revision it runs and the layers it gets (Fleet files). Argo CD renders every element (one product's configuration, packaged as a Helm chart under stack/; How an element is built) for that cluster with the same ordered list. Later files win.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
A layer is an ordinary Helm values file anywhere under values/. Nothing is matched by name, label or directory: a cluster gets a layer only when its fleet file lists it in valueFiles, as a path relative to values/.

# fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
revision: main
valueFiles:              # lowest precedence first
  - environments/prod.yaml
  - datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - platforms/aws.yaml
  • Directories are conventions. environments/, datacenters/, platforms/, tenants/ and acm/ mean nothing to the tooling. Add values/regions/emea.yaml and list it, and it works the same way.
  • Only values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml is special. <cluster> is the fleet file's name, which is the ManagedCluster name (a hub uses its hubName, see the Hub tab under Order). The file is appended to every cluster's list automatically, always last, so it overrides every shared layer. Create it only for clusters that change something.
  • One file configures many elements. Each element, enabled or not, gets its own Application per cluster, named <element>-<cluster>. A disabled one syncs nothing. Every Application receives the full list. An element reads only its own stack.<elementKey> block plus the shared top-level keys, so values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml turns on infraNodes, machineHealth and userMonitoring in one file.
  • Elements are off until a layer turns them on. Every element ships enabled: false except upgrade, which renders nothing until the fleet file sets channel or version, or a layer sets stack.upgrade.config.upstream (OpenShift upgrades). Inside an enabled element it is the reverse: every policy, template and operator is on unless the merged values set enabled: false (What renders).

Which revision a layer is read at

Fleet files are read at HEAD of the default branch. The element charts and every values file are read at the fleet file's revision (Fleet files). An edit to values/environments/prod.yaml therefore reaches only the clusters that list it and pin a revision containing the commit. A cluster pinned to a tag or SHA does not see a later edit, not even to its own values/clusters/ file, until its pin moves (Promoting and rolling back).

items.title: What goes in a layer
items.text:
Top-level key Read by What it does stack Elements One block per element, keyed by the element's chart name in camelCase: cert-manager is stack.certManager, infra-nodes is stack.infraNodes. Holds enabled, config, policies, operatorPolicies and default (How an element is built). global Every element and lifecycle/ Fleet-wide switches: dry run and catalog remapping (Global keys). placement Every element and lifecycle/ Extra settings merged into every Placement they render, the lifecycle Placement on the hub included (Placement). Never set placement.predicates: ACM ORs it with the cluster selector and sends this cluster's Policies to other clusters. A claimSelector guard (Overriding the Placement) in a layer that a built cluster lists also narrows its lifecycle Placement, so it must match the hub too. install lifecycle/ only Defaults for clusters a hub builds (Install keys). Elements never read it, so a cluster you imported into ACM yourself, rather than one a hub built, can list platforms/aws.yaml. Its install block goes unused. policyNamespace Every element Set once in the repo root values.yaml: pstack, the hub namespace every Policy goes in. Don't change it: install/ creates the namespace from its own copy in install/values.yaml, so if the two differ the Policies target a namespace that doesn't exist. The validator (tools/validator, which CI runs on every pull request; Validation) fails POLICY071 when they differ. version, channel The upgrade element, from the fleet file only Rejected in a layer (POLICY034, why). Set them in the fleet file. selector policy-library, injected by the ApplicationSet (Order) Rejected in a layer (POLICY035). If merged anyway, it narrows every Placement. policystack policy-library, injected by the ApplicationSet (Order) Rejected in a layer (POLICY035).

Any other top-level key is rejected by the validator (POLICY035).

Element settings sit under stack because policy-library, the shared chart that renders the Policies and runs in the element's own context, reads .Values.stack.<elementKey>. Each element's Chart.yaml adds the library with alias: stack, so Helm checks that key against the library's values schema.

# values/clusters/nonprod-west-1.yaml
stack:
  metallb:
    enabled: true            # turns the element on
    policies:
      addressing:
        enabled: true        # turns on a policy the element ships off
  userMonitoring:
    enabled: true
    config:
      prometheus:
        retention: 72h       # a converter setting

items.title: Order
items.text:
The policystack ApplicationSet on the hub (an Argo CD object that generates one Application per element per cluster from the fleet files; ApplicationSets) builds each Application's spec.source.helm. You never write it yourself; you write the fleet file and the layers. Below is what Argo CD hands Helm, lowest precedence first.

Managed clusterHubLifecycle

Application infra-nodes-prod-east-1, generated from the fleet file above plus channel: stable-4.20:

valueFiles:
  - values.yaml                             # (1)!
  - ../../values.yaml                       # (2)!
  - ../../values/environments/prod.yaml     # (3)!
  - ../../values/datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - ../../values/platforms/aws.yaml
  - ../../values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml  # (4)!
valuesObject:                               # (5)!
  channel: "stable-4.20"                    # (6)!
  policystack:
    libraryMajors: [4]                      # (7)!
  selector:                                 # (8)!
    matchExpressions:
      name: {key: name, operator: In, values: ["prod-east-1"]}
  1. The element's defaults, stack/infra-nodes/values.yaml. Paths are relative to the element directory.
  2. The repo root values.yaml, read by every Application of every cluster. It holds only policyNamespace. Keep it that way: put fleet-wide settings in a layer every fleet file lists, so a cluster can leave it out.
  3. One entry per valueFiles entry, in list order. Nothing sorts them.
  4. Always appended, always last, named after the ManagedCluster. Skipped when it doesn't exist (Missing files).
  5. Injected values. Argo CD ranks valuesObject above every file, so no layer can override these keys. Nothing else is injected: an element that needs to know the environment reads a key that environments/<env>.yaml sets.
  6. version and channel, only when the fleet file sets them. The upgrade element reads them (OpenShift upgrades).
  7. The policy-library majors this hub's install chart supports, set in install/templates/_helpers.tpl, not by you. policy-library fails the render when the revision's library major isn't listed, so a pin to a revision built for another major shows a ComparisonError that names the fix instead of rendering under ApplicationSets it wasn't built for (Library changes). A plain helm template sets nothing and checks nothing.
  8. policy-library turns this into the selector of each Placement the element renders, so its Policies reach this one cluster (Placement). It is a map, so Helm would merge a layer's selector entries into it, ANDed with name. No layer can change name, because valuesObject outranks every file.

ACM registers the hub as a ManagedCluster of itself, named local-cluster and labeled local-cluster. Every hub gets that name by default, so the name can't tell hubs apart. For that cluster the ApplicationSet uses hubName instead, the name you gave this hub at install (--set hubName=): it reads fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml instead of fleet/<cluster>.yaml, and uses hubName where it would use the cluster name in two places: the Application name and the cluster values file (The hub). The Placement selector still uses the ManagedCluster name, local-cluster unless ACM's localClusterName changes it.

# fleet/hubs/acm-dc1.yaml
revision: main
valueFiles:
  - environments/prod.yaml
  - datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - platforms/baremetal.yaml
  - acm/acm-dc1.yaml         # (1)!
  1. Listed by hand, like any layer. acm/ is a convention for hub-only settings, such as the acm and gitops elements that manage the hub's own ACM and Argo CD.
# Application nfd-acm-dc1: element nfd, which values/clusters/acm-dc1.yaml enables on this hub
valueFiles:
  - values.yaml
  - ../../values.yaml
  - ../../values/environments/prod.yaml
  - ../../values/datacenters/dc1.yaml
  - ../../values/platforms/baremetal.yaml
  - ../../values/acm/acm-dc1.yaml
  - ../../values/clusters/acm-dc1.yaml   # never clusters/local-cluster.yaml
valuesObject:
  policystack:
    libraryMajors: [4]
  selector:
    matchExpressions:
      name: {key: name, operator: In, values: ["local-cluster"]}

Only for clusters a hub builds; skip this tab if you import your clusters. A fleet file that sets hub (the hubName of the hub that should build this cluster) gets a lifecycle Application, lifecycle-<cluster>, which builds the cluster on that hub (Cluster lifecycle). It reads the same layers, relative to lifecycle/: values.yaml, ../values.yaml, ../values/<entry> for each valueFiles entry, then ../values/clusters/<fleet file name>.yaml. The cluster file is always named after the fleet file: the hubName swap from the Hub tab never applies.

The injected valuesObject also carries the fleet file's lifecycle keys.

valuesObject:
  hub: "acm-dc1"
  state: "present"   # (1)!
  version: "4.20.8"  # (2)!
  install: {}        # (3)!
  policystack:
    libraryMajors: [4]
  selector:
    matchExpressions:
      hub:           # (4)!
        key: name
        operator: In
        values:
          - "local-cluster"
  1. present when the fleet file sets no state.
  2. channel too, when set.
  3. The fleet file's install, {} when it sets none. It ranks above every layer and merges into their install key by key: platforms/agent.yaml sets the platform and credential, and the fleet file adds install.nodePools.
  4. The hub that builds the cluster, not the cluster itself (Placement: Lifecycle).

lifecycle/ reads install and, under stack, only the block of the engine install.engine picks (stack.hive, stack.hypershift or stack.siteconfig), so one cluster file can hold both halves:

# values/clusters/hcp-agent.yaml
install: ...   # lifecycle/ builds the cluster
stack: ...     # elements configure it once it is imported

The schema still checks the whole stack key in lifecycle/ too, so a typo in an element block fails the lifecycle Application as well (Schema).

items.title: Worked example
items.text:
The layers for prod-east-1 merge into this stack.infraNodes, trimmed:

enabled: true                 # clusters/prod-east-1.yaml, default false
policies:
  aws:
    enabled: true             # platforms/aws.yaml, default false
  vmware:
    enabled: false            # platforms/aws.yaml and element default
  workloads:
    enabled: false            # element default
  restore:
    enabled: false            # element default
config:
  replicas: 1                 # clusters/prod-east-1.yaml, default 3
  zones:                      # clusters/prod-east-1.yaml, replaces default [] (lists replace, see Merge rules)
    - us-east-1a
    - us-east-1b
    - us-east-1c
  instanceType: m6i.2xlarge   # clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
  maxPods: 250                # element default

Application infra-nodes-prod-east-1 renders, in pstack on the hub, Placement and PlacementBinding infra-nodes-prod-east-1 and Policies mcp-infra-nodes-prod-east-1, config-infra-nodes-prod-east-1, aws-infra-nodes-prod-east-1 and ready-infra-nodes-prod-east-1. vmware, workloads and restore render nothing because the merged values leave them enabled: false. Where those names come from: Rendered names.

items.title: Missing files
items.text:
Every Application sets ignoreMissingValueFiles: true: Argo CD skips any listed file that doesn't exist at the cluster's revision. It has to, because values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml is appended for every cluster and most clusters have none. The price is that a typo or a file the pinned revision lacks is skipped too.

A skipped file raises no error

The Application stays Synced and Healthy and renders from the remaining layers. What you see depends on what the lost file did:

  • It turned something on: that piece never appears.
  • It turned something off: the shared layer wins. If values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml sets remediations.enabled: false and is skipped, remediations from environments/prod.yaml keeps enforcing.
