Every cluster gets cluster-registration-secret, then the element's SecuredCluster settings merge into yours; the hub's Central gets the element's Central settings, auth config and SecurityPolicies the same way. Any field that differs changes at that point: admission control enforcement turns off unless config.admissionControl.enabled: true.
  5. Wait until central-crs-ready, secured-tls and secured-agents-ready are Compliant everywhere.

Keep the old secrets

Leave sensor-tls, collector-tls and admission-control-tls on every cluster, and let the old init bundle expire rather than revoking it: revoking cuts off every cluster still using its certificates. They are the cluster's only credentials until cluster-registration-secret exists; deleting them first fails Sensor with InitBundleSecretsMissingError.

items.title: Compliance
items.text:
The compliance element installs the Compliance Operator, scans the cluster against a benchmark (DISA STIG by default), and reports failed checks in Governance: one Policy per cluster, findings-compliance-<cluster>, with one template per severity that turns NonCompliant and names the failed results (Reading Governance). Optionally it applies the operator's fixes.

Two meanings of compliance

Every ACM policy has a compliance state (Compliant, NonCompliant, Pending; see ACM policies in brief). This element turns benchmark scan results into such states.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
# values/environments/prod.yaml
stack:
  compliance:
    enabled: true

Defaults (README):

Key under stack.compliance.config Default profiles [ocp4-stig, ocp4-stig-node, rhcos4-stig] binding stig, the ScanSettingBinding's name, whatever the profiles rawResultStorage On, default StorageClass waivers, remediations Empty

Without a default StorageClass, set rawResultStorage.storageClass or rawResultStorage.enabled: false. Otherwise the raw-results PVC stays Pending and scans never finish.

Scans run on the operator's own default ScanSetting schedule: daily, on master and worker nodes. Remediation is off (Remediations).

Hosted control planes

Red Hat ships the operator on HCP as Technology Preview, with PLATFORM=HyperShift set in the Subscription's config and a worker nodeSelector. This element sets neither, so a hosted cluster (HCP guest) can't scan and shows NonCompliant in findings-scan-state. Leave the element off there.

items.title: How a scan works
items.text:
The element writes the rows marked Element, plus spec.apply on declared remediations (Remediations); the operator does the rest.

Object Created by What it is Profile Operator content A benchmark, shipped in the operator's content. Platform profiles (ocp4-stig) check the cluster's API objects; node profiles (ocp4-stig-node, rhcos4-stig) check each node ScanSetting default Operator; the element patches storage only How and when to scan. Its schedule and roles stay the operator's Role, RoleBinding compliance-operator-agg-patch-* Element Lets the operator's remediation aggregator update ComplianceRemediations ScanSettingBinding (ssb) <binding> Element Binds the profiles to the setting. Creating it starts the first scan ComplianceSuite <binding> Operator Groups the binding's scans ComplianceScan Operator One per profile, and one per role for node profiles: ocp4-stig, ocp4-stig-node-master, rhcos4-stig-worker ComplianceCheckResult (ccr) Operator One rule's result in one scan, named <scan>-<rule>. Status PASS, FAIL, ERROR, MANUAL, INCONSISTENT and others. The rule's own name is on annotation compliance.openshift.io/rule ComplianceRemediation Operator The fix for a failed result that has one, named like the result

Each rule has three names:

Example Rule (annotation compliance.openshift.io/rule) sysctl-kernel-dmesg-restrict Results rhcos4-stig-master-sysctl-kernel-dmesg-restrict, rhcos4-stig-worker-sysctl-kernel-dmesg-restrict Remediations The same names as the results

Waivers take the rule name. Remediations take the remediation name. Governance shows result names.

items.title: What it creates
items.text:
<cluster> is the ManagedCluster name, or hubName on the hub (Rendered names). findings only reports and never changes the cluster; the other Policies enforce, apart from their -status and -state checks.

Policy Templates Waits for install-compliance-<cluster> install-compliance-ns, install-compliance (OperatorPolicy, package compliance-operator, channel stable), install-compliance-status (The install Policy) scan-compliance-<cluster> scan-setting: ScanSetting, the RBAC the operator's remediation aggregator needs, and the ScanSettingBinding install-compliance-<cluster> Compliant findings-compliance-<cluster> findings-scan-state, -high, -medium, -low, -waived, -drift scan-compliance-<cluster> Compliant remediate-compliance-<cluster> remediate-remediations, remediate-remediation-state. Only with policies.remediate.enabled: true scan-compliance-<cluster> Compliant

So findings shows Pending right after you enable the element, until the operator is installed and the binding is written. Then findings-scan-state is NonCompliant, because no results exist yet, until the first scan finishes.

items.title: Reading Governance
items.text:
In the console: Governance > Policies > findings-compliance-<cluster>, then a template.

Template Policy NonCompliant means findings-scan-state findings-compliance-<cluster> No suite or no results yet, a configured Profile doesn't exist, or a scan ended ERROR, NOT-AVAILABLE or NOT-APPLICABLE or hasn't started in 48 hours (often a cordoned node). oc get compliancescan -n openshift-compliance shows which findings-high, -medium, -low findings-compliance-<cluster> Results with that severity that failed and aren't waived. -low takes every severity other than high and medium, unset included. See below for ERROR and INCONSISTENT findings-drift findings-compliance-<cluster> A ComplianceRemediation is applied (spec.apply: true) but not declared true in config.remediations findings-waived findings-compliance-<cluster> Never. Lists each result of a waived rule with its current status remediate-remediation-state remediate-compliance-<cluster> A declared remediation hasn't reached its state. The message lists each as <name>=<applicationState>, missing when it doesn't exist

findings-scan-state has no custom message, so it shows ACM's own. compliancescans [<scan>] found but not as specified is a bad scan; its diff shows phase: Healthy, a phase no scan reaches, asserted only to flag it. compliancecheckresults not found means no results yet.

What counts as a finding:

  • FAIL, unless the rule is waived.
  • ERROR, even when waived: the check didn't run, so there is nothing to waive.
  • INCONSISTENT, which means the nodes of one role disagreed. It counts only when a node failed (unless waived) or errored, because most are NOT-APPLICABLE on some nodes.
  • Never MANUAL: the operator can't check it. Review those yourself: oc get ccr -n openshift-compliance -l compliance.openshift.io/check-status=MANUAL.

A findings message is the count, then the result names: 2 findings: ocp4-stig-api-server-audit-log-maxsize, rhcos4-stig-worker-sysctl-kernel-dmesg-restrict. With none, No findings.

Names are truncated

ACM 2.15+ caps a message at 4096 bytes, ending in ...[truncated]. Names sort, so rhcos4-* is cut first. The count stays right. For the full list, use View details > Related resources on the template.

For the raw results, which also include waived rules and harmless INCONSISTENT ones:

oc get ccr -n openshift-compliance -l 'compliance.openshift.io/check-status in (FAIL,ERROR,INCONSISTENT)'

items.title: Timing
items.text:
A rescan keeps the last results, so findings stay visible while it runs. After a failed scan they are stale until a good one.

The findings templates re-evaluate as soon as results change. findings-scan-state can't, because a scan getting old fires no event: it polls hourly while Compliant and every 10 minutes while not, so a failed or stale scan takes up to an hour to show.

To scan now instead of waiting for the schedule, use Red Hat's rescan annotation:

oc -n openshift-compliance annotate compliancescans/<scan> compliance.openshift.io/rescan=

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
config.profiles takes any mix. They share one binding, schedule and suite, and result names carry the scan, so they don't collide.

stack:
  compliance:
    config:
      profiles: [ocp4-cis, ocp4-cis-node, ocp4-stig, ocp4-stig-node, rhcos4-stig]

profiles is a list, so a layer's list replaces the default whole (Merge rules): [ocp4-cis] alone drops STIG. A misspelt profile makes findings-scan-state NonCompliant.

Replacing a profile

Dropping a profile deletes its scan, results, remediations and raw-results PVC. Applied MachineConfigs, KubeletConfig settings and created objects stay behind. Set its remediations to false and roll out before you drop it; for KubeletConfig see Reverting.

Leave config.binding alone when you change profiles. A new name writes a second ScanSettingBinding, the old one is never deleted and keeps scanning, and the findings read only the new one. If you rename it, delete the old one: oc delete ssb <old> -n openshift-compliance.

items.title: Pinning
items.text:
Keep the floating profile names (ocp4-stig, not ocp4-stig-v2r3). Red Hat supports only the latest CIS and STIG, a versioned name doesn't freeze its rules, and operator upgrades remove old versions.

The operator version freezes the content. Pin its CSV in each cluster's own layer, so a content bump, which can change results and remediations, reaches one cluster at a time (Operator versions):

# values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  compliance:
    operatorPolicies:
      compliance:
        versions:
          - <installed CSV> # (1)!
        subscription:
          startingCSV: <installed CSV>
  1. oc get csv -n openshift-compliance.

A bump can change results:

  • A rule dropped from the content loses its result and remediation, but an applied MachineConfig stays. The operator names them 75-<remediation>; find leftovers with oc get mc | grep ^75-.

  • A remediation whose fix changed is marked Outdated and keeps its old payload. It shows in remediate-remediation-state. To move it to the new payload, remove the old one. It may roll nodes:

    oc -n openshift-compliance patch complianceremediations <name> --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/outdated"}]'

Don't use Red Hat's compliance.openshift.io/apply-remediations annotation: it applies every remediation in the suite, bypassing config.remediations.

items.title: Waivers
items.text:
A waiver accepts a failed rule. The rule keeps being scanned, so the raw FAIL stays on the cluster and in the raw results (ARF, the XML reports in the raw-results PVC) as evidence; the waiver only stops it counting as a finding. git log records who approved it.

stack:
  compliance:
    config:
      waivers:
        api-server-audit-log-maxsize: "Logs ship off-cluster. SEC-1234" # (1)!
  1. The rule name, not the result name Governance shows: oc get ccr -n openshift-compliance <result> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.compliance\.openshift\.io/rule}'.

A waiver covers every result of that rule on the cluster, in every role and profile, and moves them from findings-high/-medium/-low to findings-waived. It takes effect at the next evaluation, with no rescan.

You set Result A result name (starts ocp4- or rhcos4-) Render fails: stack.compliance.config.waivers.<name> is a result name: use its compliance.openshift.io/rule annotation An empty reason Render fails: stack.compliance.config.waivers.<rule> needs a reason A misspelt rule name Nothing. It waives nothing; check that findings-waived lists it null in a later layer (listed after it, or the cluster's own file) Removes the waiver for the clusters reading that layer

To waive on some clusters only, put the waiver in their layer. To lift an environment's waiver on one cluster, set the rule to null in that cluster's file.

Limits

  • The reason stays in Git. Governance doesn't show it.
  • oc get compliancesuite -n openshift-compliance still says NON-COMPLIANT, since the operator doesn't know about waivers.
  • Waivers don't expire. A waived rule that passed and fails again raises nothing; its entry in the findings-waived message just changes, e.g. ocp4-stig-api-server-audit-log-maxsize=FAIL.

To stop scanning a rule, Red Hat documents TailoredProfile disableRules. It removes the evidence, and it isn't part of this element.

items.title: Remediations
items.text:
For each failed rule that has an automated fix, the operator creates a ComplianceRemediation; list them with oc get complianceremediations -n openshift-compliance. Nothing is applied until you turn on policy remediate and declare each one:

stack:
  compliance:
    policies:
      remediate:
        enabled: true
    config:
      remediations:
        ocp4-stig-api-server-encryption-provider-cipher: true # (1)!
        rhcos4-stig-worker-sysctl-kernel-dmesg-restrict: false # (2)!
  1. Applies it. When one fix needs several objects the operator creates <name>, <name>-1, <name>-2. List the base name: the operator sets the rest of the family to match. Two of a family with different values fail the render.
  2. Reverts it.

true sets the remediation's spec.apply, and the operator applies the payload: a MachineConfig (the Machine Config Operator then reboots that pool's nodes), a KubeletConfig, or an object it creates or patches. The result turns PASS only after the next scan.

  • Both remediate templates do nothing while a scan runs, because the operator rewrites remediations mid-scan: remediate-remediation-state reads Compliant until every scan is DONE.
  • A name that doesn't exist is never created. remediate-remediation-state reports a true one as missing, unless its result passes, since a passing rule has no remediation.
  • A false name that doesn't exist isn't reported at all, so check the spelling.
  • A value other than true or false fails the render.

Turning remediate off stops managing spec.apply. What is applied stays applied.

items.title: Reverting
items.text:
Removing an entry doesn't revert anything: it stays applied and shows in findings-drift. Set it to false, and remove the entry once its state is NotApplied.

Remediation false does MachineConfig Deletes it and reboots the pool Object the operator created Deletes it KubeletConfig Nothing. Status says NotApplied, the setting stays, and remediate-remediation-state stays NonCompliant until you follow Red Hat's manual removal and drop the entry. Affected nodes reboot. Object the operator patched Nothing, and status says NotApplied. Nothing here detects it.

Deleting a ComplianceRemediation doesn't revert it either. After any revert, rescan: results don't change until the next scan.

items.title: Turning it off
items.text:
enabled: false deletes the Policies but nothing they created: no template sets pruneObjectBehavior, the ACM setting that deletes a template's objects with its Policy, and the operator stays installed (Removal and pruning). The binding keeps scanning daily and applied remediations stay. To stop scanning and keep the results:

oc patch scansetting default -n openshift-compliance --type merge -p '{"suspend":true}'

Deleting the binding (oc delete ssb stig -n openshift-compliance, or your config.binding) also deletes the results and raw-results PVCs.

items.title: File Integrity
items.text: The file-integrity element installs the File Integrity Operator, which runs AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) on every Linux node. AIDE records checksums, permissions and SELinux labels of the files under each node's /boot, /root, /usr and /etc. It rescans every 15 minutes and reports any file that changed since. Nodes with changes show in Governance: findings-file-integrity-<cluster> turns NonCompliant and names them.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
# values/environments/prod.yaml
stack:
  fileIntegrity:
    enabled: true

Defaults (README):

Key under stack.fileIntegrity.config Default gracePeriod 900 seconds between scans aideExclusions /etc/machine-config-daemon/previous-logs (Exclusions)

The AIDE pods tolerate every taint, so control plane, infra, storage and other dedicated nodes are all scanned. Windows nodes are skipped. Red Hat supports RHCOS nodes only, all on the same RHCOS version.

Hosted control planes

Red Hat doesn't document the operator on hosted clusters, and it is untested there. Leave the element off on HCP guests.

items.title: What it creates
items.text:
Policy Templates Waits for install-file-integrity-<cluster> Namespace openshift-file-integrity, the OperatorPolicy (package file-integrity-operator, channel stable) and its status check (The install Policy) config-file-integrity-<cluster> config-file-integrity, in this order: the namespace's pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged label, ConfigMap file-integrity-aide, FileIntegrity file-integrity install Compliant findings-file-integrity-<cluster> findings-file-integrity-active, findings-file-integrity-nodes (Reading Governance) config Compliant

One FileIntegrity covers every node. Per-role instances would scan schedulable control plane nodes twice, because those nodes are workers too.

items.title: How AIDE is configured
items.text:
The operator ships a default AIDE configuration. A FileIntegrity's spec.config replaces that default whole; you can't add to it. The element follows Red Hat's custom-configuration procedure:

  1. ConfigMap file-integrity-aide holds the operator's default, copied from operator 1.5.0, followed by one !<path> rule per aideExclusions entry.
  2. The FileIntegrity points at it.
  3. The operator rewrites the database paths, prefixes /hostroot to each path, and stores the result in ConfigMap file-integrity, which the AIDE pods read.

Edit neither ConfigMap on the cluster. ACM restores file-integrity-aide, and the operator overwrites file-integrity.

Operator upgrades

Clusters keep the 1.5.0 copy of the default until an element release updates it, even after the operator changes its own. Red Hat changed the default once between 1.3.4 and 1.5.0. If every node goes Errored right after an operator upgrade, the operator has moved to a newer AIDE that rejects the copy. Pin the operator to the previous version until an element release refreshes it.

items.title: Exclusions
items.text:
The machine config daemon copies its log to /etc/machine-config-daemon/previous-logs on every restart. The operator's default doesn't exclude that path. Without the element's default exclusion, every daemon restart would make a node Failed for a change nobody made.

stack:
  fileIntegrity:
    config:
      aideExclusions:
        /etc/myapp/cache: "Rewritten by myapp on start. OPS-123"

The key is the host path without /hostroot. It must start with / and contain no spaces, or the render fails. It is an AIDE regular expression matched from the start, so /etc/myapp also excludes /etc/myapp2 and everything below both. End it with $ to match one file. Layers merge the map, and null in a later layer removes an entry, the default one included.

A configuration change re-initializes

Any change to the ConfigMap, whether from aideExclusions or from an element release that refreshes the default, makes the operator rebuild the database on every node from the files as they are at that moment. A change made before the rebuild is never reported.

items.title: Reading Governance
items.text:
Template NonCompliant means findings-file-integrity-active The FileIntegrity isn't Active: Pending (no daemon set yet), Initializing (database being rebuilt) or Error (AIDE couldn't run on a node; see the next row) findings-file-integrity-nodes A node's latest scan is Failed (files changed) or Errored (AIDE couldn't run). ACM's message names the FileIntegrityNodeStatus objects, file-integrity-<node>

Initializing is expected for a few minutes in three cases:

  • after install, because the operator always runs one re-init when it switches to the custom configuration
  • after a configuration change
  • on each node after a Machine Config Operator update

The operator pauses scans during an MCO update and re-initializes afterwards, so a MachineConfig rollout raises no Failed nodes.

The operator also fires the NodeHasIntegrityFailure alert in cluster monitoring.

items.title: After a failure
items.text:
1. Read what changed:

    oc get fileintegritynodestatus file-integrity-<node> -n openshift-file-integrity \
  -o jsonpath='{.lastResult.resultConfigMapName}'
oc get cm <failure-cm> -n openshift-file-integrity -o jsonpath='{.data.integritylog}'

    Logs over 1 MB are stored as a base64 gzip archive, marked by the annotation file-integrity.openshift.io/compressed. Extract those with:

    oc get cm <failure-cm> -n openshift-file-integrity -o json | jq -r '.data.integritylog' | base64 -d | gunzip

  2. Treat an unexpected change as an incident. A path that changes routinely belongs in Exclusions. To accept a one-off change, re-initialize the failed nodes:

    oc annotate fileintegrities/file-integrity -n openshift-file-integrity file-integrity.openshift.io/re-init-on-failed=

    file-integrity.openshift.io/re-init= re-initializes every node. The finding clears after the next scan.

  3. Once it's handled, delete the failure ConfigMap with oc delete cm <failure-cm> -n openshift-file-integrity. The operator keeps failure ConfigMaps as a record and never deletes them.

Never manage the re-init annotations from a policy

The operator removes them once the re-init starts. An enforced policy would add them back on every evaluation and rebuild the database in a loop, so no change would ever be reported.

items.title: Disconnected clusters
items.text:
Read How PolicyStack works and Installation first; this page changes those steps for a site with no internet.

A disconnected cluster cannot reach the internet. PolicyStack normally pulls from five places on the internet, and each one is replaced by something you run at the site:

Normally reached By Disconnected replacement Set up GitHub Argo CD on the hub, your repository's CI, and copier Internal Git. policy-library, the chart every element renders through, is in the repo (lib/), so Git is all Argo CD reads By hand (PolicyStack releases) Container images and operator catalogs Every cluster oc-mirror's mirror sets and CatalogSources, applied by the disconnected element; global.catalogSources points every operator at the mirrored catalog Site layer Public certificate authorities Every cluster Your mirror registry's CA and your internal servers' CAs, applied by the disconnected element Site layer Red Hat's upgrade graph Every cluster's CVO Your OSUS, set by the upgrade element or the HostedCluster Update Service Release images and RHCOS ISOs on quay.io and mirror.openshift.com The hub, for clusters it builds install.releaseRepository, and per-engine mirror settings Clusters the hub builds

Terms used on this page:

Term Meaning oc-mirror v2 copies release images and operator catalogs into your registry and writes the cluster objects that point clusters at it into working-dir/cluster-resources/. You run it; PolicyStack applies its output. CVO Cluster Version Operator. Runs on every cluster, reads ClusterVersion, fetches the upgrade graph and performs upgrades. OSUS OpenShift Update Service. Serves a local copy of the upgrade graph. You run it; PolicyStack only points clusters at it. Site layer A values layer holding one datacenter's mirror data, such as values/datacenters/dc2.yaml. Every cluster at the site lists it in its fleet file's valueFiles. HostedCluster, standalone A HostedCluster is the hub object describing a hosted control plane cluster, whose control plane runs as pods on the hub. Any other cluster is standalone.

Other terms: Glossary.

Order of work: mirror, set up Git, write the site layer, bring up the hub, then add spokes.

items.title: What to mirror
items.text:
The mirrored operator catalog must hold every package, at the channel, that the elements you enable subscribe to. Otherwise that element's install OperatorPolicy stays NonCompliant, with the Subscription reporting that no operator was found in the channel. No tool generates the list; read it from the elements:

yq -N '.stack[].operatorPolicies[] | .subscription.name + " " + .subscription.channel' \
  stack/{acm,gitops,metallb}/values.yaml  # the elements you enable
# advanced-cluster-management release-2.17
# openshift-gitops-operator latest
# metallb-operator stable

The elements you enable are the stack.<key>.enabled: true entries in the layers your fleet files list. A layer that overrides a channel sets stack.<key>.operatorPolicies.<op>.subscription.channel; mirror that channel too. Two more things go in the list:

  • Every package an operator requires. ODF's odf-operator, for one, pulls in ocs-operator, mcg-operator and more; take the list from the product's disconnected docs.
  • Every version a layer pins. A missing version fails the same way. A channel listed without minVersion/maxVersion keeps only its newest bundle, so a layer that pins versions (Operator versions) needs a range on that channel covering the pin.

Every shipped element subscribes from redhat-operators; your own elements may use certified-operators or others, which then need their catalog mirrored too.

# imageset-config.yaml
kind: ImageSetConfiguration
apiVersion: mirror.openshift.io/v2alpha1
mirror:
  platform:
    channels:
      - name: stable-4.20
        minVersion: 4.20.8
        maxVersion: 4.20.12 # (1)!
    architectures: [multi] # (2)!
    graph: true # (3)!
  operators:
    - catalog: registry.redhat.io/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.20
      packages:
        - name: advanced-cluster-management
          channels: [{name: release-2.17}]
        - name: multicluster-engine # (4)!
          channels: [{name: stable-2.12}]
        - name: openshift-gitops-operator
          channels: [{name: latest}]
        - name: metallb-operator
          channels: [{name: stable}]
  1. Cover every version a fleet file targets and every hop on the way. A version outside the range is not in your OSUS graph, so its bump waits at the guard (Update Service).
  2. The payload architecture your clusters run (amd64 in oc-mirror is the x86_64 release tag). Clusters the hub builds with hypershift or hive run multi, siteconfig clusters run amd64 (Clusters the hub builds). Imported clusters keep the payload they were installed with. List both when you have both.
  3. Mirrors the graph data your OSUS serves, and makes oc-mirror write an updateService.yaml for it.
  4. ACM installs it itself, so no element lists it. Mirror the channel that pairs with your ACM release: stable-2.12 for ACM 2.17 (ACM release notes).

items.title: PolicyStack releases
items.text:
Your repository is created and updated from upstream's Git tags (Installation), so the site needs a copy of upstream's repository, tags included. policy-library is in it (lib/); there is no chart repository to mirror.

  1. Mirror upstream on a connected machine, then carry it across and push it to your Git server. Repeat to pick up new releases:

    git clone --mirror https://github.com/PolicyStack/PolicyStack.git
git -C PolicyStack.git push --mirror https://git.example.internal/mirrors/PolicyStack.git

  2. On every machine that runs copier, send the upstream URL to the mirror:

    git config --global url."https://git.example.internal/mirrors/PolicyStack.git".insteadOf \
  https://github.com/PolicyStack/PolicyStack.git

    copier reaches upstream only through git, so the answers files keep the upstream URL in _src_path and every command in Installation and Upgrading PolicyStack works unchanged.

    Global or system config only

    copier clones upstream into a temporary directory, where your repository's own .git/config doesn't apply. Set the rewrite with --global or --system, or for one shell with GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=url.<mirror>.insteadOf GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=<upstream>. A rewrite in your repository's own config is ignored, and copier tries GitHub.

  3. Install copier from your Python package mirror: pipx install copier with PIP_INDEX_URL pointing at it. mise install installs the pinned copier the same way.

CI in your repository needs the tools in mise.toml and the validator's Go modules (GOPROXY pointing at your Go module proxy). The CRDs the validator checks against are committed in tools/validator/crds/, so it needs nothing else from the internet (CRD schemas).

items.title: Git and the hub's Argo CD
items.text: Argo CD on the hub reads your repository before any Policy exists, and PolicyStack never manages that Argo CD instance (the hub layer turns off the gitops element's instance policy, Installation). So trustedCA below never reaches it. If your Git server uses a private CA, add it to Argo CD by hand, as a repository TLS certificate.

items.title: Site layer
items.text:
One file holds everything about the site's mirror. Every cluster at the site lists it in its fleet file:

# fleet/prod-west-1.yaml
revision: main
valueFiles:
  - environments/prod.yaml
  - datacenters/dc2.yaml

Build clusterResources from oc-mirror's output, which it writes under the directory you passed as --workspace or file://. Each object becomes one list item:

cd <dir>/working-dir/cluster-resources
yq ea -p yaml -o yaml -P '[.] | map(del(.status)) | {"clusterResources": .}' \
  $(ls | grep -v -e updateService -e signature-configmap.yaml)
  • updateService.yaml is an UpdateService, which needs the OSUS operator, so resources goes NonCompliant on any cluster without it. Apply it by hand on the cluster that runs OSUS.
  • oc-mirror writes the signature ConfigMap twice, as signature-configmap.json and signature-configmap.yaml. The command keeps the JSON copy; -p yaml reads it, as JSON is valid YAML.

Paste the output, indented, as stack.disconnected.config.clusterResources:

# values/datacenters/dc2.yaml
global:
  catalogSources:
    redhat-operators: cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20 # (1)!

stack:
  disconnected:
    enabled: true # (2)!
    config:
      clusterResources: # (3)!
        - apiVersion: config.openshift.io/v1
          kind: ImageDigestMirrorSet
          metadata:
            name: idms-operator-0
          spec:
            imageDigestMirrors:
              - mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/redhat]
                source: registry.redhat.io/redhat
        - apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
          kind: CatalogSource
          metadata:
            name: cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20
            namespace: openshift-marketplace
          spec:
            image: mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.20
            sourceType: grpc
      registryCAs:
        mirror.dc2.example.com..8443: | # (4)!
          -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
          ...
      trustedCA: | # (5)!
        -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
        ...
  remediations:
    config:
      allowedRegistries: # (6)!
        - mirror.dc2.example.com:8443
        - quay.io
        - registry.redhat.io
        - image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000
      allowedRegistriesForImport:
        - domainName: mirror.dc2.example.com:8443
          insecure: false
        - domainName: quay.io
          insecure: false
        - domainName: registry.redhat.io
          insecure: false
  upgrade:
    config:
      upstream: https://osus.dc2.example.com/api/upgrades_info/v1/graph # (7)!
  1. Every Subscription names its catalog, and every shipped element names redhat-operators, which oc-mirror does not create: it names the mirrored catalog cs-<index>-<tag>. This map renames the source in every OperatorPolicy the elements render, and in the hub's bootstrap Subscriptions. With it, metallb renders source: cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20. Add one key per catalog you mirror.
  2. global applies to every cluster that lists this layer, whether or not it enables the element. Enabling the element in the same file keeps the mapping and the CatalogSource it points to together. Otherwise a cluster that lists the layer but leaves the element off has every operator pointed at a catalog it does not have, and no operator installs or upgrades. Your repository's CI validator (POLICY038) only checks that a source is a known catalog name or a catalogSources key, not that the CatalogSource exists on the cluster.
  3. The yq output. Applied as is, with musthave: the listed fields are set and nothing else on the object is touched (ACM policies in brief).
  4. The mirror registry's CA, keyed by host. A ConfigMap key cannot contain :, so OpenShift reads .. as the port separator.
  5. CAs of your other internal HTTPS servers: Git, Helm, OSUS, the RHCOS image server.
  6. The remediations element restricts which registries the cluster may pull from. It only takes effect where it is enabled, and then blocks every registry not listed, the mirror included. Keep the source registries: pods still reference images by their source name and the mirror sets redirect the pull. Lists replace across layers (Merge rules), so restate the element's defaults.
  7. Your OSUS graph URL (Update Service). The upgrade element ships enabled, so this repoints every standalone cluster that lists the layer, the hub included, at once.

registryCAs or trustedCA

registryCAs becomes ConfigMap openshift-config/registry-cas, referenced by the cluster image config's additionalTrustedCA: trusted for image pulls, builds and image stream imports. trustedCA goes into the cluster-wide trust bundle through the Proxy's trustedCA, which the CVO, operators and every ConfigMap labelled config.openshift.io/inject-trusted-cabundle use. Put the mirror registry's CA in registryCAs and every other internal server's CA in trustedCA. A server used both ways goes in both. The CVO trusts only the cluster trust bundle, so an OSUS CA in registryCAs alone leaves RetrievedUpdates=False.

Before you enable the element

  • Existing image config CA. An image config whose additionalTrustedCA names another ConfigMap is repointed at registry-cas, and that ConfigMap's registries stop being trusted for pulls. Copy its keys into config.registryCAs first: oc get image.config cluster -o jsonpath={.spec.additionalTrustedCA.name}.
  • Default catalogs disappear. The operatorhub policy sets disableAllDefaultSources: true, so redhat-operators and the other default CatalogSources go away. Any Subscription not renamed by global.catalogSources, including ones created by hand, stops resolving. Put the mapping and the mirrored CatalogSource in place in the same commit that enables the element.
  • Release signatures. Before an upgrade the CVO checks the release image's signature. A disconnected cluster reads it from ConfigMap openshift-config-managed/mirrored-release-signatures, which oc-mirror writes when it mirrors releases. Without a signature for the release, the upgrade stops with ClusterVersion ReleaseAccepted=False and a message that the release cannot be verified. Each oc-mirror run writes that ConfigMap with only its own releases (Changing the site data).

items.title: Check it
items.text:
On the hub, oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n <cluster> lists pstack.resources-disconnected-<cluster>, pstack.registry-ca-disconnected-<cluster>, pstack.trusted-ca-disconnected-<cluster> and pstack.operatorhub-disconnected-<cluster>, all Compliant. A NonCompliant one names the object at fault (Compliance states). On the cluster:

oc get imagedigestmirrorsets,catalogsources -A
oc get packagemanifests -n openshift-marketplace -l catalog=cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20 # the mirrored packages
oc get mcp # nodes take new mirror sets through a pool update; wait for UPDATED True

items.title: The hub
items.text:
The hub needs the mirrored catalog before PolicyStack exists to apply it, because the bootstrap installs ACM and GitOps from it.

  1. Install the hub disconnected, following Red Hat's docs, with the mirror registry's CA in the install-config additionalTrustBundle. The steps below apply no CA, so the hub must already trust the mirror.

  2. Apply oc-mirror's output by hand, except the UpdateService:

    cd working-dir/cluster-resources
for f in $(ls | grep -v updateService); do oc apply -f "$f"; done

  3. Install the operators, adding the site layer with -f values/datacenters/dc2.yaml. Its global.catalogSources points the ACM and GitOps Subscriptions at the mirrored catalog.

  4. Install PolicyStack with --set gitRepo=<your internal Git URL>, once Argo CD can reach Git (Before you start).
  5. List datacenters/dc2.yaml in the hub's fleet file, fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml (hubName is the name you installed the hub with, Hub file). The disconnected element then enforces the same objects by name, so ACM manages the ones you applied instead of creating copies. If they differ from clusterResources, the Policy changes them to match.

items.title: What the element applies
items.text:
Every policy is on; turn one off with policies.<policy>.enabled: false. With empty input, resources, registry-ca and trusted-ca apply nothing; the Policy stays, Compliant.

Policy Applies resources config.clusterResources, as is. registry-ca ConfigMap openshift-config/registry-cas from config.registryCAs, and additionalTrustedCA on image.config.openshift.io/cluster. trusted-ca ConfigMap openshift-config/trusted-cas, with the Proxy's trustedCA pointing at it. Lands in every injected trust bundle, including the one the gitops element mounts into the repo server of an Argo CD instance it manages (not the hub's own, above). operatorhub OperatorHub disableAllDefaultSources: true.

items.title: trusted-cas
items.text:
trusted-cas = user-ca-bundle (the installer's additionalTrustBundle) + config.trustedCA. The user-ca-bundle part is an ACM template that the cluster evaluates on every check, so a later change to user-ca-bundle is picked up. user-ca-bundle itself is never written.

Existing Proxy trustedCA

A Proxy pointing at a ConfigMap other than user-ca-bundle is repointed, and its CAs leave the trust bundle. Copy them into config.trustedCA first.

Turning trusted-ca off

Turning trusted-ca off or emptying config.trustedCA leaves the Proxy on a stale trusted-cas, still trusted. Clean up by hand:

oc patch proxy/cluster --type merge -p '{"spec":{"trustedCA":{"name":"user-ca-bundle"}}}' # (1)!
oc delete configmap trusted-cas -n openshift-config
  1. Use "name":"" if user-ca-bundle does not exist.

items.title: Changing the site data
items.text:
No template sets pruneObjectBehavior (ACM's setting that deletes what a policy created once the policy goes, Removal and pruning). So an object dropped from clusterResources, a policy turned off, or the element disabled stays on the cluster: an old CatalogSource keeps its pod running and the OperatorHub stays disabled. The two CA ConfigMaps are mustonlyhave, so a removed key does disappear, but emptying registryCAs or trustedCA leaves the last ConfigMap and its reference in place. Delete them by hand.

  • A new oc-mirror run. Regenerate the list and replace clusterResources whole: oc-mirror v2's mirror sets cover the entire image set on every run, and a list in a later layer replaces the earlier one rather than adding to it, so a second layer cannot hold "the new objects".
  • Old signatures. Each run writes one ConfigMap, mirrored-release-signatures, with only that run's releases. Clusters keep keys they already have (musthave never removes them), but a new cluster gets only the current run's. Keep minVersion low enough to cover every release a cluster may still upgrade to, or copy the earlier run's binaryData entries into the new ConfigMap.
  • A new catalog version (v4-20 to v4-21, when clusters move minor):
    1. Mirror the new index and add its CatalogSource to clusterResources, next to the old one.
    2. Once a cluster finishes its upgrade to 4.21, set global.catalogSources.redhat-operators: cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-21 in values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml. The new index may hold bundles that need 4.21. Maps merge, so this one key overrides the site's.
    3. Once every cluster has moved, change the site mapping, drop the cluster overrides and the old CatalogSource, then oc delete catalogsource cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20 -n openshift-marketplace on each cluster.

items.title: Update Service
items.text:
The upgrade element holds a fleet version until it appears in the ClusterVersion's availableUpdates, which the CVO fills from the upgrade graph (The upgrade element). A disconnected cluster gets no graph unless stack.upgrade.config.upstream points at your OSUS (Site layer), so every version bump waits forever. Hosted clusters take it from the HostedCluster instead (Hosted clusters).

OSUS only offers releases in your mirror. availableUpdates empty or missing the target means one of:

  • The target is outside the mirrored minVersion/maxVersion.
  • oc-mirror did not mirror the cluster's payload architecture (What to mirror), so the graph has no entries for it.
  • The CVO cannot reach or trust OSUS: oc get clusterversion version -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="RetrievedUpdates")]}' says why.

items.title: Clusters the hub builds
items.text:
The credential, the hub Secret named by install.credential (Install keys), must have the mirror registry's auth in its pullSecret, for every engine.

Every engine pulls the release image by tag, as <install.releaseRepository>:<version>-<arch> (-x86_64 or -multi). An ImageDigestMirrorSet only redirects pulls by digest, so it does not cover this one. Point releaseRepository at the repository oc-mirror put the release images in:

# values/datacenters/dc2.yaml
install:
  releaseRepository: mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release-images

install in a layer is read only by the lifecycle-<cluster> Application of a cluster the hub builds, so imported clusters at the site ignore it. Set it before the hub builds a cluster: on a running hypershift cluster a new releaseRepository changes the HostedCluster's and NodePools' release image, which rolls the control plane and replaces or updates every node. Each engine also needs the mirrors and the mirror CA for the install itself, set as below.

items.title: Hosted clusters
items.text:
HyperShift writes a hosted cluster's image config, Proxy, node mirror configuration and, with the default olmCatalogPlacement: management, its OperatorHub from the HostedCluster, so policies writing them inside the guest would fight it. Set them on the HostedCluster, through install.hostedCluster. On the guest, the disconnected element keeps only the CatalogSource. For the same reason, turn off the remediations element's registries policy on guests and set the allowlist in install.hostedCluster.spec.configuration.image (registrySources, allowedRegistriesForImport).

Site layerCluster values 
# values/datacenters/dc2.yaml
install:
  releaseRepository: mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release-images
  hostedCluster:
    spec:
      imageContentSources: # (1)!
        - source: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-release
          mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release-images]
        - source: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-v4.0-art-dev
          mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release]
        - source: registry.redhat.io/redhat
          mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/redhat]
        # ...one entry per imageDigestMirrors item in oc-mirror's idms-oc-mirror.yaml
      configuration:
        operatorhub:
          disableAllDefaultSources: true # (2)!
      updateService: https://osus.dc2.example.com/api/upgrades_info/v1/graph # (3)!
  1. Copy every entry of oc-mirror's ImageDigestMirrorSets (source/mirrors keep the same shape). Missing the ocp-v4.0-art-dev entry fails the install while pulling payload images.
  2. Replaces the guest's operatorhub policy, turned off in the cluster values.
  3. The hosted CVO runs on the hub, so use an OSUS URL the hub reaches. Without it, a version bump with channel set is held forever. hive and siteconfig clusters ignore install.hostedCluster.
# values/clusters/hcp-agent.yaml
install:
  hostedCluster:
    spec:
      additionalTrustBundle:
        name: hcp-agent-mirror-ca # (1)!
  manifests: # (2)!
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: ConfigMap
      metadata:
        name: hcp-agent-mirror-ca
        namespace: clusters # (3)!
      data:
        ca-bundle.crt: |
          -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
          ...
stack:
  disconnected:
    policies:
      registry-ca:
        enabled: false
      trusted-ca:
        enabled: false
      operatorhub:
        enabled: false
    config:
      clusterResources: # (4)!
        - apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
          kind: CatalogSource
          metadata:
            name: cs-redhat-operator-index-v4-20
            namespace: openshift-marketplace
          spec:
            image: mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.20
            sourceType: grpc
  1. A hub ConfigMap with key ca-bundle.crt, in the HostedCluster's namespace. Name it per cluster: install.manifests are deleted when their cluster is destroyed, so a ConfigMap two clusters share disappears with the first one.
  2. Hub objects created before the cluster (Install keys). A list, so it replaces any manifests from another layer, and the fleet file's install overrides this file's. Keep all of a cluster's manifests in one place.
  3. install.namespace, clusters by default.
  4. Replaces the site's list, CatalogSources only. Restate each in full: without this, the guest inherits the site's mirror sets and signature ConfigMap.

items.title: Hive clusters
items.text:
The OpenShift installer takes the mirrors and the mirror CA from the install-config. install.hive.installConfig is merged into it as is:

# values/platforms/vmware.yaml, or the cluster's own file
install:
  hive:
    installConfig:
      imageDigestSources: # (1)!
        - source: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-release
          mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release-images]
        - source: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-v4.0-art-dev
          mirrors: [mirror.dc2.example.com:8443/openshift/release]
        # ...one entry per imageDigestMirrors item in oc-mirror's idms-oc-mirror.yaml
      additionalTrustBundle: |
        -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
        ...
  1. Copy every entry of oc-mirror's ImageDigestMirrorSets (source/mirrors keep the same shape). Missing the ocp-v4.0-art-dev entry fails the install while pulling payload images. Once the cluster is built and imported, the disconnected element manages its mirror sets like any other cluster's.

Warning

Keep install.hive out of layers that other engines read. The lifecycle schema rejects it on a hypershift or siteconfig cluster, and its lifecycle-<cluster> Application shows a ComparisonError: install.hive: Must have at most 0 properties.

items.title: Bare metal
items.text:
siteconfig clusters install through the hub's assisted service, the multicluster engine component that builds the discovery ISO each host boots to install (Cluster lifecycle). So the hub holds their mirrors. The cim element, which configures the assisted service through AgentServiceConfig agent, reads the disconnected config from the hub's own layers, whether or not disconnected is enabled there:

From To ImageDigestMirrorSets in clusterResources (ImageTagMirrorSets are ignored: the installer pulls by digest) registries.conf in ConfigMap multicluster-engine/assisted-mirror, referenced as AgentServiceConfig mirrorRegistryRef registryCAs ca-bundle.crt in the same ConfigMap trustedCA, only when osImages is set: the image service needs it only to download your self-hosted ISOs over HTTPS ConfigMap image-service-additional-ca, referenced as OSImageCACertRef

Assisted writes the mirrors and CAs into the discovery ISO and into each spoke's install-config, so the spoke installs from the mirror with its ImageDigestMirrorSet in place.

# values/clusters/<hubName>.yaml
stack:
  cim:
    enabled: true
    config:
      osImages: # (1)!
        "4.20":
          version: 9.6.20251015-1 # (2)!
          url: https://images.dc2.example.com/rhcos-4.20-x86_64-live.iso
  1. Replaces the default list, which points at mirror.openshift.com. List every version the hub's siteconfig clusters install, and host the ISOs yourself.
  2. RHCOS version of the ISO.

Limits of hub-side mirrors

  • One mirror set per hub: every siteconfig cluster it builds gets the hub's mirrors, even one at another site. The stock SiteConfig templates have no per-cluster mirror.
  • ibi (image-based install) does not use the assisted service, so mirrorRegistryRef never reaches it. Put an ImageDigestMirrorSet in a ConfigMap through install.manifests and list that ConfigMap in siteconfig.extraManifests.

Removing entries

The AgentServiceConfig is musthave, which never removes fields. A removed osImages entry, or a mirrorRegistryRef once no mirrors remain, stays on it. Remove it with oc edit agentserviceconfig agent.

items.title: Global Hub
items.text:
Read this only if your ACM hubs are, or will be, imported into a Multicluster Global Hub. PolicyStack does not need one: several hubs can share one repository, each installed with its own hubName.

Import each managed hub in hosted mode (a Global Hub import mode, unrelated to hosted control planes; see Import modes) unless you want the global hub to configure and build clusters for it. In hosted mode every hub keeps running PolicyStack for itself and nothing in the repo changes. Default mode removes the managed hub's local-cluster, rules out hypershift on it, and makes its hub templates resolve on the global hub.

items.title: What Global Hub does
items.text:
Global Hub is an operator on one ACM hub, the global hub. The ACM hubs it imports are managed hubs. An agent on each managed hub streams its Policies, compliance, events and ManagedClusters through Kafka into PostgreSQL, and Grafana reads them there. It can also move clusters between managed hubs (ManagedClusterMigration, Technology Preview).

It does not push configuration: global policy distribution was removed in 1.7. Each hub's PolicyStack and ACM still deliver everything.

Minimum version

Use Global Hub 1.8.2 (RHSA-2026:68515) or 1.7.3 (RHSA-2026:67842) or later. Earlier releases let one managed hub spoof another's compliance data (CVE-2026-71576). 1.8 pairs with ACM 2.17, 1.7 with 2.16.

items.title: What the mode decides
items.text:
Terms used below:

  • Day-2: the element Policies the policystack ApplicationSet renders for a cluster. Lifecycle: building and destroying clusters, rendered by policystack-lifecycle (Cluster lifecycle).
  • local-cluster: the ManagedCluster a hub creates for itself. PolicyStack needs it to find the hub's own fleet file, fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml, and to place the Policies that build clusters.
  • Klusterlet: ACM's agent through which a hub manages a cluster.

A hub's ApplicationSets see only the ManagedClusters that hub manages: its GitOpsCluster turns each one into an Argo CD cluster secret, and the ApplicationSets pair those secrets with fleet files (ApplicationSets). Global Hub only mirrors status, so the global hub has no secret for a cluster under a managed hub, and that cluster's Day-2 always renders on the managed hub. The import mode decides two other things: which hub renders the managed hub's own Day-2, and which hub builds clusters whose fleet hub names the managed hub.

items.title: Import modes
items.text:
You import a managed hub into the global hub's ACM like any cluster, following Red Hat's Global Hub import procedure; PolicyStack does not do it. A label on its ManagedCluster, on the global hub, picks the mode. Without the label, the hub gets no Global Hub agent.

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: ManagedCluster
metadata:
  name: hub-a # (1)!
  labels:
    global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/deploy-mode: default # (2)!
  1. Use the managed hub's hubName. In default mode the global hub knows the hub only by this name: it reads fleet/hubs/<name>.yaml and values/clusters/<name>.yaml, and fleet hub: keys must use it. hub-a's own PolicyStack install still needs a hubName, but in default mode hub-a has no local-cluster, so it renders nothing for itself and never reads that value. Set it to the same name anyway, so the files work in both modes and Global Hub's dashboards match.
  2. default or hosted.
default hosted Managed hub's klusterlet runs on The managed hub The global hub Managed hub has local-cluster No. ACM requires disableHubSelfManagement: true on its MultiClusterHub Yes Global hub's Policies reach the managed hub Yes No. Global Hub's admission webhook turns off the policy and application add-ons for that hub Renders the managed hub's Day-2, from fleet/hubs/<managed-hub>.yaml Global hub Managed hub Builds clusters whose hub is the managed hub Global hub, Policies placed on the managed hub (Lifecycle) Managed hub hypershift engine on the managed hub No Yes When to set the label Any time Before import. An already-imported cluster is ignored Hosted mode requirements
  • The global hub has its own local-cluster (the ACM default).
  • The kubeconfig you give at import stays valid: use a token that doesn't expire, such as a service-account token, not an oc login token. When it expires the global hub loses the managed hub until you regenerate auto-import-secret in the managed hub's namespace on the global hub.
  • The global hub reaches each managed hub's API.
  • Red Hat does not support backup and restore of a hosted-mode managed hub, which Hub disaster recovery relies on.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
Install PolicyStack on the global hub and on every managed hub, all with the same gitRepo and each with its own hubName (Install PolicyStack). All hubs read the same fleet/.

fleet/
  hubs/gh.yaml      # the global hub; Day-2 rendered by gh
  hubs/hub-a.yaml   # default-mode managed hub; Day-2 rendered by gh
  hubs/hub-b.yaml   # hosted-mode managed hub; Day-2 rendered by hub-b
  edge-1.yaml       # hub: hub-a; Day-2 rendered by hub-a, built by gh on hub-a
  edge-2.yaml       # hub: hub-b; Day-2 rendered and built by hub-b

items.title: Import a managed hub
items.text:
Hosted modeDefault mode

Set the label on the ManagedCluster before importing. Nothing else changes: the managed hub keeps local-cluster, reads its own fleet/hubs/hub-b.yaml and builds its own clusters.

No fleet/hub-b.yaml

The global hub has a cluster secret for hub-b with neither local-cluster nor the default label, so its Day-2 ApplicationSet looks for fleet/hub-b.yaml. If that file exists, the global hub creates <element>-hub-b Applications whose Policies never reach hub-b and never report compliance. A hub the global hub builds is imported as soon as it is built, before you could set the hosted label, so it can't use hosted mode: use default mode.

For hub-a:

  1. Install PolicyStack on hub-a and commit fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml, as for any hub. An existing PolicyStack hub has both. hub-a's PolicyStack applies step 2 and keeps rendering Day-2 for hub-a's managed clusters.

  2. Turn off self-management in hub-a's layer. The acm element must be on, which means handing the operators to PolicyStack first:

    # values/acm/hub-a.yaml, listed in fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml
stack:
  acm:
    enabled: true
    config:
      selfManaged: false

    Merge. hub-a's own PolicyStack sets disableHubSelfManagement: true and ACM removes local-cluster. With it go hub-a's Applications for itself (the Policies are deleted, what they created stays) and its lifecycle-<cluster> Applications: clusters with hub: hub-a are abandoned, not destroyed, until step 4. oc get managedcluster local-cluster on hub-a returns NotFound when done.

    From here until step 4, nothing enforces hub-a's own Policies or runs its builds. Do steps 3 and 4 together.

  3. Import hub-a into the global hub (Red Hat's procedure).

  4. Label it on the global hub:

    oc label managedcluster hub-a global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/deploy-mode=default

    The global hub now reads fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml, creates <element>-hub-a Applications, and takes over building the clusters with hub: hub-a. It re-adopts the abandoned ones by their ownership marker.

A hub the global hub builds with hive or siteconfig has two fleet files: fleet/hub-a.yaml, holding its lifecycle keys, and fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml. Until the label is set, the global hub renders hub-a's Day-2 from fleet/hub-a.yaml; after, from fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml. Both carry a version, and each drives upgrades while the global hub reads it: fleet/hub-a.yaml before the label, fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml after. Keep them equal, and label hub-a as soon as it is imported.

The label picks the fleet file

With the label, the global hub reads fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml; without it, fleet/hub-a.yaml. Removing the label deletes hub-a's Day-2 Policies and the lifecycle-<cluster> Applications for every cluster with hub: hub-a, which leaves those clusters abandoned (What deletes an Application). Restoring the label re-adopts them.

Hub templates resolve on the global hub

An ACM hub template ({{hub ... hub}}) resolves on the hub that delivers the Policy. hub-a's own Day-2 Policies now come from the global hub, so the acs element on hub-a registers hub-a with the global hub's Central, and fails if the global hub runs none. Either run Central on the global hub, or keep stack.acs.enabled: false in hub-a's layer. hub-a's managed clusters still use hub-a's Central. acs is the only element that uses hub templates.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
policystack-lifecycle has two generators, the parts of an ApplicationSet that each produce one Application per match (Lifecycle generator). "Placed on" means the lifecycle Placement selects that ManagedCluster, so ACM runs the build steps there.

Generator Matches fleet files whose hub is Places the Policy on 1 This hub's hubName, if this hub has local-cluster local-cluster 2 A ManagedCluster of this hub labeled deploy-mode=default That managed hub

The global hub and hosted-mode hubs build their own clusters with generator 1. A default-mode hub has no local-cluster, so it renders nothing and the global hub builds for it with generator 2.

# fleet/edge-1.yaml, rendered by gh, Policy placed on hub-a
revision: main
hub: hub-a
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: hive
  credential:
    namespace: hive-credentials
    name: aws                     # (1)!
  baseDomain: aws.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      aws:
        region: us-east-2
  1. The Secret must exist on hub-a, not the global hub.

ACM delivers the Policies to hub-a, and their lookup and fromSecret calls are managed-cluster template functions, evaluated on the cluster the Policy lands on. Lifecycle uses no hub templates, so credential and BMC Secrets live on the managed hub in both modes. To watch a default-mode build:

oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io present-lifecycle-edge-1 -n pstack  # on the global hub
oc get configurationpolicy -n hub-a                # on hub-a: each step and its message

No hypershift on a default-mode hub

ACM installs the HyperShift operator through the hypershift-addon on a hub's own local-cluster, which a default-mode hub does not have. present-lifecycle-<cluster> stays NonCompliant. Use hive, siteconfig, or hosted mode.

items.title: Changing a managed hub's mode
items.text:
Fleet files stay where they are. Detach means deleting hub-a's ManagedCluster on the global hub (oc delete managedcluster hub-a), ACM's way to remove a cluster from management.

hive and siteconfig clusters survive the change. Losing the hub that builds them (detaching from the global hub, or removing hub-a's local-cluster) deletes their lifecycle-<cluster> Applications, but no lifecycle template sets pruneObjectBehavior, so nothing is deleted on hub-a (Removal and pruning). The hub that takes over adopts them by their marker because hub is unchanged (Abandon). hypershift clusters of a hosted-mode hub keep it in hosted mode: destroy them first, since a default-mode hub can't run hypershift.

Hosted to defaultDefault to hosted
  1. Detach hub-a from the global hub.
  2. Run steps 2 to 4 of Default mode. hub-a's own PolicyStack still runs, so it applies selfManaged: false.

hub-a has no local-cluster, so after detaching nothing delivers its Policies, and selfManaged: true renders no disableHubSelfManagement field that could undo the old setting. Flip it by hand:

  1. Detach hub-a from the global hub. Its Day-2 and lifecycle Applications on the global hub are deleted; its clusters are abandoned, not destroyed.
  2. Set selfManaged: true, or remove the key, in hub-a's layer and merge. Otherwise step 3 brings back hub-a's own PolicyStack, which removes local-cluster again.

  3. On hub-a:

    oc patch multiclusterhub multiclusterhub -n open-cluster-management --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"disableHubSelfManagement":false}}'

    local-cluster returns. hub-a's PolicyStack reads fleet/hubs/hub-a.yaml again and adopts its clusters.

  4. Re-import hub-a with the hosted label set before import.

items.title: Do not
items.text:
• Label a PolicyStack hub global-hub.open-cluster-management.io/hub-role. That turns on Hub HA, Global Hub's active/standby feature, which copies the ApplicationSets, Applications, Policies and ArgoCD CR to the standby, where they enforce the same Policies and build the same clusters. PolicyStack's recovery path is ACM backup plus a reinstall with the same hubName (Hub disaster recovery).
  • Enable the ACM gitops-addon or Argo CD Agent on a managed hub. They replace openshift-gitops, which runs that hub's PolicyStack.
  • Name a managed cluster after the hub that manages it, in default mode. ACM puts a cluster's Policies in a namespace named after that cluster: the global hub's Policies for hub-a land in namespace hub-a on hub-a, and hub-a keeps the Policies for each of its own clusters in a namespace named after that cluster, so a managed cluster hub-a would share it.
  • Reuse a cluster name across hubs. fleet/ is shared, and migration needs unique names.
  • Migrate a lifecycle-built cluster with ManagedClusterMigration. It moves the ManagedCluster, not its Policies or Applications, and hypershift clusters cannot migrate. Imported clusters migrate cleanly: the source hub deletes their Argo CD secret, and with it their Applications and Policies, pruning nothing on the cluster (What happens on the managed cluster). The target hub pairs its new secret with the same fleet/<cluster>.yaml and recreates them. If acs is enabled, run steps 2-3 of Re-register a cluster, since Central is now the target hub's.

items.title: Building clusters
items.text:
You build, upgrade, scale and destroy OpenShift clusters by editing fleet files. Read Cluster lifecycle first: it explains how a fleet file with hub: becomes a Policy on the hub that drives ACM's own installers, and which engine to pick (Pick an engine). Every key and generated object is in Lifecycle keys.

Every engine and platform is a preview

Lifecycle follows the framework's version, but no engine or platform is stable yet: a framework minor may change their converters, behaviour and defaults not fixed at create, with the steps in its release notes. Their install keys and the names of the objects they create change only in a major (Maturity). Pin clusters the hub builds to tags.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
On every hub that builds clusters:

  • ACM 2.16 or later.
  • The hub manages itself: oc get managedcluster -l local-cluster=true returns one cluster (ACM creates it by default). Without it the hub's lifecycle ApplicationSet creates no lifecycle-<cluster> Application, and nothing reports an error. Exception: a hub imported into Multicluster Global Hub in default mode has no local-cluster; see Global Hub.
  • fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml exists, the hub's own fleet file (Add the hub's fleet file). Your repository's CI fails a cluster whose hub has no hub file (POLICY050), which catches a typo that would leave the cluster with no hub to build or destroy it. The hub file's valueFiles are also where hub-side settings go, such as stack.cim for bare metal.
  • For engine: hypershift: the hypershift-addon is Available (oc get managedclusteraddon hypershift-addon -n local-cluster shows AVAILABLE True). It is on by default.

items.title: Build a cluster
items.text:
1. Create the credential Secret on the hub with oc, in any namespace, and never commit it. It holds pullSecret, ssh-publickey and, for hive, the cloud login; each example below shows the exact keys and command. The hub copies its keys into per-cluster Secrets on every Policy evaluation, so a rotated key reaches existing clusters without a merge. Destroy never deletes it.
  2. Add fleet/<cluster>.yaml with hub, version and install (Examples). The file name is the cluster name. install can also come from any values layer (Values).
  3. Merge to the default branch. Fleet files are read only there (Fleet files). Within about 6 minutes oc get applications.argoproj.io -n openshift-gitops lifecycle-<cluster> shows the Application. It renders the lifecycle/ chart at the fleet file's revision (branch, tag or SHA, Revision), so revision: main follows the default branch.
  4. Follow the build (Watching a build). The hub creates Policy present-lifecycle-<cluster>, whose steps run in order: guard, credentials, manifests, cluster, ready (The step chain, with the full AWS render in Worked example).

Cluster name

A DNS label of at most 30 characters. Day-2 element names are built from it and must stay under ACM's 63-character limit; CI fails a name that pushes any Policy past it (POLICY001, Naming limits).

Most install keys are fixed at create

Changing one later is refused, not rebuilt (Immutable fields). install.hive.installConfig raises no error: a change only rewrites the install-config Secret, and the running cluster ignores it.

Imported clusters cannot be adopted

Adding hub to the fleet file of a cluster that was imported, or built by hand or in the console, builds nothing. The guard step finds an object named <cluster> without the lifecycle ownership marker and stays NonCompliant with ... not built by lifecycle (no lifecycle.policystk.io/hub annotation); refusing to build it. Remove hub, state and install again; the cluster keeps its Day-2 config as an imported cluster.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Copy one, change names and addresses, merge. Values moves the shared parts into a layer.

AWSGCPAzurevSphereBare metalKubeVirtAgentNone

Needs a public Route 53 zone for baseDomain and EC2 quota.

oc create namespace hive-credentials
oc create secret generic aws -n hive-credentials \
  --from-literal=aws_access_key_id=<key> --from-literal=aws_secret_access_key=<secret> \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub # (1)!
  1. Optional: the labels cluster.open-cluster-management.io/credentials= and cluster.open-cluster-management.io/type=<type> list the Secret under Credentials in the console. Nothing else reads them.
# fleet/ocp-aws.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1 # (1)!
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: hive
  credential:
    namespace: hive-credentials
    name: aws
  baseDomain: aws.example.com
  hive:
    platform: # (2)!
      aws:
        region: us-east-2
    installConfig: # (3)!
      controlPlane:
        name: master
        architecture: amd64 # (4)!
        replicas: 3
        platform:
          aws:
            type: m6i.xlarge
      compute:
        - name: worker
          architecture: amd64
          replicas: 3
          platform:
            aws:
              type: m6i.xlarge
  1. hubName of the hub that builds the cluster.
  2. Exactly one of aws, gcp, azure or vsphere. hive ignores install.platform, which is for hypershift only.
  3. Any install-config content. The chart sets apiVersion, metadata.name, baseDomain (from install.baseDomain) and platform (from hive.platform), and these win over the same keys here. Other keys under platform and metadata are merged in. Leave out pullSecret: Hive fills it in from the ClusterDeployment's pull secret. sshKey comes from the credential's ssh-publickey unless you set it here.
  4. Keep it, or the install follows the hub node's architecture.

Single node: in installConfig, set controlPlane.replicas: 1 and compute[0].replicas: 0, and raise the control-plane type to m6i.2xlarge, because one node then also runs every workload.

Needs a public Cloud DNS zone for baseDomain, a service account with the installer's roles or Owner, and the compute, dns, iam, cloudresourcemanager and serviceusage APIs.

oc create namespace hive-credentials   # once per hub
oc create secret generic gcp -n hive-credentials \
  --from-file=osServiceAccount.json=sa-key.json \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub

# fleet/ocp-gcp.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: hive
  credential:
    namespace: hive-credentials
    name: gcp
  baseDomain: gcp.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      gcp:
        projectID: my-project
        region: us-central1
    installConfig:
      controlPlane:
        name: master
        architecture: amd64
        replicas: 3
        platform:
          gcp:
            type: n2-standard-4
      compute:
        - name: worker
          architecture: amd64
          replicas: 3
          platform:
            gcp:
              type: n2-standard-4

Needs an Azure DNS zone for baseDomain in baseDomainResourceGroupName, and a service principal with Contributor and User Access Administrator on the subscription.

cat > sp.json <<EOF
{"subscriptionId":"<sub>","clientId":"<appId>","clientSecret":"<password>","tenantId":"<tenant>"}
EOF
oc create namespace hive-credentials   # once per hub
oc create secret generic azure -n hive-credentials \
  --from-file=osServicePrincipal.json=sp.json \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub

# fleet/ocp-azure.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: hive
  credential:
    namespace: hive-credentials
    name: azure
  baseDomain: azure.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      azure:
        region: eastus
        baseDomainResourceGroupName: dns-rg
    installConfig:
      controlPlane:
        name: master
        architecture: amd64
        replicas: 3
        platform:
          azure:
            type: Standard_D8s_v5
      compute:
        - name: worker
          architecture: amd64
          replicas: 3
          platform:
            azure:
              type: Standard_D4s_v5

Needs vCenter and ESXi 7.0.2+, vCenter on port 443, DNS for api.<cluster>.<baseDomain> and *.apps.<cluster>.<baseDomain> pointing at the VIPs, and DHCP on the network unless hive.platform.vsphere.hosts sets static IPs (see Static IPs below). Inventory paths are absolute. More than one failure domain needs the openshift-region and openshift-zone tag categories attached to the datacenters and clusters. The hub downloads the RHCOS OVA unless topology.template names one.

cacertificate is the vCenter CA in PEM, from https://<vcenter>/certs/download.zip (certs/lin/*.0). It is required even for a publicly trusted vCenter. Use --from-literal for the login: a trailing newline fails the install.

oc create namespace hive-credentials   # once per hub
oc create secret generic vsphere -n hive-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=<user> --from-literal=password=<password> \
  --from-file=cacertificate=vcenter-ca.pem \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub

# fleet/ocp-vsphere.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: hive
  credential:
    namespace: hive-credentials
    name: vsphere
  baseDomain: vsphere.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      vsphere: # (1)!
        apiVIPs: [10.0.10.5]
        ingressVIPs: [10.0.10.6]
        vcenters:
          - server: vcenter.example.com # (2)!
            datacenters: [dc1]
        failureDomains:
          - name: dc1-cl1
            region: dc1
            zone: cl1
            server: vcenter.example.com
            topology:
              datacenter: dc1
              computeCluster: /dc1/host/cl1
              datastore: /dc1/datastore/ds1
              networks: [ocp-vlan10]
    installConfig:
      controlPlane:
        name: master
        architecture: amd64
        replicas: 3
      compute:
        - name: worker
          architecture: amd64
          replicas: 3
      networking:
        machineNetwork:
          - cidr: 10.0.10.0/24 # (3)!
  1. The installer's platform.vsphere, also the ClusterDeployment's infrastructure. Fixed at create.
  2. Every vCenter logs in with the credential. user and password here are refused.
  3. Holds the node IPs and both VIPs.
Static IPs, two failure domains

hosts lists exactly one bootstrap, then one entry per control-plane and compute replica.

vsphere:
  apiVIPs: [10.0.10.5]
  ingressVIPs: [10.0.10.6]
  vcenters:
    - {server: vcenter.example.com, datacenters: [dc1]}
  failureDomains:
    - {name: dc1-cl1, region: dc1, zone: cl1, server: vcenter.example.com,
       topology: {datacenter: dc1, computeCluster: /dc1/host/cl1, datastore: /dc1/datastore/ds1, networks: [ocp-vlan10]}}
    - {name: dc1-cl2, region: dc1, zone: cl2, server: vcenter.example.com,
       topology: {datacenter: dc1, computeCluster: /dc1/host/cl2, datastore: /dc1/datastore/ds2, networks: [ocp-vlan10]}}
  hosts:
    - {role: bootstrap, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.10/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: control-plane, failureDomain: dc1-cl1, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.11/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: control-plane, failureDomain: dc1-cl2, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.12/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: control-plane, failureDomain: dc1-cl1, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.13/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: compute, failureDomain: dc1-cl1, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.21/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: compute, failureDomain: dc1-cl2, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.22/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}
    - {role: compute, failureDomain: dc1-cl1, networkDevice: {ipAddrs: [10.0.10.23/24], gateway: 10.0.10.1, nameservers: [10.0.0.53]}}

Static IPs and Day-2 nodes

With hosts, the installer creates the workers as standalone Machines and leaves the worker MachineSets at 0, drawing addresses from an IPPool. Nothing installs an IPAM controller for that pool, so new Machines (from oc scale machineset, or the infraNodes and storageNodes elements) never get an address. Use DHCP if you plan to add nodes after install, or install an IPAM controller on the cluster yourself.

No hibernation

Hive cannot hibernate vSphere clusters, so leave install.hive.clusterDeployment.spec.powerState unset.

Rotating the vCenter password

Update both:

  • The credential on the hub. The hub copies it to <cluster>-creds, which Hive uses to destroy the cluster.
  • kube-system/vsphere-creds on the cluster, used by its storage and machine controllers. Nothing updates it for you.

Needs:

  • The cim element on the hub (central infrastructure management): stack.cim.enabled: true in a values file the hub reads, one listed in fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml or values/clusters/<hubName>.yaml, not the new cluster's files. It manages the Provisioning CR, AgentServiceConfig agent and the MultiClusterHub siteconfig component. Policy ready-cim-<hubName> is Compliant once they run (oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack ready-cim-<hubName>).
  • On the hub, yourself: a default StorageClass (or stack.cim.config.storage.storageClass) and the bare-metal ports. On an AWS hub, Red Hat's procedure for enabling central infrastructure management on AWS also adds an ingress controller backed by a Network Load Balancer so hosts can reach the assisted service (Clusters).
  • Hosts with a virtual-media BMC the hub reaches. Hosts reach the hub's image service and API.
  • DNS for api.<cluster>.<baseDomain> from hosts and hub. Multi-node adds api-int and *.apps.
  • Disconnected: mirrors and RHCOS images on the hub (Bare metal).
oc create namespace bm-credentials
oc create secret generic hostinventory -n bm-credentials \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub # (1)!
oc create secret generic bmc -n bm-credentials --from-literal=username=<user> --from-literal=password=<password>
  1. One key only: the stock templates fold a second into the first, so present-cluster-<cluster> fails before create with install.credential ssh-publickey must hold one key. Use RSA or ECDSA with siteconfig.fips: FIPS mode disables ed25519, so the example's id_ed25519.pub fails before create.
# fleet/sno-edge.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  engine: siteconfig
  credential:
    namespace: bm-credentials
    name: hostinventory
  baseDomain: edge.example.com
  siteconfig:
    bmcCredential: # (1)!
      namespace: bm-credentials
      name: bmc
    machineNetwork: [10.20.30.0/24]
    nodes: # (2)!
      sno-edge.edge.example.com:
        bmcAddress: idrac-virtualmedia://10.20.0.11/redfish/v1/Systems/System.Embedded.1 # (3)!
        bootMACAddress: "00:11:22:33:44:55" # (4)!
        rootDeviceHints:
          deviceName: /dev/sda
  1. username and password, used for every node.
  2. Keyed by host name. role defaults to master; set role: worker for workers. All keys.
  3. idrac-virtualmedia:// for Dell, ilo5- or ilo4-virtualmedia:// for HPE, redfish-virtualmedia:// otherwise (all variants). Other schemes need a provisioning network, which the cim default doesn't have, so the schema refuses them.
  4. Keep the quotes: an unquoted MAC is not read as a string by YAML.

Fixed after create

SiteConfig allows no spec change until the install completes, and after it only adding and removing workers. A failed install is not retried: destroy it and build again (When a build fails). Check addresses and networks before merging.

BMC certificates

The stock BareMetalHost template hard-codes disableCertificateVerification: true, with no setting to change it. Keep BMCs on a restricted network.

Three nodes

One entry per host; HighlyAvailable follows from the masters:

install:
  siteconfig:
    machineNetwork: [10.20.40.0/24]
    apiVIPs: [10.20.40.5]
    ingressVIPs: [10.20.40.6]
    nodes:
      m0.bm-ha.dc1.example.com:
        bmcAddress: redfish-virtualmedia://10.20.0.21/redfish/v1/Systems/1
        bootMACAddress: "00:11:22:33:44:01"
      m1.bm-ha.dc1.example.com: ...
      m2.bm-ha.dc1.example.com: ...
Image-based install

siteconfig.templates: ibi. Single node only. Needs the multicluster engine image-based-install-operator component, which you enable yourself, and a host preinstalled with a seed image at version.

See Scaling to add and remove workers.

Needs OpenShift Virtualization and a LoadBalancer implementation such as MetalLB on the hub; the hosted API server is a LoadBalancer Service.

oc create secret generic kubevirt-secret -n open-cluster-management \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub

# fleet/hcp-kubevirt.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  platform: KubeVirt # (1)!
  credential:
