    namespace: open-cluster-management
    name: kubevirt-secret
  nodePools:
    workers: # (2)!
      replicas: 2
  1. engine defaults to hypershift; platform has no default, and without it the render fails with install.platform is required. Without baseDomain, HyperShift uses the hub's ingress domain.
  2. NodePool hcp-kubevirt-workers. The chart generates clusterName, the platform and management.upgradeType (Replace on KubeVirt), and merges this map over them. It always sets the release image itself and ignores release here. Without replicas the pool has 0 nodes.

Needs:

  • An AgentServiceConfig (stack.cim on the hub, as for bare metal) and a LoadBalancer implementation on the hub, as for KubeVirt.
  • An InfraEnv in agentNamespace, with hosts booted from its discovery ISO, approved, and labeled to match agentLabelSelector. PolicyStack creates none of this; follow Host inventory (create the InfraEnv, boot the ISO, approve with oc patch agent <id> -n hardware-inventory --type merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}', then oc label agent <id> -n hardware-inventory example.com/cluster=hcp-agent).
  • DNS for *.apps.<cluster>.<baseDomain> at the guest ingress. In values/clusters/hcp-agent.yaml, the metallb element runs as Day-2 config on the hosted cluster and gives its router a fixed address (10.20.13.10) for that record. The hub-side MetalLB pool for the hosted API comes from the same file's install.manifests.
oc create namespace hcp-credentials
oc create secret generic hostinventory -n hcp-credentials \
  --from-file=pullSecret=pull-secret.json --from-file=ssh-publickey=id_ed25519.pub

# fleet/hcp-agent.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  platform: Agent
  credential:
    namespace: hcp-credentials
    name: hostinventory
  baseDomain: dc1.example.com
  agentNamespace: hardware-inventory
  nodePools:
    workers:
      replicas: 2
      platform:
        agent:
          agentLabelSelector: # (1)!
            matchLabels:
              example.com/cluster: hcp-agent
  1. A pool without a selector claims any free Agent in agentNamespace.

Use it for VMs or hosts that ACM cannot provision. No machines are created: you boot each worker from the NodePool's Ignition. No InfraEnv or Agents are involved. Needs a credential with pullSecret and ssh-publickey, created like the Agent tab's hcp-credentials/hostinventory, a hub LoadBalancer, and DNS for *.apps.<cluster>.<baseDomain> at the workers (router on host ports 80/443).

# fleet/hcp-none.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
install:
  platform: None
  credential:
    namespace: hcp-credentials
    name: hostinventory
  baseDomain: dc1.example.com
  nodePools:
    workers: {}

Add a worker once the HostedCluster is up. The hosted control plane runs in namespace <install.namespace>-<cluster> (clusters-hcp-none here); the admin kubeconfig Secret is in install.namespace (clusters).

# Ignition pointer config with the ignition server URL, token and CA
oc get secret -n clusters-hcp-none -o name | grep user-data-hcp-none-workers \
  | xargs oc get -n clusters-hcp-none -o jsonpath='{.data.value}' | base64 -d > worker.ign
# Boot RHCOS with worker.ign as Ignition or cloud user data, then approve its CSRs twice,
# a minute apart: client, then serving certificate
oc extract secret/hcp-none-admin-kubeconfig -n clusters --to=- > hcp-none.kubeconfig
oc --kubeconfig hcp-none.kubeconfig get csr -o name | xargs oc --kubeconfig hcp-none.kubeconfig adm certificate approve

Workers on AWS

The default service network 172.31.0.0/16 is the AWS default VPC range. Set hostedCluster.spec.networking.serviceNetwork to another range at create. A single worker also needs hostedCluster.spec.infrastructureAvailabilityPolicy: SingleReplica.

items.title: Values
items.text:
Lifecycle uses the same values cascade as Day-2, starting from lifecycle/values.yaml, the lifecycle chart's defaults (every install key, commented). The fleet file's install ranks above every layer.

Upstream's example layers. copier doesn't copy them into your repository: copy the one you need from upstream's values/platforms/ into your values/platforms/, and read it first (Example files).

Layer Sets values/platforms/aws.yaml engine: hive, credential hive-credentials/aws, 3 control-plane + 3 worker m6i.xlarge, OVNKubernetes with machine network 10.0.0.0/16 values/platforms/vmware.yaml engine: hive, credential hive-credentials/vsphere, 3 control-plane + 3 worker amd64 at installer default size values/platforms/baremetal.yaml engine: siteconfig, credentials bm-credentials/hostinventory and bm-credentials/bmc values/platforms/kubevirt.yaml platform: KubeVirt, credential open-cluster-management/kubevirt-secret, 2 workers values/platforms/agent.yaml platform: Agent, credential hcp-credentials/hostinventory, agentNamespace: hardware-inventory

aws, vmware and baremetal also select the matching infraNodes and storageNodes Day-2 policies, so imported clusters on those platforms list the same layer; lifecycle reads only its install.

The AWS example, with a copy of platforms/aws.yaml:

# fleet/ocp-aws.yaml
revision: main
hub: acm-dc1
version: 4.20.8
channel: stable-4.20
valueFiles:
  - platforms/aws.yaml
install:
  baseDomain: aws.example.com
  hive:
    platform:
      aws:
        region: us-east-2

version and channel belong in the fleet file only; CI rejects them in a layer (POLICY034, why). For per-cluster install settings you'd rather keep out of the fleet file, use values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml: it is read last, after every listed layer, and can also hold the cluster's Day-2 stack settings.

Shared layers reach the build too

  • Maps merge, lists replace (Merge rules): installConfig.compute in the fleet file replaces the layer's list.
  • Changing a fixed-at-create key like baseDomain in a layer turns every existing cluster reading it NonCompliant.
  • The lifecycle chart schema-checks every stack.* key in the layers it reads, so an element typo in a shared layer, such as certManager: Additional property enabeld is not allowed, also fails every lifecycle-<cluster> render that reads it.
  • global.remediationAction: inform (Dry run) also sets the lifecycle Policy to inform: nothing is built, and state: absent destroys nothing.

items.title: Watching a build
items.text:
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack present-lifecycle-<cluster>  # Compliant = built
oc get configurationpolicy -n local-cluster | grep <cluster>    # each step (Global Hub default-mode hub: run on the global hub with -n <managed-hub>)
oc get applications.argoproj.io lifecycle-<cluster> -n openshift-gitops -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'   # render errors
# each step's latest message. ACM's copy of the Policy in the hub's own namespace is named
# <policy-namespace>.<policy> (concepts/acm.md, How a Policy reaches a cluster)
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n local-cluster pstack.present-lifecycle-<cluster> \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.details[*]}{.templateMeta.name}{": "}{.history[0].message}{"\n"}{end}'
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack | grep <cluster>   # Day-2 elements, not covered by present-lifecycle

NonCompliant with Waiting for … on ready is normal until the install finishes; read the first step that isn't Compliant (The step chain). Errors and fixes: Troubleshooting.

Engine Progress Typical time hive oc get clusterdeployment -n <cluster>oc logs -f -n <cluster> -l hive.openshift.io/install=true -c installer 45 min on AWS siteconfig oc get clusterinstance,bmh,agentclusterinstall,agent -n <cluster> 1 h single node hypershift oc get hostedcluster,nodepool -n <install.namespace> (default clusters) Varies with platform

What each step does per engine: Policy chains.

items.title: When a build fails
items.text:
On hive and siteconfig a failed install is final: Hive gets installAttemptsLimit: 1, and SiteConfig refuses spec changes during install. present-ready stays NonCompliant either way.

Engine Failure shows as Recover hive ClusterDeployment condition ProvisionStopped=True Destroy and rebuild (steps below) siteconfig ClusterInstance condition Provisioned False Destroy and rebuild hypershift Step message; HyperShift keeps reconciling Fix a mutable value and merge; a fixed-at-create one needs the steps below 
oc get clusterdeployment -n <cluster> <cluster> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ProvisionStopped")]}'

To start over:

  1. Set state: absent and merge (Destroy). Keep install and its layers.
  2. Wait for absent-lifecycle-<cluster> to be Compliant.
  3. Fix the values, then remove state (or set state: present) and merge. The guard finds nothing left, so the build starts fresh.

On hive and siteconfig, present-credentials-<cluster> can report because it is being terminated until Namespace <cluster> from the destroy is gone. It clears on its own. Engine-specific failures: Troubleshooting.

items.title: Upgrades
items.text:
Bump version, and channel on a minor bump (OpenShift upgrades):

 # fleet/hcp-kubevirt.yaml
-version: 4.20.8
-channel: stable-4.20
+version: 4.21.2
+channel: stable-4.21
Engine How hive, siteconfig On the cluster, by the Day-2 upgrade element, like imported clusters. The hub keeps the install release image: Hive rejects changes to it, and the chart reads the siteconfig image set back from the live object. hypershift From the hub: the cluster step sets the HostedCluster release image to <install.releaseRepository>:<version>-multi, then each NodePool once the control plane reaches version (rules). KubeVirt pools replace VMs; others upgrade in place. Disconnected, channel needs install.hostedCluster.spec.updateService pointing at your OSUS, or the bump waits forever (Hosted clusters).

Watch a hypershift upgrade from the hub, reading the VERSION column:

oc get hostedcluster <cluster> -n <install.namespace>
oc get nodepool -n <install.namespace> | grep <cluster>

present-lifecycle-<cluster> is NonCompliant until the control plane and every NodePool reach version. A held downgrade, such as a reverted bump after the control plane moved, keeps it NonCompliant until version is back at or above the control plane's version. hypershift and hive clusters install from the -multi payload, so they are multi-architecture. siteconfig installs -x86_64 and stays single-architecture.

Minor upgrade blocked by ClusterVersionUpgradeable=False

HyperShift sets ClusterVersionUpgradeable=False on the HostedCluster when the guest reports a minor upgrade unsafe (for example, removed APIs still in use), and present-ready keeps waiting. Fix the cause if you can. To override, set the annotation to the exact release image. It forces only the image it names, so remove it after the upgrade:

install:
  hostedCluster:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        hypershift.openshift.io/force-upgrade-to: quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-release:4.21.2-multi

items.title: Scaling
items.text: Workers change after create through install.nodePools (hypershift: add a key for a new pool, change replicas to scale) and install.siteconfig.nodes (siteconfig). On hive, installConfig is read once at install; scale with MachineSets on the cluster (oc scale machineset, or the infraNodes/storageNodes elements).

items.title: Removing a NodePool
items.text:
Lifecycle creates NodePools with musthave, the ACM compliance type that makes sure an object exists and never deletes it (ACM policies in brief). Removing a nodePools entry only stops managing the pool; its nodes keep running. Remove the entry, then delete the pool:

oc delete nodepool <cluster>-<pool> -n clusters

A pool from a shared layer, like workers in platforms/kubevirt.yaml, cannot be removed from a higher layer (the schema rejects null). Scale it down:

install:
  nodePools:
    workers:
      replicas: 0

items.title: Scaling SiteConfig workers
items.text:
Note

Red Hat documents this flow for clusterType: SNO. On HighlyAvailable, SiteConfig accepts the same changes and its sample output shows it, but no doc covers it explicitly.

Scale out. Add a host with role: worker under install.siteconfig.nodes. The chart adds it to the ClusterInstance only after the install completes; that is also true for workers listed at create on a one-master cluster, which join by scale-out after the master is up. Before you merge:

  • The hub's admin kubeconfig for the cluster (Secret <cluster>-admin-kubeconfig in namespace <cluster>) still works. If the API certificate changed, update it first.
  • The bmcCredential Secret still exists on the hub. Without it present-credentials-<cluster> fails and present-cluster-<cluster> never applies the change.

present-ready-<cluster> stays NonCompliant until the host's Agent reports Done, and names the host once its BareMetalHost exists.

Scale in. Set remove: true on the worker. Masters and arbiters cannot be removed.

install:
  siteconfig:
    nodes:
      w0.bm-ha.dc1.example.com:
        role: worker
        bmcAddress: redfish-virtualmedia://10.20.0.24/redfish/v1/Systems/1
        bootMACAddress: "00:11:22:33:44:04"
        remove: true

present-cluster-<cluster> then runs SiteConfig's documented scale-in. Each write waits for the previous one:

Step Written to the node Waits for 1 extraAnnotations remove-agent-and-node-on-delete The annotation on the BareMetalHost 2 pruneManifests: BareMetalHost, InfraEnv, NMStateConfig BareMetalHost gone, SiteConfig done (observedGeneration) 3 Node dropped

BMAC (the BareMetal Agent Controller in assisted-service) drains the Node, deprovisions the host and removes the Agent and Node. Follow it with oc get bmh,agent -n <cluster>. Once present-ready-<cluster> is Compliant, delete the host's entry under install.siteconfig.nodes. Do not delete the fleet file: that abandons the cluster (Abandon). Cleaning is metadata only: data stays on the disks.

You do Result Delete a live node's entry, or rename it present-cluster fails with not install.siteconfig.nodes: SiteConfig would accept the drop and delete nothing, stranding the BareMetalHost, Agent and Node. Add a master to a live cluster present-cluster fails: is a new master. Clear remove before step 2 Scale-in cancelled. Clear remove after step 2 present-cluster fails: cannot be cancelled. remove on a worker still joining present-cluster fails: has not finished joining. Its drain would loop until SiteConfig's 30-minute timeout pauses the ClusterInstance. remove on a worker whose Node you already deleted Not detected: the hub cannot see spoke Nodes. The drain fails the same way, and the BareMetalHost's drain-status annotation shows failed to drain node. Removing a worker that never joined, or whose Node is gone

Either finish the install, or annotate its BareMetalHost so the drain gives up. BMAC honours this annotation, but no Red Hat doc covers it:

oc annotate bmh <host> -n <cluster> bmac.agent-install.openshift.io/drain-timeout=5m

The value is a Go duration, counted from the first drain attempt. If the ClusterInstance has already paused, also remove its paused annotation.

items.title: Destroy
items.text:
The hub detaches the cluster from ACM, deletes it through its engine, then cleans up the copied Secrets and install.manifests (Destroy and abandon). The credential is never deleted.

  1. Set state: absent and merge. Change nothing else:

     # fleet/ocp-aws.yaml
 revision: main
 hub: acm-dc1
+state: absent

    Keep install and its layers

    The absent Policy finds the cluster's objects through install.engine. Stripped of install and the valueFiles that set it, the engine falls back to hypershift: on a hive cluster the Policy detaches the ManagedCluster, "deletes" a HostedCluster that never existed and goes Compliant, while the ClusterDeployment and its cloud resources keep running. Deleting the fleet file after that orphans them.

  2. Wait for absent-lifecycle-<cluster> to be Compliant. Deleting the fleet file earlier abandons the cluster mid-destroy.

    oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n pstack absent-lifecycle-<cluster>  # Compliant = gone

  3. Delete the fleet file and values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml. To build a new cluster under the same name instead, remove state again (When a build fails).

  4. If the cluster ran the acs element and you will re-create it under the same name, delete it in ACS first, or Central refuses to register the new one under the old name (Re-register a cluster, step 1).

Until step 3, the absent Policy keeps running and deletes these again if anything re-creates them:

Engine Deleted hive Namespace <cluster>, install.manifests siteconfig Namespace <cluster>, ClusterImageSet lifecycle-<cluster>, install.manifests hypershift Secrets <cluster>-pull-secret, -ssh-key and -etcd-encryption-key in install.namespace, install.manifests Engine Left behind hive Nothing. Hive deprovisions the cloud resources or VMs, usually within 20 minutes. vSphere: the DNS records you created. siteconfig Hosts still running, disks not wiped. Power off or reuse. A worker scaled in is powered off with its disk metadata cleaned; data stays on disk. hypershift Agent Agents return to the InfraEnv for the next cluster. hypershift None Your workers and their DNS. Delete them.

items.title: Abandon
items.text:
Abandoning stops lifecycle from managing a cluster without destroying it (Destroy and abandon). The cluster keeps running and stays an ACM ManagedCluster: deleting a lifecycle Policy never deletes what it created.

You do Lifecycle Day-2 Remove hub, state and install together from the fleet file Abandoned Keeps its Applications and Policies Delete the fleet file Abandoned Its Applications and Policies are deleted too (Removal and pruning)

Remove all three keys: the validator rejects state or install without hub (POLICY050). Layers in valueFiles that set install can stay; nothing reads them without hub.

helm uninstall policystack leaves the ApplicationSets in place (helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, Install chart), so it abandons nothing. Deleting the ApplicationSets with oc delete abandons every cluster the hub built. To re-adopt, restore the keys or file with the same install: the root object still carries the ownership marker, so the guard accepts it.

Changing hub

Moving a cluster between hubs is not supported. Changing hub abandons the cluster on the old hub, which keeps running it. The new hub's lifecycle ApplicationSet now matches the file and runs the present Policy there; its guard finds no root object, so it builds a second, same-named cluster. It only takes over a root object that was restored or migrated onto it with the marker. Destroy the cluster on the old hub first. ACS: run steps 2-3 of Re-register a cluster after the move.

items.title: Hub disaster recovery
items.text:
A DR hub takes over the hubName of the hub it replaces (The hub). ACM backup leaves out PolicyStack's ApplicationSets and their Applications (velero.io/exclude-from-backup), so a passive hub (one receiving ACM backups but not managing clusters) builds nothing. Do not install PolicyStack on it before takeover: with the same hubName, its lifecycle ApplicationSet would match the same fleet files and, finding no root objects of its own, build a second copy of every cluster. To take over:

  1. Make sure the old hub stays down, or delete its ApplicationSets (oc delete applicationset -n openshift-gitops policystack policystack-lifecycle). Two hubs with one hubName both act on the same fleet files.
  2. Run the ACM activation restore with veleroManagedClustersBackupName: latest in the Restore resource (Business continuity). ClusterDeployments, ClusterInstances and ManagedClusters come back with their annotations.
  3. hypershift: restore the HostedClusters with the OADP procedure in Hosted control planes. ACM backup does not include them, and without them the hub builds new, empty control planes.
  4. Install PolicyStack with the old hub's hubName. No fleet edits: the restored root objects carry the ownership marker, so the new hub owns them.

items.title: Operator versions
items.text: How to pin, upgrade, stop managing and uninstall the OLM operators elements install. The examples use the metallb element.

items.title: How an element installs an operator
items.text:
Term Meaning Subscription Asks OLM for an operator package from a catalog channel. CSV ClusterServiceVersion: one installed version of the operator, such as metallb-operator.v4.20.0-<build>. InstallPlan OLM's proposal to install or upgrade to a CSV; it runs only once approved. OperatorGroup Tells OLM which namespaces the operator watches.

An element declares each operator under stack.<element>.operatorPolicies.<key> in its values.yaml. The element's README lists them under Operators, with package, channel and namespace (stack/metallb/README.md). Each entry renders Policy install's three templates, install-<key>-ns, OperatorPolicy install-<key> and the install-<key>-status check (The install Policy). This page is about the OperatorPolicy.

The OperatorPolicy owns the Subscription's approval mode:

  • Enforced, with upgradeApproval: Automatic (the default) and an empty versions list, it sets the Subscription to installPlanApproval: Automatic. OLM then installs every new CSV the channel offers as soon as it appears, on every cluster, whatever the cluster's fleet revision.
  • Enforced in every other case, it sets Manual and approves InstallPlans itself, only for CSVs it allows. Under inform it leaves the Subscription's approval mode as it is.

Elements ship with versions: [], so by default every operator follows its channel.

items.title: Choosing a behavior
items.text:
Set these on stack.<element>.operatorPolicies.<key> in a values layer.

Goal Set Result when enforced Follow the channel Nothing (default) OLM installs every upgrade the channel offers. Pin versions and subscription.startingCSV (Pinning) Approves an InstallPlan only for a CSV in versions or startingCSV. Unpin versions: [] and subscription.startingCSV: "" in a later layer, or delete the pin Back to following the channel. startingCSV is a separate key, so versions: [] alone leaves it set and a new cluster installs that old CSV first. Install once upgradeApproval: None Approves the first install only, never an upgrade. Change channel subscription.channel (Changing channel) The Subscription moves to the new channel. Stop managing enabled: false (Stopping and uninstalling) The operator stays installed, unmanaged. Uninstall complianceType: mustnothave (Stopping and uninstalling) Deletes the Subscription, the CSV and an unused OperatorGroup.
  • The OperatorPolicy owns approval. subscription.installPlanApproval fails the render with a schema error. upgradeApproval accepts only Automatic or None: Manual renders, CI fails it (POLICY030), and on a cluster the Policy reports the OperatorPolicy's validation error. A manual policy is a versions pin or upgradeApproval: None.
  • Under inform, including a dry run, nothing is approved or created. A new cluster gets no operator and the Policy reports NonCompliant. A non-empty versions also flags an installed CSV missing from it. An installed operator whose Subscription is Automatic keeps upgrading: OLM approves those InstallPlans itself.
  • versions holds exact CSV names; wildcards are not supported.
  • The hub's ACM and GitOps operators follow the same rules once their elements are on (Hand the operators to PolicyStack).

items.title: Pinning
items.text:
operatorPolicies is a map, so a layer sets only the fields it changes (Merge rules):

# values/environments/prod.yaml
stack:
  metallb:
    operatorPolicies:
      metallb: # (1)!
        versions:
          - metallb-operator.v4.20.0-<build> # (2)!
        subscription:
          startingCSV: metallb-operator.v4.20.0-<build> # (3)!
  1. The key the element defines in its values.yaml. A layer cannot add an operator: a key the element doesn't define, such as the typo metalb, fails the render with operatorPolicies.metalb has no subscription.name - a values layer may set an operator the element does not define, and CI fails it as POLICY032 (Validator rules). Add operators in the element.
  2. The CSV the clusters run: oc get csv -n metallb-system on a managed cluster.
  3. A new Subscription starts at the channel head, the newest CSV in the channel. If that isn't in versions, its InstallPlan is never approved, the operator never installs and the Policy stays NonCompliant. startingCSV makes OLM install the pinned CSV instead. Omit it only when the pin is the channel head.

A pin in a shared layer applies to every cluster reading it

A cluster running a CSV not in versions goes NonCompliant (ClusterServiceVersion (<csv>) is not an approved version) and its next upgrade is held. List every CSV the clusters in that layer run, or pin in each cluster file.

items.title: Bumping
items.text:
A pinned operator with an upgrade available stays Compliant, so nothing flags it. The held upgrade appears only in the compliance message, as an InstallPlan to update to [<csv>] is available for approval.

To bump a pinned operator:

  1. Find the held CSV in the message:

    # on the hub: the replicated install Policy of the element
oc describe policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n prod-east-1 pstack.install-metallb-prod-east-1

# on the managed cluster: the OperatorPolicy, in the namespace named after the cluster
oc get operatorpolicy install-metallb -n prod-east-1 \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="InstallPlanCompliant")].message}'

  2. Add that CSV, not a later one, next to the old one, and leave startingCSV alone. Promote it (Promoting and rolling back): the change is one commit, so clusters pinned to that branch get it at merge, and tag-pinned clusters get it one fleet PR at a time.

  3. Once every cluster reading the layer runs the new CSV, drop the old one, set startingCSV to the new one, and promote again.

Dropping the old CSV from both versions and startingCSV in one change makes every cluster still on it NonCompliant until it upgrades, and forever if the new CSV isn't its next step. Bumps don't roll back: OLM cannot downgrade, so removing the new CSV after clusters upgraded leaves them NonCompliant on the same message.

Why only the next CSV can be approved

OLM picks that CSV from the channel's upgrade graph: each CSV names the ones it replaces, so OLM offers only the next step from the running CSV, not the channel head. The OperatorPolicy only approves or holds it. Only the CSV in the message can be approved: listing a later one holds the upgrade forever, and reaching a target can take several bumps. One InstallPlan can carry the CSVs of several operators in the same namespace. On a versions pin the message ends with but approval for [<csv>] is required, listing every CSV in it that no OperatorPolicy in that namespace allows yet. Once all are allowed, the InstallPlan is approved.

# each channel of a package and its newest CSV
oc get packagemanifest <package> -n openshift-marketplace \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.channels[*]}{.name}: {.currentCSV}{"\n"}{end}'

items.title: Changing channel
items.text:
Set subscription.channel in a layer. The OperatorPolicy updates the Subscription, and OLM offers the new channel's upgrade. An unpinned operator upgrades as soon as the new channel is set. With a pin, add the CSV it offers as in Bumping. Move one minor at a time: OLM's upgrade graph only links a CSV to the versions it replaces, so skipping a channel can leave no path from the running CSV, and the upgrade never comes.

stack:
  lvm:
    operatorPolicies:
      lvms:
        subscription:
          channel: stable-4.21 # was stable-4.20

items.title: Stopping and uninstalling
items.text:
enabled: false stops managing the operator. It stays installed, and its Subscription keeps the approval mode the OperatorPolicy last set: a pinned or None operator stays on Manual and never upgrades again unless someone approves InstallPlans by hand; an unpinned one stays Automatic and keeps upgrading with nothing watching it. To manage it again, write enabled: true in a later layer or remove the false (What renders).

complianceType: mustnothave uninstalls it through the OperatorPolicy's removalBehavior. The Namespace template is not rendered, so other operators in a shared namespace are untouched. install-<key>-status reads NonCompliant until the CSV is gone.

removalBehavior key Default Other value operatorGroups DeleteIfUnused Keep subscriptions Delete Keep clusterServiceVersions Delete Keep customResourceDefinitions Keep Delete, which also deletes every resource of those CRDs cluster-wide

Operands stay

Uninstalling deletes the operator but leaves what it manages. The MetalLB instance, IPAddressPools and other custom resources stay, with no controller and, with CRDs kept, nothing to clean them up. Templates that wait on the operator cannot prune them either: CI rejects pruneObjectBehavior on any template with a dependency (POLICY033).

To uninstall cleanly, remove the operands while the operator still runs to process their finalizers:

  1. PR: turn off the templates that create operands, so nothing recreates them. Their objects stay on the cluster.

    # values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  metallb:
    policies:
      config:
        templates:
          metallb-instance:
            enabled: false # (1)!
      addressing:
        enabled: false # (2)!
    1. The only template of Policy config, which waits on metallb. With it off, config-metallb-<cluster> is no longer rendered. policies.config.enabled: false does the same.
    2. addressing depends on Policy config. The render doesn't check Policy dependencies, so if it were on it would still render and, on the cluster, sit Pending on a Policy that no longer exists. Turn off every Policy that depends on one you remove. addressing ships off; this line only matters where a layer turned it on.

  2. On the cluster, delete the operands: oc delete metallb,ipaddresspools,l2advertisements,bgpadvertisements,bgppeers -n metallb-system --all.

  3. PR: in the same layer as step 1, set the operator to mustnothave:

    # values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  metallb:
    # policies: as in step 1
    operatorPolicies:
      metallb:
        complianceType: mustnothave

Keep both changes in one layer. The render checks each cluster's merged values and fails, for enabled: false as for mustnothave, while an enabled template still waits on the operator:

waitForOperator "metallb" on policy "config" matches no enabled entry in operatorPolicies
waitForOperator "metallb" on policy "config" names an operator with complianceType mustnothave, which is being uninstalled

items.title: Rolling out changes
items.text:
How a change gets from a commit to your clusters, how to preview it, and how to take things away. Adding a cluster is in First cluster, operator versions in Operator versions.

Rollout follows from two facts (Fleet files has the full model):

  1. Argo CD reads fleet/<cluster>.yaml only from the default branch, so any edit to it, a pin move included, takes effect when it merges there.
  2. Everything else (stack/, values.yaml, values/) is read at the commit the file's revision names, so each cluster can run a different commit.

items.title: Choosing a pin
items.text:
revision A change reaches the cluster Use for Branch, such as main Within minutes of every merge to that branch, with no further step Lab and nonprod clusters you want current Tag, such as v1.5.0 Only when a fleet PR moves revision to a tag that has it Production: each move is reviewed and gets its own Render Diff Commit SHA Same as a tag One-off pins, such as a dry run

A common setup: nonprod pins main, prod pins tags, and a fleet PR promotes prod one cluster or one wave at a time.

What a pin does not freeze

Operators left on versions: [] upgrade whenever their channel ships a new CSV (Operator versions). The fleet keys version and channel apply when the fleet file merges, whatever the pin (OpenShift upgrades).

A branch pin bypasses fleet/ review

Protecting fleet/ (Protect the repository) only gates pin moves. A cluster with revision: main takes every merge to stack/, values/ and values.yaml without a fleet/ reviewer. That includes install keys that resize hub-built clusters, or that the engine refuses, which then blocks that cluster's later changes (Immutable fields). Pin production to tags, or also require review on values/ and stack/.

Tags are yours to create: Argo CD reads only your repository, and copier copies none of upstream's tags into it. Tag the commit you want to release:

git tag v1.5.0 <sha>
git push origin v1.5.0

Argo CD follows a tag wherever it points. Anyone with push rights can move or delete it, which changes every cluster pinned to it, or stops generation if it is gone (When a revision breaks). Protect v* with a GitHub tag ruleset that blocks updates and deletion, or pin SHAs.

items.title: Reviewing a change
items.text:
On a PR to the default branch, the Render Diff job renders every fleet cluster at its revision before and after the merge and comments what each cluster's Policies gain, lose or change. Read it before you merge: it is the only place a PR shows its effect on real clusters.

It shows only clusters whose rendered output changes. A change to stack/ or values/ doesn't appear for clusters pinned to a tag; it appears later, in the PR that moves their pin.

No comment means no fleet cluster changes, but only if the Render diff check ran and passed. It is also absent when:

  • the render job failed: the comment job depends on it, so check the run;
  • the PR touches none of stack/, lifecycle/, values/, values.yaml, fleet/ (install/ is never rendered, see Upgrading PolicyStack);
  • the PR targets a branch other than the default branch;
  • your repository has no fleet files yet;
  • the PR comes from another repository, such as a personal fork of your repository: its result goes to the run's job summary instead.

items.title: Promoting and rolling back
items.text:
Promote a tag- or SHA-pinned cluster with a fleet PR. Its Render Diff shows the Policy changes for that cluster:

 # fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
-revision: v1.4.0
+revision: v1.5.0

Moving a pin updates the cluster in place. Application names are <element>-<cluster> and carry no revision, so Argo CD patches the existing Policies rather than deleting and recreating them: nothing is removed from the cluster and compliance history continues. The Placement selects the cluster by its name label, which doesn't change with the revision, so the Policies stay bound throughout. An element that exists only at the new revision gets a new Application. One missing there loses its Application and its Policies (Removing an element).

Roll back the same way you rolled forward:

Cluster pins Roll back by Review A tag or SHA Setting the old revision in the fleet file, or reverting the pin commit fleet/ review applies A branch git revert of the commit that changed stack/ or values/ Whatever protects those paths. fleet/ review does not apply.

What a rollback leaves on the cluster

  • Templates default to complianceType: musthave, which only adds and patches. Fields the newer revision added stay unless the template is mustonlyhave; objects it added stay unless the template sets pruneObjectBehavior (ConfigurationPolicy).
  • A Policy that exists only in the newer revision is deleted. What it created stays, unless its template sets pruneObjectBehavior (What happens on the managed cluster).
  • OLM cannot downgrade an operator. Putting the old CSV back in versions leaves the Policy NonCompliant: ClusterServiceVersion (<csv>) is not an approved version (Operator versions).
  • Rolling back past the commit that added an element deletes that element's Application and Policies.

items.title: Dry run
items.text:
A dry run makes every Policy report what it would change instead of changing it. Set global.remediationAction: inform in any layer (Global keys). policy-library, the Helm library every element renders through (How an element is built), writes it into every Policy's spec.remediationAction, lifecycle Policies included, and ACM applies a Policy's action to all its templates, OperatorPolicies too. Nothing is created, patched, deleted or approved.

Read the result per Policy (Compliance states):

  • Compliant: enforcing would change nothing.

  • NonCompliant: enforcing would change something. The template's status message names the objects that differ:

    oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n prod-east-1  # replicated Policies, on the hub
oc describe policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n prod-east-1 pstack.<policy>-<element>-prod-east-1

To dry-run one cluster, put the key in its cluster file, at the revision the cluster reads:

# values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
global:
  remediationAction: inform # (1)!
  1. enforce is rejected by the schema. Remove the key to return to each Policy's own action. Templates set remediationAction: InformOnly stay inform either way: they are checks other templates wait on, and ACM never enforces them.

How you get the key to the cluster depends on its pin:

Branch pinTag pin

Two PRs. The first adds the key together with the change; check the Policies once they evaluate. The second removes the key, and enforcement starts.

A tag-pinned cluster reads its cluster file at the tag, so a key added on the default branch never reaches it. To preview v1.5.0 on a cluster at v1.4.0:

  1. Branch from v1.5.0, commit the key, and push the branch.
  2. Fleet PR: pin that commit's SHA. Check the Policies.
  3. Fleet PR: pin v1.5.0. It lacks the key, so enforcement resumes.

Keep the branch until step 3 merges. A commit no branch or tag reaches can stop being fetchable, which stops generation (When a revision breaks).

Limits of a dry run

  • It does not stop removal. Only Policies that still exist at the new revision get the inform update. A Policy the new revision drops or renames is deleted from the hub, and its copy on the cluster was last seen as enforce. If its template sets pruneObjectBehavior, its objects are deleted (What happens on the managed cluster). Argo CD also keeps pruning and self-healing as usual. Check the "removed" counts in the PR's Render Diff first.
  • It undoes nothing already applied.
  • On a new cluster it previews only the first Policy of each dependency chain. A Policy that depends on another (Dependencies) needs it Compliant; under inform nothing is applied, so the first stays NonCompliant and the rest stay Pending without evaluating. In metallb, config waits on install and addressing waits on config, so only install reports.
  • An OperatorPolicy under inform installs nothing, but an installed operator whose Subscription is Automatic keeps upgrading: OLM approves those InstallPlans itself (Operator versions).

items.title: Disabling an element
items.text:
Set enabled: false in a layer listed after every layer that enables the element (Order). values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml is always last, so it can turn off anything for one cluster. Upstream's example environments/prod.yaml enables dns; to turn it off on prod-east-1:

# values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  dns:
    enabled: false
  remediations:
    policies:
      samples:
        enabled: false # (1)!
  1. enabled: false on a policy, template or operator turns off one part of an element (How an element is built).

What happens:

  1. The element renders nothing. Its Application stays and syncs to zero objects; allowEmpty lets it, where Argo CD would otherwise refuse to prune an Application down to nothing (Applications).
  2. Argo CD prunes the element's Policies, Placement and PlacementBinding from the hub.
  3. ACM removes the policies from the cluster. What they created stays, unless a template sets pruneObjectBehavior (What happens on the managed cluster).

If the render fails, nothing is pruned: the Application shows ComparisonError and sync status Unknown, and the last Policies stay in place until the error is fixed (When an Application fails).

items.title: Removing an element
items.text:
To drop an element from the repository:

  1. Delete stack/<element>.
  2. In the same PR, delete every stack.<elementKey> block (the element name in camelCase, cert-manager → certManager) under values/ and in values.yaml. CI checks every values file, listed in a fleet file or not, and fails a key that names no element (POLICY035).
  3. Promote as usual. When a cluster's revision no longer has the element, the ApplicationSet deletes that cluster's Application and its Policies. Clusters pinned to older revisions keep it until their pin moves.

Disabling and deleting both delete the Policies and leave the objects. Disabling is per cluster and reversible with one line. Deleting removes it everywhere, cluster by cluster as pins move. Other events that delete Applications: What deletes an Application.

items.title: Offboarding a cluster
items.text:
Delete fleet/<cluster>.yaml in a PR, and values/clusters/<cluster>.yaml with it (otherwise CI warns that no fleet file reads it). The cluster's Applications and Policies are deleted, and what the Policies created stays unless a template prunes. The cluster stays imported in ACM; detach it there if you want it gone.

If the file sets hub, the hub built the cluster and you choose what happens to it (Cluster lifecycle):

DestroyAbandon

Set state: absent, wait for Policy absent-lifecycle-<cluster> to be Compliant, then delete the file (Destroy).

Delete the file, or remove hub, state and install together (POLICY050 rejects state or install without hub). Either way lifecycle-<cluster> and its Policies are deleted, the cluster keeps running and stays in ACM, and lifecycle never changes or destroys it again (Abandon). Removing the keys keeps its element Applications. Deleting the file deletes those too, and templates with pruneObjectBehavior prune on the still-attached cluster.

Don't reuse a cluster name while its fleet file exists

The hub finds a cluster's fleet file by ManagedCluster name only. Any cluster imported under that name immediately gets Applications for every element the file and its layers enable.

items.title: Pausing removals
items.text:
The element Applications follow the cluster Secrets in openshift-gitops: if a cluster's Secret, or its clusterID label, disappears even briefly, the ApplicationSet deletes that cluster's Applications and their Policies. Pause deletions before an ACM upgrade or any work on those Secrets. An ACM upgrade that changes how GitOpsCluster builds cluster Secrets can replace one under a new name.

Pause both ApplicationSets. policystack-lifecycle pairs fleet files with the hub's own Secret, and losing its Applications abandons every cluster the hub built.

# pause deletes; creates and updates continue
for a in policystack policystack-lifecycle; do
  oc patch applicationset $a -n openshift-gitops --type merge \
    -p '{"spec":{"syncPolicy":{"applicationsSync":"create-update"}}}'
done

While paused, a deleted fleet file or element keeps its Applications and Policies. They are deleted when you resume.

Resume once every ManagedCluster has a Secret with a clusterID:

oc get managedclusters
oc get secrets -n openshift-gitops -l argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type=cluster -L clusterID
for a in policystack policystack-lifecycle; do
  oc patch applicationset $a -n openshift-gitops --type json \
    -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/syncPolicy/applicationsSync"}]'
done

Note

helm upgrade of the install chart does not remove the patch; resume by hand. The field has no effect if the Argo CD ApplicationSet controller runs with an explicit --policy, which takes precedence.

items.title: OpenShift upgrades
items.text: You set the OpenShift version each cluster should run in its fleet file. PolicyStack moves the cluster there, never backwards, and reports progress as Policy compliance on the hub.

items.title: The target is in the fleet file
items.text:
version and channel are keys of fleet/<cluster>.yaml (fleet/hubs/<hubName>.yaml for a hub). Like every fleet key, they are read from the default branch, not at the cluster's revision (Fleet files), and the ApplicationSet passes them to each of the cluster's Applications as Helm values. A merged bump reaches the cluster within about 6 minutes even if the cluster pins an old tag. The revision only decides which version of the upgrade element's code runs.

Fleet key Effect version OpenShift release x.y.z the cluster should run. Unset, nothing upgrades the cluster. On a cluster a hub builds it is required, because it first picks the install image; the lifecycle render fails with version is required without it. Bumping it never reinstalls a hive or siteconfig cluster: the upgrade element upgrades it like any standalone cluster. channel Update channel, such as stable-4.21. Unset, the cluster's channel is left as it is.

Always the full x.y.z

version: 4.20 is read as the number 4.2 (Quote numbers and booleans). CI rejects any version that isn't x.y.z (POLICY050). If one is merged without CI, the upgrade-guard check stays NonCompliant and nothing upgrades.

Not in a values layer

CI rejects version: or channel: at the root of a values file, outside stack: (POLICY034). The fleet keys outrank every values file, so a layer's version would be ignored where the fleet file sets one and would silently upgrade every other cluster reading the layer, with no fleet diff to review. POLICY034 is a CI check: Argo CD itself would apply the layer value.

items.title: The cluster must offer the target
items.text: On a standalone cluster version must be a direct update from the running version, listed under Recommended updates by oc adm upgrade on the cluster (ClusterVersion status.availableUpdates). That list comes from the update graph for the cluster's channel, served by Red Hat (api.openshift.com) or by your own OpenShift Update Service (Update service). That is why a minor bump changes channel too.

items.title: Who upgrades what
items.text: Cluster Upgraded by Writes Standalone: imported, built by hive or siteconfig (Pick an engine), and every hub The upgrade element, a Day-2 element on by default, running on the cluster ClusterVersion spec.channel, spec.upstream, spec.desiredUpdate Hosted control plane built by a hub (hypershift engine) That hub's present-lifecycle-<cluster> Policy, rendered by Application lifecycle-<cluster> (How a Policy builds a cluster) HostedCluster and NodePool release (Hosted control planes) Hosted control plane PolicyStack did not build Nobody. Upgrade its HostedCluster on the hub that hosts it

items.title: Upgrade a cluster
items.text:
These steps are for standalone clusters. For a hypershift-built cluster do step 2 only and watch as in Hosted control planes.

  1. On the cluster, run oc adm upgrade and pick a version under Recommended updates. For a minor upgrade the list only shows the new minor once the channel moves: merge the channel change alone first (it upgrades nothing), then read the list again.

  2. Edit the fleet file in a PR:

     # fleet/prod-east-1.yaml
 revision: v3.0.0
-version: 4.20.8
+version: 4.20.12
 channel: stable-4.20

    On a minor bump channel moves too (stable-4.20 to stable-4.21), in this commit or already merged in step 1. The Render Diff comment lists the cluster, because its upgrade Policy changes.

  3. Merge. Within about 6 minutes the cluster's upgrade-upgrade-<cluster> Policy (policy upgrade of element upgrade, see Rendered names) turns NonCompliant and the upgrade starts. Watch it.

Several fleet files bumped in one commit upgrade at the same time: nothing orders or staggers clusters. To stage a fleet, use one PR per group and open the next once the last group's Policies are Compliant.

items.title: The upgrade element
items.text:
The element is on by default for every cluster. It renders nothing, not even a Placement, until the fleet file sets version or channel or a layer sets stack.upgrade.config.upstream. With version: 4.20.12 and channel: stable-4.20 on cluster prod-east-1 it renders two Policies:

Policy Renders when Template (ConfigurationPolicy) Action Does channel-upgrade-prod-east-1 channel or stack.upgrade.config.upstream set channel-pin enforce Sets ClusterVersion spec.channel and spec.upstream, each only when set. Not held by the guard, so a disconnected cluster reaches its update service before the guard needs it. upgrade-upgrade-prod-east-1 version set upgrade-guard InformOnly NonCompliant unless version is in availableUpdates, is already the desired version, or is at or below the running version. upgrade-trigger enforce Waits for the guard. Sets desiredUpdate.version only while version is newer than the running version and no update is progressing. Clears image and force (Brownfield clusters). upgrade-progress InformOnly Waits for the trigger. NonCompliant until the cluster has completed version.
  • In the Policy names, <cluster> is the ManagedCluster name, or hubName on a hub.
  • InformOnly is an action ACM keeps at inform even when the Policy says enforce, so the guard and progress checks never change the cluster (inform, enforce and InformOnly).
  • Waits for is an ACM dependency (Waiting and ordering). While the guard is NonCompliant the trigger is Pending and writes nothing. ignorePending counts Pending as Compliant, so the Policy's status shows the guard's reason, not a wall of Pending.
  • The guard and progress templates show as mustnothave on ClusterVersion version in the console. That object always exists, so the check is a deliberate way to report NonCompliant. Both are InformOnly: nothing deletes your ClusterVersion.
  • The NonCompliant message ends with the ClusterVersion conditions that explain it: always Progressing, Failing or Invalid when True, and ReleaseAccepted or RetrievedUpdates when False.

items.title: Watch an upgrade
items.text:
# on the hub: each template's latest message
oc get policies.policy.open-cluster-management.io -n prod-east-1 pstack.upgrade-upgrade-prod-east-1 \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.details[*]}{.templateMeta.name}{": "}{.history[0].message}{"\n"}{end}'
# on the cluster
oc adm upgrade

For a hub, the namespace is local-cluster and the name uses hubName: -n local-cluster pstack.upgrade-upgrade-<hubName>.

Phase upgrade-guard upgrade-trigger upgrade-progress Held NonCompliant, with Progressing and, if they explain it, RetrievedUpdates or ReleaseAccepted Pending Pending Running Compliant Compliant NonCompliant, ...; Progressing: Working towards 4.20.12... Done Compliant Compliant Compliant

items.title: When it does not move
items.text: You see Cause Fix Guard NonCompliant, minor bump channel still names the old minor (or is unset), whose graph has no edge to version Set channel to the new minor. Guard NonCompliant, version is in the channel version needs an intermediate hop, is only a conditional update (known risks, listed by oc adm upgrade --include-not-recommended), or availableUpdates is empty Pick a version oc adm upgrade recommends; hop in several bumps. Conditional updates are not supported: keep version at the running version, run oc adm upgrade --allow-not-recommended --to <version> by hand, and set version to it once the update completes. Empty list: check the channel and the update service (Update service). Progress NonCompliant, the ReleaseAccepted message names a failed precondition Upgradeable=False blocks a minor upgrade, often an admin-ack Fix the cause on the cluster, such as setting the acknowledgement in ConfigMap admin-acks in openshift-config as the message says. There is no force for standalone clusters. All Compliant, cluster runs an older version than the fleet's Lowered or reverted version: a target at or below the running version counts as reached OpenShift does not downgrade. Set version to what the cluster runs. A bump reverted after the update started still finishes. All Compliant, cluster runs a newer version than the fleet's Someone ran oc adm upgrade --to past the fleet version. The trigger only moves clusters forward to version, so it lets this through and nothing flags it Set version to what the cluster runs.

items.title: Brownfield clusters
items.text: A brownfield cluster is one upgraded by hand before PolicyStack. The Cluster Version Operator (CVO) ignores desiredUpdate.version while desiredUpdate.image is set, and oc adm upgrade and the console leave the running image there. The trigger therefore writes image: '' and force: false next to the version, leaving desiredUpdate.architecture (set when a cluster moved to the multi-arch payload) as it is. While the fleet version is newer than the running one, a pending oc or console request that has not started is replaced, and a hand-set force (or --to-image) does not survive.

items.title: Update service
items.text:
channel-pin sets spec.upstream from stack.upgrade.config.upstream. Empty (the default) leaves the cluster's value alone; a cluster with none uses Red Hat's public graph. A disconnected cluster has no reachable graph, so availableUpdates stays empty and every bump holds at the guard. Point it at a local OpenShift Update Service (OSUS) in a values layer, and see Disconnected clusters for the CA and mirrored images it also needs:

# values/datacenters/dc1.yaml
stack:
  upgrade:
    config:
      upstream: https://osus.example.internal/api/upgrades_info/v1/graph

Warning

Removing the key leaves the last URL on the cluster, since the template then stops setting the field. To go back to the public graph, set upstream: https://api.openshift.com/api/upgrades_info/v1/graph. policies.channel.enabled: false stops managing upstream too.

items.title: Holding and pausing
items.text:
To hold one cluster back, leave its version alone.

To stop PolicyStack writing ClusterVersion on a cluster altogether, turn the policies off in a layer the cluster reads:

# values/clusters/prod-east-1.yaml
stack:
  upgrade:
    policies:
      upgrade:
        enabled: false # (1)!
      channel:
        enabled: false # (2)!
  1. Deletes upgrade-upgrade-<cluster>. What the trigger already wrote stays on ClusterVersion, so an update the trigger already requested still runs.
  2. Stops managing the channel and upstream. The cluster keeps the last values.

Pause before you bump

Values layers are read at the cluster's revision, but version is read at the default branch. A tag-pinned cluster sees the pause only once its revision includes it: tag the pause commit and move the pin in a fleet PR merged before the bump (same steps as the Tag pin tab in Dry run). And the trigger writes desiredUpdate on its first evaluation after the bump, so a pause merged after the bump is usually too late.

global.remediationAction: inform in a layer also stops the trigger, along with every other Policy of the clusters reading that layer (Dry run).

items.title: Hosted control planes
items.text:
A hosted control plane's ClusterVersion is owned by HyperShift, so the upgrade element's Policies report Compliant there and change nothing. For a hypershift-built cluster the hub's present-lifecycle-<cluster> Policy moves HostedCluster spec.release when version changes, then each NodePool once the control plane completes. Unlike the standalone path:

  • With channel set it waits until version is in the HostedCluster's status.version.availableUpdates. Without channel it moves at once, with no availability check.
  • It never applies a version below the control plane's desired version.
  • There is no pause switch: leave version where it is.

Watching, held downgrades and forcing a blocked minor upgrade are in Building clusters.

Why not ClusterCurator or TALM?

ClusterCurator is ACM's resource for running an upgrade, with hooks, on a managed cluster as a one-shot Job. A failure is not retried, and a Policy owning the ClusterCurator cannot tell a finished upgrade from a new one. TALM (Topology Aware Lifecycle Manager) batches policy remediation across clusters with a ClusterGroupUpgrade, also one-shot, and needs its own inform policies. ClusterVersion is declarative, so a Policy can keep enforcing it.

items.title: Upgrading PolicyStack
items.text: Your repository was created with copier from an upstream release tag (Installation). Upgrading means running copier update to merge a newer release into a branch, the framework first and then each element you want, opening a PR, then rolling the result out like any other change. No bot, script or hosted service is involved. Argo CD never reads upstream.

items.title: How releases are versioned
items.text:
Upstream has one tag line, vX.Y.Z, semver. Each release tag holds the framework and every element. Your repository records which release each part came from, in its own answers file:

Part Recorded in Covers Framework /.copier-answers.yml install/, lifecycle/, policy-library in lib/, tools/, the CI workflows and hooks Element stack/<element>/.copier-answers.yml That element only

Because each part has its own record, you can update them at different times: the framework to v1.3.0 this week, odf next month, acm not at all. One rule orders them: an element is never on a newer release than the framework, so take the framework first. An element on an older release than the framework keeps working within the same major (Versions).

A major breaks something you depend on, and its release notes say what to change. A stable element breaks only in a major; a preview element may break in a minor, with notes. Each element's README.md shows which it is (Element stability). Lifecycle engines and platforms are all preview.

Each part reaches your clusters on its own path:

Part Delivered by Reaches clusters Elements, lifecycle/, policy-library (lib/) Argo CD, from your repository at each fleet file's revision Clusters pinned to the default branch, often the hub: within minutes of the merge. Clusters pinned to a tag or SHA: when you move the pin. Validator and CI GitHub Actions in your repository On the update PR itself ACM and GitOps operators The acm and gitops elements, after handover Like any element, at the hub's revision (ACM and GitOps) Install chart (install/) helm upgrade, run by you on each hub When you run it, for every cluster on that hub at once (Install chart)

items.title: Checking for updates
items.text:
copier check-update compares one answers file's _commit with upstream's tags:

copier check-update .            # the framework
copier check-update stack/odf    # one element

Current version is 1.0.0, latest version is 1.2.0.

To check the framework and every tracked element at once, loop over them. With --quiet, copier prints nothing and exits 2 when a newer release exists:

for d in . stack/*/; do
  [ -f "$d/.copier-answers.yml" ] || continue  # (1)!
  copier check-update --quiet "$d"; [ $? -ne 2 ] || echo "update available: $d"
done
  1. Elements you wrote or ejected have no answers file and are skipped.

copier asks the Git server in _src_path for its tags, so this works against an internal mirror too (Disconnected clusters). It only reads. Prereleases, such as v1.3.0-rc.1, are ignored unless you pass --prereleases.

Nothing checks for releases on its own. Run the loop when you plan updates, or watch upstream's releases on GitHub.

items.title: Taking an update
items.text:
Use copier at the version mise.toml pins (mise install). Start from an up-to-date default branch:

git switch main && git pull
git switch -c update/v1.2.0
copier update --defaults .                                 # (1)!
git add -A && git commit -m "chore(deps): update framework to v1.2.0"
fw=$(sed -n 's/^_commit: //p' .copier-answers.yml)
copier update --defaults --vcs-ref "$fw" stack/odf          # (2)!
git add -A && git commit -m "chore(deps): update odf to $fw"
  1. The framework, to the newest release. Add --vcs-ref vX.Y.Z for another one.
  2. An element, to the framework's release. Without --vcs-ref copier takes the newest release, which is newer than your framework unless you just updated it to the newest.

Review each diff, resolve any conflict markers (Resolving conflicts), then push the branch and open a PR. ci and Render Diff run on it like on any PR, and pr-title needs a Conventional Commit title such as the ones above.

copier update merges upstream's changes between your _commit and the new release with your edits, and moves _commit. One update covers any number of releases. It leaves the result uncommitted.

  • copier refuses to update a path that has uncommitted changes in it. For the framework that path is the whole repository, so commit each update before the next.
  • Give the framework its own PR when you can: it has steps before the merge (Framework updates). Elements can share a PR, but one PR per element keeps each Render Diff to that element and lets you merge or drop each on its own.
  • copier prints Make sure Git >= 2.24 is installed to improve updates. on every update, whatever your Git version. Ignore it.

OSError: [Errno 39] Directory not empty: '/tmp/copier._main.new_copy...'

A framework update sometimes ends with this traceback and exit code 1. Git's automatic housekeeping is still writing to copier's temporary clone when copier deletes it. The update itself has been applied: git status shows the changes and _commit names the new release. Review it as usual, and delete the leftover directory. To avoid it, turn housekeeping off for the command:

GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=2 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=gc.auto GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=0 \
  GIT_CONFIG_KEY_1=maintenance.auto GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1=false copier update --defaults .

Always pass --vcs-ref for an element

Unless your framework is on the newest release, copier update without --vcs-ref takes the element past it. POLICY061 fails the PR, because an element newer than the framework may need framework code you don't have yet. Update the framework first, or take the element back with --vcs-ref and the framework's tag.

items.title: Framework updates
items.text:
copier update . applies upstream's changes between your _commit and the new release to every framework file, and moves _commit. It never touches stack/, fleet/ or values/. A file upstream deleted is deleted in your repository too.

A framework file you deleted stays deleted

copier doesn't recreate it, and drops upstream's later changes to it without a conflict or a message. Delete a framework file only if you never want it back.

Open the PR as in Taking an update, then:

  1. Read the release notes of every release between your _commit and the new tag (releases). A note about hubs, the install chart or lifecycle applies to step 4.
  2. Fix what CI reports. The PR runs the new validator against your fleet and values. A new error, such as POLICY035 for a key an element dropped, is fixed in the same PR. Warnings such as POLICY039 (a deprecated key) can wait until the version they name. A conflict means you edited a framework file (Resolving conflicts).
  3. Read the Render Diff.
  4. Upgrade the install chart on every hub from the PR branch (Install chart).
  5. Merge.
  6. Move tag-pinned clusters to a revision that has the update (Roll it out).

Hubs before pins

Within a major, a hub is only guaranteed to render revisions up to its own install chart's release. Upgrade every hub before you move any pin to a revision with a newer framework. A pin moved first can fail its render on a hub still on the older install chart (Hub and revision skew). Clusters that follow the default branch move the moment you merge, which is why step 4 comes before step 5.

items.title: Majors
items.text:
Take majors one at a time. A hub on major N is only guaranteed to render revisions on N and on the last N-1 release (Hub and revision skew):

  1. Take the last release of your current major, for the framework and every element, and move every fleet pin to a revision that has it.
  2. Take the next major for the framework and every element in one PR: upgrade every hub from the update's PR branch, then merge it. POLICY061 fails the PR while any element is still on the older major.
  3. Move pins to the new major, cluster by cluster.

POLICY052 checks only the major: on the update PR, a fleet file whose revision is more than one major behind, or on a newer major than the branch, fails. It can't tell whether an N-1 revision is the last N-1 release, so step 1 is yours to check. copier update without --vcs-ref takes the newest release, whatever its major. For step 1, or when the newest release is two majors ahead, name the tag from the releases page: copier update --defaults --vcs-ref v1.9.2 ..

items.title: Element updates
items.text:
copier update stack/odf merges upstream's changes to odf since your _commit with yours and moves _commit. Nothing outside stack/odf/ changes.

  • Read the element's entries in the release notes, prefixed with its name (odf:), and the Render Diff. For a preview element any minor may rename keys or Policies; search those entries for breaking:.
  • If the element needs a newer policy-library than your framework has, its render fails and POLICY060 says so. Taking the element at the framework's release, as above, avoids it.
  • A file upstream deleted is deleted from stack/odf/ too, even if you edited it, without a conflict. Check the PR diff for deleted files and move any edit you need into a values layer.
  • An element upstream removed (POLICY092 warned while it was deprecated) can't be updated: copier update fails with a FileNotFoundError naming stack/<element> in copier's temporary clone. Eject it to keep it as yours, or remove it.
  • Elements update independently, so merge their PRs in any order.

items.title: Skip, freeze, eject, roll back
items.text: To Do Skip a release Don't take it, or take a later one with --vcs-ref. copier check-update keeps reporting the newest release until you take it. Freeze an element Don't run copier update on it. It keeps working on newer framework releases of the same major. A framework major ends the freeze: POLICY061 fails until the element is on the new major. Eject an element git rm stack/odf/.copier-answers.yml. copier and the check loop stop tracking it, the validator stops checking its answers file, and the element is yours (Tiers). copier update stack/odf then fails with a Python traceback ending in TypeError: Template not found. To track it again, delete the directory and copy it again (Add elements). Remove an element git rm -r stack/odf. Its Applications and Policies are deleted (Removing an element). Roll back git revert the update's merge commit. The answers file reverts with it, so copier check-update reports the update again. Clusters pinned to a tag never had it.

items.title: Answers files
items.text:
.copier-answers.yml at the root and in each tracked element is copier's record of what it copied: _commit is the release tag, _src_path the upstream URL, and element the element, empty for the framework. copier rebuilds the old release from _commit to work out what you changed, copier check-update reads both to find newer releases, POLICY052 reads the root file at each fleet revision to check skew, and POLICY061 checks every one.

Never edit an answers file by hand

A _commit that doesn't match the files makes the next update merge against the wrong base: your changes are reported as conflicts, or upstream changes are skipped. Change it only with copier update, or git revert an update. POLICY061 fails a _commit that isn't a release tag, an element answers file whose element isn't its directory, and an element newer than the framework.

items.title: Resolving conflicts
items.text:
copier merges three versions of each file: the old release, the new release and yours. Where you and upstream changed the same lines, it leaves both in the file, between conflict markers:

A conflict in stack/odf/values.yaml

<<<<<<< before updating
      storageClassName: fast-ssd
=======
      storageClassName: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd
>>>>>>> after updating

before updating is your repository, after updating is the new release. The ci check fails while a marker is left (the check-merge-conflict hook), so a conflicted PR can't merge. Resolve them before you commit:

  1. git diff --check lists every file and line with a marker.
  2. Edit each file to what you want, deleting the markers. In a framework file, take after updating: a framework you modified is not supported, and the conflict comes back on every update.
  3. Run git diff --check again until it prints nothing, then commit. Don't touch the answers file.

A conflict in an element you edited means the edit and upstream's change overlap. If they keep overlapping, move the setting to a values layer, where updates never reach it, or eject the element.

Change settings in layers, not in elements

Every setting an element exposes can be set from values/. Editing an element's values.yaml or converters instead makes it yours to merge on every update.

items.title: Reading Render Diff
items.text:
On an update PR, Render Diff shows what the merge changes for every cluster pinned to the default branch. A framework update shows changes from lib/ and lifecycle/ across elements; an element update, that element only. Tag-pinned clusters show theirs on the PR that moves their pin.

  • removes Policy names a Policy the update deletes. A rename shows as a removal plus an addition: the Policy is recreated and its compliance history starts over (Policy names).
  • render failed means the update breaks that cluster. The error is in the cluster's block. Fix it in the PR.
  • install/ is not rendered. Read its diff in the PR (Install chart).

items.title: Roll it out
items.text:
Clusters pinned to the default branch already run the update. For the rest, tag the merge commit in your repository and move pins cluster by cluster (Promoting and rolling back):

git switch main && git pull
git tag v1.5.0 && git push origin v1.5.0

These are your repository's tags, unrelated to upstream's. POLICY052 reads the framework release from each pinned commit's answers file, not from the tag name.

items.title: ACM and GitOps
items.text:
Before handover, install/operators created the Subscriptions with automatic approval on the channel stack/acm/values.yaml and stack/gitops/values.yaml named at the time. OLM upgrades within that channel; a new channel from an element update does not reach the hub. Hand the operators over, or rerun Install the operators with the new values.

After handover, the channel is subscription.channel of the element's operatorPolicies entry. An element update that changes it, or your own layer, moves the hub's Subscription to that channel once the hub's fleet revision includes it. Nothing steps through minors for you, and ACM upgrades only from the previous minor. To go from release-2.15 to release-2.17, set release-2.16 in the hub's layer, wait until oc get csv -n open-cluster-management shows the 2.16 CSV Succeeded, then set release-2.17 or take the acm update. Pin or hold versions as in Operator versions.

items.title: Install chart
items.text:
install/ holds the two ApplicationSets and their supporting objects (Install chart). No Argo CD Application reads it, so merging a framework update changes nothing on a hub until someone runs helm upgrade there. From then on, the new ApplicationSets generate the Applications of every cluster on that hub, whatever revision each pins. Render Diff does not render install/, so read its diff on the update PR.

The release's chart version is the framework release it was installed from. Compare it with the framework update's PR branch, or with the default branch once the update is merged:

git fetch origin && git switch --detach origin/<branch>   # the PR branch, or main
helm list -n openshift-gitops   # CHART: policystack-1.2.0
grep '^version' install/Chart.yaml

If they differ, upgrade, in the hub's kube context:

helm upgrade policystack ./install -n openshift-gitops --reset-then-reuse-values

--reset-then-reuse-values (Helm 3.14 or later) takes the new chart's defaults and keeps every value set at install or a later upgrade, normally just hubName and gitRepo.

Within a major the ApplicationSets only add injected values, so clusters pinned to older revisions keep rendering. The exception is a fleet file's install, passed through as written: a key newer than the cluster's revision fails that revision's lifecycle schema (Lifecycle). A policy-library major is checked at render: the chart passes policystack.libraryMajors, and a revision built on a library major the hub's chart doesn't list fails its render with a ComparisonError that says to move the pin or upgrade the hub.

Roll back with helm rollback policystack <revision> -n openshift-gitops.

items.title: CI workflows
items.text:
PolicyStack's GitHub Actions workflows live in .github/workflows/. Four of them check a fleet repository and run unchanged in yours: copier copies them with the framework, and framework updates change them, so don't edit them (Tiers). Upstream (upstream.yml) checks PolicyStack itself and runs only in upstream PolicyStack. For an adopter, the checks that cover real clusters are the fleet/ pass of Policy Validate and Render Diff; the rest guard the framework.

Workflow Trigger Fails when In your repository CI (ci.yml) Every PR and main push A hook or the validator fails Runs PR Title (pr-title.yml) Every PR, including title edits The title is not a Conventional Commit Runs Policy Validate (validate.yml) Called by CI A validator error, a bad fleet pin, a broken install chart Runs, including the fleet/ pass Render Diff (render-diff.yml) PRs into the default branch changing stack/, lifecycle/, lib/, values/, values.yaml, fleet/, tools/validator/ or Render Diff itself Never: it only comments Comments only when fleet/ has files, so only in yours Upstream (upstream.yml) Every PR and main push The policy-library lint or tests, a validator lint or test, a stale CRD, the doc generator tests or the site build fails Absent: copier leaves it out

A new push to a PR cancels its running CI, Upstream and Render Diff checks. CI, Upstream and Policy Validate can also be started from the Actions tab.

items.title: Required checks
items.text:
A required check is one GitHub won't let a PR merge without. ci and pr-title are the required checks for main, set in a GitHub repository ruleset. Rulesets live in the repository settings, not in the files copier copies, so your repository has none until you add one: without it, a red PR still merges. Create a branch ruleset on the default branch that requires the status checks ci and pr-title (Protect the repository has the steps, plus code owner review on fleet/). The ruleset matches checks by job name, so renaming ci or pr-title leaves PRs waiting on a check that never reports.

ci is the last job in ci.yml. It always runs and fails if any job it needs failed, was cancelled or was skipped (alls-green). A new job goes in its needs, not in the ruleset.

Upstream PolicyStack's ruleset requires a third check, upstream, the same kind of last job in upstream.yml. A job in one workflow can't wait on a job in another, and ci.yml can't call upstream.yml because that file is missing from your repository, so upstream PRs are gated by the two checks together.

Note

No gating workflow has a paths filter. A required check whose workflow is skipped by on.paths never reports, so the PR waits on it forever.

items.title: CI (ci.yml)
items.text:
Job Runs lint prek run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure: the hooks in .pre-commit-config.yaml. It installs only the hooks' tools from mise.toml validate Policy Validate ci The required check over lint and validate

Tool versions come from mise.toml. Run the same checks locally: Setup.

items.title: Hooks
items.text:
prek is a pre-commit-compatible hook runner, installed by mise install. It reads .pre-commit-config.yaml; you don't need pre-commit itself.

Hook Checks check-yaml, trailing-whitespace, end-of-file-fixer, check-merge-conflict, check-added-large-files prek builtins. check-merge-conflict runs with --assume-in-merge, so it also fails the conflict markers a copier update commits actionlint (workflow syntax), zizmor (workflow security audit) Workflows. zizmor runs offline shellcheck Shell scripts ruff-check, ruff-format tools/*.py element-readmes Regenerates stack/*/README.md, except for elements with a .copier-answers.yml: their README is upstream's (Element reference) lychee Link checker: relative links in docs/, offline

check-yaml, trailing-whitespace, end-of-file-fixer and check-added-large-files skip templates/, converters/ and __snapshot__/, which are YAML only once rendered. check-merge-conflict checks them too. Every hook skips tools/validator/crds/, which holds upstream's files as fetched.

A hook that rewrites a file (trailing-whitespace, end-of-file-fixer, ruff-format, element-readmes) fails. Commit what it wrote:

prek run --all-files   # rewrites what it can
git add -u             # stage the rewritten files; add a new element's README by path

Tip

prek install runs the hooks on every commit.

items.title: Upstream
items.text:
upstream.yml checks PolicyStack itself (the library, the validator code and the docs site), then publishes the site and cuts releases. It runs on every PR and main push in upstream PolicyStack. copier leaves it out of an adopter's copy, so none of this runs there.

Job Runs library policy-library in lib/: ct lint --config lib/ct.yaml, which fails a change to lib/policy-library without a version bump and runs helm lint --strict; then the helm-unittest suites in lib/tests (untt --strict), failing on a snapshot that is not committed (Library changes) validator make -C tools/validator lint (golangci-lint, go mod tidy -diff, govulncheck) and test; then make crds, failing when tools/validator/crds/ differs from the files the Makefile pins (CRD schemas) docs Doc generator tests (python -m unittest tools/test_doc_generator.py), then zensical build --strict upstream The required check over library, validator and docs publish main pushes in PolicyStack/PolicyStack only, after upstream: the site to gh-pages release main pushes in PolicyStack/PolicyStack only, after upstream: release-please opens or updates the release PR and, once it merges, tags it vX.Y.Z (Releases)

items.title: Documentation site
items.text:
The docs job builds docs/ with zensical build --strict, which fails on a relative .md link or anchor that doesn't resolve, or a missing snippet file. On main, publish pushes site/ to the gh-pages branch as a single commit, using a GitHub App. The site is unversioned: for an older revision, read docs/ at that revision on GitHub.

Not checked by strict mode

Absolute links, nav and the content of included snippets (Docs layout).

items.title: PR Title
items.text:
Squash merges make the PR title the commit subject and the release-note line, so it must match:

<type>(<scope>)!: <subject>

type is one of feat fix docs chore ci refactor test perf build revert. (<scope>) (lowercase, digits, -) and ! (breaking) are optional.

feat(validator): real POLICY080       # ok
fix!: rename hubName                  # ok
feat(odf): breaking: rename config.pools  # ok: preview break, a minor
Revert "feat: add metallb"            # fails: retitle to revert: feat: add metallb

Editing the title re-runs the check. Upstream, release-please reads the squash commits to pick each release's version and write its notes (Releases). In your repository the titles only keep history readable; if you don't want the check, drop pr-title from your ruleset.

items.title: Policy Validate
items.text:
Runs the validator. Findings are annotated on the PR at the file and line to fix. Errors fail the job, warnings only annotate.
